all.title: P1/P6 need context, scopes and t as read inputs, but the locked query(embedding, limit) has no way to receive them
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:434 (P1), :439 (P6), :463 (X3), :134 (deposit carries scope), :247-253 (QueryRecord); G2-1 at :228
all.claim: P1 says a read depends only on (prefix, embedding, limit, context, scopes, t). P6 says time is an argument and no read reads a clock. X3 keeps the four agent signatures unchanged, and the locked read is query(embedding, limit). So context, scopes and t can reach the read only through state that is neither an argument nor a G1 node: handle or config state for context and scopes, and the substrate's own clock for t. The paper never names a binding mechanism (grep for handle/init/bound/URI/session finds none). Counterexample: the host logs QueryRecord{context=A, scopes={s1}} while the substrate instance was configured for context B, or with no scope filter at all, which is v1's only behaviour. Replaying the logged inputs gives Resolved(A, n), not what was served, so the logged returned ids disagree with the replay. Nothing in G1 or the echo can detect the mismatch, because the echo's context is whatever ambient value the substrate used. The same gap applies to the scope on the G1 deposit node: deposit(payload, embedding, protected_floor) carries no scope, so the deposit scope also comes from unjournaled ambient state. Under X3, P6 cannot be met: t must come from the substrate's clock at call time, as v1 does at api.py:399, and P6 forbids exactly that.
all.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:34-39 locks `query(embedding: List[float], limit: int = 5)` and `deposit(payload, embedding, protected_floor)`; src/moneta/api.py:328-333, :379-380 (no context/scope/t params), :399 `now = time.time()`; v1 has no scope concept at all (grep of api.py finds none). BLUEPRINT_v6.md:95 says the inputs belong to v5's `recall`, which takes five inputs including context and scopes, not v1's query. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:463 X3 keeps the signatures unchanged; :134 deposit carries scope; :248 echo includes context.
all.proposed_fix: State which surface 'a read' is. Option 1: v5's recall(embedding, limit, context, scopes, t) is a harness op and agents keep query(). In that case P1 applies only to recall, and the paper must say what context, scopes and t an agent query() uses. Option 2: context and scope are bound at handle construction and journaled as a typed event (e.g. `bind{context, scopes}`) that each read's echo cites by seq, so G1 captures them. Reword P6 to 'the substrate reads the clock once per read, echoes t, and never reads it again; seams take t as an argument'. If neither option fits within X3, adding arguments to query/deposit is a signature change and goes to the MONETA.md §9 Round 4 brief alongside E1–E4.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds; I could not refute it. P1 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:434) and P6 (:439) make context, scopes and t inputs to a read. X3 (:463, and :86 "its signatures don't change") keeps the four agent signatures. Those signatures are locked at ARCHITECTURE.md:36-37 as deposit(payload, embedding, protected_floor) and query(embedding, limit=5), and api.py:379-380 matches. G1's deposit node carries a scope (:134), and QueryRecord holds context and caller scopes (:248-249). The paper never says which surface takes these inputs or how they reach query()/deposit(). Grep finds no handle-bind, session or per-call context mechanism. G2's `Context` at :202 is a policy binding, not a call binding. P1's source, BLUEPRINT_v6.md:95, credits the five inputs to v5's `recall`, not v1's `query`.

The paper half-acknowledges the problem in four places, but none of them closes it:
- P1 is tagged "false in v1 [V, api.py:399-401]" (:434).
- P6 and Q3 (:584) note that v1 reads time.time() at api.py:399.
- Attack 1 (:686) lists "the clock source" as an open question.

These flag that v1 differs. They do not say how v7 meets P1/P6 under X3. Context and scope binding is never raised at all. So the counterexample stands: a logged QueryRecord{context=A} served under ambient context B replays wrong, and G1 cannot detect it. As written, P6 ("no read reads a clock") conflicts with X3 for an agent-facing query(), because t has to come from somewhere other than an argument.

On severity, "critical" is arguable. This is a design paper that already flags v1 gaps, so "major" may fit better. Even so, P1/P2/V-REPLAY rest on it, so it is not cosmetic.
verdicts.better_fix:
The fix is right in direction, but its last branch overstates the cost. Option 2 already fits within X3, with no §9 needed for binding. ARCHITECTURE.md:43-47 (§2.1, Ruling B) makes init() and MonetaConfig harness-level, outside the four-op surface, and X3 (:463) cites that same precedent. Concrete edits:

(1) Add a harness-level bind at init/handle construction, journaled as a typed G1 event: bind{context fingerprint, scopes, deposit scope}. Signing rule: unsigned, or signed if scopes widen authorization (relates to C4/G2-5). Every later deposit node and every QueryRecord echo cites the bind's seq with a typed backward edge (principle 6). A rebind is a new event, never an in-place change.

(2) Reword P6: "Seams and Resolved() take t as an argument. The agent-facing read samples the clock exactly once, at entry, echoes t, and uses only that t. Replay uses the echoed t." Do the same for deposit's timestamp (api.py:375 `now`).

(3) Reword P1: "A read is a pure function of (prefix, embedding, limit, bind@seq, t)." Add a V-check with a sabotage: serving under an unjournaled ambient context must fail replay.

(4) Send it to §9 only if per-call context or scopes are required, i.e. one handle serving many contexts. That would change a signature, so it goes into the Round 4 brief next to E1–E4. Also add it to O-list/attack 1, so the owner sees that per-call scoping is lost under X3.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute the finding. Every cited fact checks out.

- **The paper's claims:** P1 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:434) lists (prefix, embedding, limit, context, scopes, t) as the read inputs. P6 (:439) says time is an argument and no read reads a clock. X3 (:463, and :80) keeps all four agent signatures unchanged. The G1 `deposit` node carries a scope (:134). The QueryRecord echo carries context and the caller's scopes (:247-253).
- **The locked API:** ARCHITECTURE.md:34-39 locks `query(embedding, limit=5)` and `deposit(payload, embedding, protected_floor)`. v1 matches at src/moneta/api.py:328-333 and :379-380. Neither takes a context, scope or t argument, `now = time.time()` is read at :399, and a grep of api.py for scope or context finds no such concept (the hits are the context-manager protocol).
- **Where the five inputs come from:** BLUEPRINT_v6.md:95 attributes them to v5's `recall`, not to v1's `query`.
- **No binding mechanism:** nowhere does the paper say how context and scopes reach an agent `query()` or `deposit()`. Its mentions of handle, binding and session concern other things: the G2 `Context` node definition (:202), signature binding (:160-162), the tuner holding no handle (:190), and the seam rule (:103).
- **Partial acknowledgment only:** §10 attack 1 (:686) asks about "the clock source" as an open question. That flags the clock half of the problem but resolves nothing, and says nothing about context or scope. No O-item closes it either.

So the paper does not already handle the gap. The counterexample stands: the logged QueryRecord context can differ from the ambient context the substrate actually used, and nothing in G1 detects it. The P6-versus-X3 conflict is real as written.
verdicts.better_fix:
The fix is directionally right, with one correction: severity should be high rather than critical, because Option 2 fits inside X3 with no signature change. I would make Option 2 the default and spell it out.

1. **Binding.** Context and the scope set are bound when the harness constructs the handle. That fits Ruling B precedent: `init`/`MonetaConfig` are harness-level (ARCHITECTURE.md:46-50), and v1's handle is already URI-locked (api.py:1).
2. **Journaling.** Construction appends a typed G1 `bind{context fingerprint, scopes}` event. Every `deposit` node and every QueryRecord echo cites that event's seq with an **at** edge. This also covers the deposit-scope half of the finding.
3. **Rebinding.** A rebind is a new handle and a new `bind` event, never a mutation of the existing one.
4. **Rewording P6.** Change it to: "the agent read path reads the clock exactly once per call and echoes t; Resolved, the folds and every seam take t as an argument". Add the clock source to the open item from attack 1.
5. **New check.** Add a V-BIND check with this sabotage: serve under context B while the echo claims A, or apply no scope filter while the `bind` event lists scopes. It passes only if replaying from the logged QueryRecord plus the cited `bind` reproduces the returned ids.
6. **Clarifying P1.** State that P1's inputs for an agent `query()` are (prefix, embedding, limit, bind seq, echoed t). The five-argument v5 `recall` form survives only as an internal or harness function.

If the owner wants context switched per call rather than per handle, that is a signature change. It belongs in the Round 4 brief alongside E1-E4, as the finding proposes.

all.title: R4a exclusion applied at build time makes the eval set and fold for prefix n depend on events after n
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:296 (G3-5), :298 (G3-7), :282 (recall-fold excluded set), :329-331 (G4-5), :517 (V-POOL), :671 (O6 default), :558 (fold_recall signature)
all.claim: G3-5 says the eval set rebuilds byte-identically from `Prefix + QueryRecords + Labels`, and V-POOL says the referee's top k equals the read path's. O6's default keeps rolled-back attention in the recall fold, so live reads include it. G3-7/V-LEAK, by contrast, removes generation g's attention from every eval set built after g's rollback. Counterexample: g is Promoted from seq 100 to 200, and attention events at seqs 120-180 are stamped g. A QueryRecord at n=150 was served with g's attention in the recall anchors, which can lift record r2 above r1. After the rollback at 200, the eval builder drops g's attention for that same query. The referee's pool and top k for query n=150 then differ from the served returned ids, so V-POOL fails on exactly the queries from g's window. The eval-set leaf is also a function of the head's excluded-generation set, which no `Prefix(n,h)` input captures. The excluded set is an input to fold_recall (:558) with no rule that bounds it to the prefix, and :282 skips the excluded set without saying 'as of n'. If the owner later rules O6 'yes', live reads at n would also depend on rollbacks after n, and G2-1/P1 purity breaks outright. This is a consequence of the R4a ruling, not a reopening of it.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:296 G3-5 inputs; :298 G3-7; :671 O6 default 'retention only, as ruled; eval sets also exclude it (V-LEAK)'; :517 V-POOL exact top-k equality; :558 `fold_recall(..., excluded_gens)`; :282 'Attention whose produced_under generation is in the excluded set is skipped'; RULINGS.md R4(a) (retention fold only).
all.proposed_fix: Add the excluded-generation set, i.e. the seq of the latest rollback the builder honoured, as an explicit built_from input of the eval-set leaf and of every fold checkpoint, and rewrite G3-5 as 'from Prefix(head) + QueryRecords + Labels'. State that a read at (n, t) uses the excluded set as of n, which is empty for rollbacks after n. Exempt V-POOL for queries served while an excluded generation was live, or compare those queries against a replay that includes g. Ask the owner to rule on O6 with this consequence in view: if the recall fold excludes as-of-head, P1 must gain 'excluded set at evaluation time' as an input.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds up, though one part is overstated.

What holds:
1. The paper requires the eval set to exclude g's attention after a rollback (G3-7 at :298, V-LEAK at :499, O6 default at :671).
2. Under the O6 default, the read path's recall fold keeps g's attention. Only the retention fold drops it (R4a, RULINGS.md:20; G4-5 at :329-331).
3. The recall-fold oracle at :282 and `fold_recall(..., excluded_gens)` at :558 take an excluded set. Nothing says whose set it is (read path or eval builder) or as of which seq.
4. V-POOL at :517 requires the referee's top k to equal the read path's, and the paper does not say which excluded set either side uses. For any query served inside g's window, the referee scores a pool without g's attention while the read path includes it. That breaks top-k equality. The paper does not address this anywhere: no exemption, and nothing about which excluded set the read path uses.
5. G3-5 at :296 says the eval set rebuilds from `Prefix + QueryRecords + Labels` without saying which Prefix. Each QueryRecord's **at** edge points to Prefix(n) (:247). A builder that honours a rollback at seq 200 for a query at n=150 therefore reads past that query's own prefix, and G3-5 does not say so.
6. The conditional is right. If the owner rules O6 'yes' and exclusion applies as of head, replaying a read at n would depend on events after n. That breaks G2-1 at :228 and P1 at :434.

What is overstated:
1. The claim that "no Prefix input captures the excluded set" is too strong. Rollback is a journaled, signed `govern` event (G4-2), so a leaf built from Prefix(head) already determines the excluded set. The real defect is that G3-5 and the leaf's `built_from` do not name that head prefix.
2. The failure is latent on real stores until mile 4. G4-6 keeps every real-store generation in Proposed, so no real rollback happens before then. V-POOL becomes a gate at mile 3 (:517, :654), so the conflict appears once rollbacks exist: on test stores at mile 4, and on real stores after that. It is still a contradiction in the spec as written.

Major severity is defensible but at the high end; it could fairly be rated moderate. The finding does not reopen R4a.
verdicts.better_fix:
The proposed fix is mostly right. I would change three things:

1. **Name the head prefix, not a separate rollback seq.** Rewrite G3-5 as "from Prefix(h_build) + QueryRecords + Labels". Name Prefix(h_build) in the `built_from` of the eval-set leaf and of every fold checkpoint. The excluded set is computed from the `govern` rollback events at or before h_build, so a separate "latest-rollback seq" input adds nothing.

2. **Fix V-POOL by giving both sides the same excluded set, not by exempting queries.** Make `excluded_gens` an explicit parameter of the read path, the same way `fold_recall` takes it at :558. Then state V-POOL as: the referee's top k equals the read path's when both run with the same excluded set. An exemption would leave every query in g's window untested, and that window is exactly where the misattribution in attack 3 happens. Add a fixture with a query inside a rolled-back window, and a sabotage case where the referee and the read path use different excluded sets.

3. **State the read path's excluded set for each O6 outcome.**
   - O6 'no' (current default): the live read path always uses an empty excluded set.
   - O6 'yes': a read at (n, t) uses the excluded set as of n. This keeps G2-1 and P1 unchanged. The alternative, excluding as of head, would require adding the evaluation-time excluded set as a P1 input.

   Attach this consequence to O6 at :671 for the owner, and note at :282 that the oracle's excluded set is supplied by the caller.

verdicts.reason:
The central tension is real, and nothing in the paper resolves it.

1. **Exclusion moves the eval set off the served path.** G3-7 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:298) and V-LEAK (:499) strip g's attention from every eval set built after the rollback. O6's default (:671) keeps that attention in the recall fold, so the reads actually served at n inside g's window used anchors that included it. The referee is fed raw attention runs carrying a gen tag and calls the fold oracle (:556). For those queries, its pool and anchors therefore differ from what the read path computes at the same n.

2. **The tests assume they match.** V-POOL (:517) requires exact top-k equality between referee and read path. V-EXCL (:524) says a fold with g excluded equals a fold of a journal that never held g's attention. Together they make exclusion a different journal history from the one actually served. No section reconciles this: G3-2 (:293) and the misattribution note (:343) cover the stamp window, not eval/serve divergence.

3. **The excluded set has no "as of".** G3-5 (:296) names an unparameterized "Prefix". The recall-fold rule (:282) and `fold_recall(..., excluded_gens)` (:558) never say whose excluded set applies. The paper only half-handles this: if "Prefix" means the head prefix, the build-time dependence is captured, but nothing says so.

**Overstatements in the finding:**
- **P1 does not "break outright".** P1/G2-1 (:434) defines a live read at n over the journal prefix at n, which cannot contain a rollback after n. What would break under an O6 "yes" with an as-of-head excluded set is replay or rebuild determinism (P2/G3-5), not live-read purity.
- **The failure is not reachable at mile 3, where V-POOL first gates (:654).** Under G4-6 (:303) nothing on a real store leaves Proposed through mile 4, so no rollback happens there. The failure first becomes reachable on test stores at mile 4, and on real stores at mile 5 (:657).
- **"Major" is fair.** It is a latent contradiction between two of the paper's own checks (V-LEAK/G3-7 vs V-POOL). It is a consequence of R4a plus the O6 default, not a reopening of a ruled item.
verdicts.better_fix:
The fix is mostly right; four changes would make it correct.

1. **Make the excluded set an explicit input.** Each eval-set leaf and fold checkpoint records in its built_from the seq of the latest rollback it honoured, which is the head prefix it was built from. Rewrite G3-5 as "from Prefix(head_at_build) + QueryRecords + Labels".

2. **Recast the P1 point.** Live reads are already as-of-n. Add to P1/G2-1 that a read at n uses the excluded set as of n, which is empty for any rollback after n. State that replay and rebuild of a read at n uses that same as-of-n set. Then an O6 "yes" does not break P1; it only fixes which set replay uses.

3. **Narrow V-POOL instead of exempting queries.** Define V-POOL's read path as the read recomputed at Prefix(n) under the eval set's own excluded set. Equality then holds by construction. Add a separate disclosed count of queries whose served ids differ from the eval-set pool because of exclusion. Exempting the g-window queries outright would hide exactly the queries attack 3 is about.

4. **Owner note.** Ask the owner to rule on O6 knowing that the default (retention-only plus eval exclusion) means the referee scores the g-window queries against a history that was never served.

all.title: Vector bytes and embedder identity have no home in G1; G3-4 and replay after erase or revector are unsatisfiable as drawn
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:134 (deposit carries only a vector digest), :138 (revector 'as in v5 [A]'), :262 (vector index is a derived leaf), :295 (G3-4), :376 (store layout), :493 (V-LEAF), :496 (V-REBUILD), :250 (QueryRecord embedding without an embedder pin)
all.claim: The deposit event commits only a vector digest. The store layout has journal/, payloads/ (record payloads), blobs/ and derived/, and no place for vector bytes. The vector index is a derived leaf. So G3-4 and V-LEAF ('deleting every derived file changes no answer once leaves are rebuilt') fail: delete derived/ and the index can't be rebuilt from the journal, which holds only digests. If vectors are payloads instead, an erase at seq m deletes them. Every QueryRecord at n < m whose pool contained the erased record then can't have its cos f64 pool row recomputed, so G3-5/V-REBUILD fail for any train or held-out window that predates the erase. The read at n stays a function of the prefix, but it is no longer computable from what the store keeps. revector has no defined content or edges. If it overwrites vectors in place without keeping the old digest and bytes, a replay at n < revector compares the old-model query embedding with new-model record vectors, and the cosines differ from what was served. Neither the QueryRecord nor the G1 deposit/revector nodes name the embedder, so nothing can tell when a query embedding and record vectors come from different models. In v1 the caller supplies the embedding (api.py:330), so Moneta can't infer the embedder.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:134, :138, :262, :295, :376 ('payloads/<sha256> record payloads ... Erase deletes a file'), :493, :496, :250; attack item 5 (:690) leaves 'Is a vector a payload?' open. src/moneta/api.py:328-333 (embedding supplied by the caller), :372-374 (vector_index.upsert holds the vector bytes; that index is authoritative in v1 per ARCHITECTURE.md:146). BLUEPRINT_v6.md:544 defines revector as 'replace vectors after an embedder swap'.
all.proposed_fix: Answer attack 5 in the schema. Vector bytes get their own non-derived content-addressed store (e.g. `vectors/<sha256>`), committed by the deposit's vector digest. Say whether erase deletes the vector too. If it does, declare that queries whose pools contain an erased record leave the rebuildable eval set, and pinned eval-set blobs remain the record of them. If it doesn't, state that the embedding survives erase, which is a privacy consequence the owner must accept. Make revector a typed event carrying an **about** edge and the new vector digest, keeping the old bytes for replay at earlier prefixes. Add an embedder id to genesis or `govern{const}` content and to each revector, and add it to the QueryRecord echo, so mixed-embedder pools can be detected.

verdicts.reason: The finding holds. The paper raises the problem but never answers it. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:134 gives `deposit` only a "vector digest". The only **commits** edge is deposit → payloads/<sha> (:179). G1-6 (:191) checks payload digests but has no matching rule for vectors. The store layout (:375-382) has no place for vector bytes, and the vector index is listed as a derived leaf (:262, :378). So under G3-4 (:295) and V-LEAF (:493), deleting derived/ leaves no non-derived source to rebuild the index from. The paper never says "vectors are payloads". It leaves that open at attack 5 (:690, "Is a vector a payload?") and attack 1 (:686, "The embedder version ... payload availability after an erase?"). Those are open questions to reviewers, not schema. Either branch fails. If vectors are payloads, erase deletes the file (:376), and G3-5 (:296) can no longer rebuild the eval set byte-identically from Prefix + QueryRecords + Labels, because it needs the cosine against the erased record's vector. If they aren't payloads, the store has nowhere to keep them. Two more gaps hold: `revector` is only "as in v5 [A]" (:138), with an **about** edge (:173) but no content, and the QueryRecord (:247-253) carries no embedder identity. In v1 the caller supplies the embedding (src/moneta/api.py:328-333) and only vector_index holds the bytes (:372-374; ARCHITECTURE.md:146), so the substrate can't infer the embedder. RULINGS.md and pass1_rulings_brief.md rule nothing on vectors, erase or revector. The only related line is brief :88, where the host logs the full query embedding, which covers the query side and not the record vectors.
verdicts.better_fix: The fix is right in direction and needs four changes. (1) The embedder id has to be **host-declared**, not substrate-derived, because the substrate can't infer it (api.py:328-333). Carry it as a declared field on each `deposit` and in the QueryRecord echo. A `const` pin in genesis or `govern{const}` is a check that a declared id matches, not a source of identity. (2) Add a G1-6 analogue, call it G1-6v: a **commits_vector** edge deposit/revector → vectors/<sha>, with canonical() replacing vector bytes by their digest, as Q2 does for payloads (:170). (3) Erase has to delete every vector version of the record, including old bytes kept for revector. Otherwise revector's "keep old bytes for replay" quietly becomes an erase bypass. So the rule should read: revector keeps the old bytes only until an erase of that record, and after that the paper's declared eval-set exclusion applies. (4) State the exclusion as an amendment to G3-5 and V-REBUILD: rebuild is byte-identical for QueryRecords whose pool held no record erased at or before rebuild time, and the pinned eval-set blob in blobs/ stays the record for the rest. Because erase is owner-signed (O9), the owner has to accept this choice. Mark it needs_owner and tie it to O9 and E1 (:301), since keeping vector bytes non-derived is itself part of the E1 authority question.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute the finding. The paper does not handle it, and the factual claims check out against the paper and v1 code.

1. The deposit node carries only a "vector digest" (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:134). The store layout (:374-383) has journal/, payloads/ ("record payloads ... Erase deletes a file", :376), blobs/ (referee, eval and label sets only, :377) and derived/ (:378, which lists the vector index as a leaf). No non-derived location holds vector bytes.
2. G3-4 (:295) and V-LEAF (:493) therefore depend on rebuilding the index from inputs that are never stored. G1-6 (:191) and T6 (:432) cover payload bytes only.
3. revector is left "as in v5 [A]" (:138). It gets an **about** edge (:173) but no defined content. The only definition is v6's "replace vectors after an embedder swap" (BLUEPRINT_v6.md:544), which says nothing about keeping the old vectors.
4. The QueryRecord (:245-251) holds the f64 embedding but no embedder id. Neither genesis nor deposit names one (:133-134).
5. The paper only raises these as open questions in §10: attack 1, "The embedder version ... payload availability after an erase?" (:686), and attack 5, "Is a vector a payload?" (:690). Posing a question in the attack list does not answer it in the schema. The invariants and gates as written stay unsatisfiable.
6. RULINGS.md has no ruling on erase, payloads or embeddings (grep is empty), so the finding does not reopen a ruled item.
7. v1 confirms the caller supplies the embedding (src/moneta/api.py:328-333) and the vector index stores the bytes (:372-374). Moneta cannot infer the embedder.
8. The G3-5/V-REBUILD consequence after an erase also holds. An eval-set row for a query at n < m needs the erased record's vector. If the vector is deleted with the payload, the row can only come from the pinned blob, not from a rebuild.

One limit on scope: E1 (:301, :629) is still unruled. If the owner rules against E1, the index becomes a second authority and the G3-4 half of the finding goes away. The erase, revector and embedder-identity halves survive either way.
verdicts.better_fix:
The proposed fix is sound and correctly flagged needs_owner, because the privacy trade-off on erase is the owner's call. Four refinements:

(a) Name the alternative that keeps v5's "the journal is the database": put the vector inline in the deposit and revector events instead of in a separate vectors/ store. Then attack 5 has to weigh journal size and the 1.0 s open at 10k. The fix as written should state why it picks a separate CAS store.

(b) Fold vector bytes into G1-6/T6 under a separate clause, so V-ERASE asserts whatever the owner chooses. Either the vector is gone and its digest stays, or the vector survives.

(c) Because the host supplies the embedding (api.py:328-333), put the embedder id on the API's deposit and query inputs, or in a govern{const} pin that the host must echo. It cannot come from the substrate alone. If a QueryRecord's embedder id disagrees with the record vectors' current id, that query falls out of the rebuildable eval set, the same treatment as an erase.

(d) Tie this to E1. If E1 is ruled against, restate G3-4 to exclude the index rather than requiring rebuild of it.

all.title: G1 attention and deposit nodes carry no timestamp, yet the fold and referee need t_event and t0
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:134-135 (G1 node table), :282 (fold uses t_event), :556 (EvalBuf attention runs carry t f64), :558 (fold_recall takes t0)
all.claim: The fold is `u ← decay_value(u, t_last, floor, λ_recall, t_event)`, and fold_recall takes per-record t0 and per-event t. The G1 node table lists deposit as (record id, H(payload), vector digest, scope, protected floor) and attention as ({record id: weight}, gen), with no time. If t sits in an unlisted envelope, Q2's canonical encoding must name it, or V-CHAIN can't cover it and an edited t would change anchors without failing the chain. Its source also needs stating. v1 stamps attention with wall-clock time.time() at signal (api.py:429-431), which is not monotone in seq. With per-event folding sorted by (record, seq), a backward clock step at seq 11 (t=90 after t=100 at seq 10) sets t_last back to 90, because the negative Δt clamps to 0 at decay.py:66-67 and then t_last ← t_event. Later decay is then charged from 90 rather than 100. That is deterministic from the journal only if t is in it.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:134-135, :282, :556 `(t f64, w f64, gen u32)`, :558; src/moneta/api.py:429-431 `now = time.time()` and `self.attention.append(entity_id, w, now)`; src/moneta/attention_log.py:73; src/moneta/decay.py:66-67.
all.proposed_fix: Add `t` (f64 bit pattern, substrate clock at append) to the deposit and attention rows, or to a declared common envelope covered by Q2's canonical bytes. Declare the clock source (monotone or wall) and whether the fold uses t_last ← max(t_last, t_event). Add a V-ORACLE-FOLD fixture with a backward clock step.

verdicts.reason: The finding holds. The G1 node table at BLUEPRINT_v7.md:134-135 gives `deposit` as (record id, H(payload), vector digest, scope, protected floor) and `attention` as ({record id: weight}, gen). Neither row has a time field. No common envelope declares one either. `prev` at :170 and Q2 at :583 define canonical bytes but never say a time field is in them. The fold still consumes per-event time: `t_event` at :282, attention runs `(t f64, w f64, gen u32)` in EvalBuf at :556, and `t0` / `until_t` in `fold_recall` at :558. P6 (:439) and Q3 (:584) say only that time is an argument to seams. They don't say where the journal stores it, so G2-1 purity (:228) can't hold for the fold unless t is in the journal. The only place the paper touches the v1 timestamp is :341 and Q7 (:588), and both are about the `gen` stamp, not about carrying `t`. The backward-step scenario is right. `t_last ← t_event` is unconditional at :282, and `decay_value` clamps a negative Δt to 0 (decay.py:65-67), so t_last can move backwards. One more point strengthens the finding. v1 never uses the per-entry timestamp at all: the reducer passes its own `now` into `apply_attention` and `decay_all` (attention_log.py:107-131; ecs.py:211-214). So v7's per-event fold depends on a time value v1 stamps (api.py:429-431) but never reads. The paper has to declare that value's source and coverage. It can't inherit them from v1.
verdicts.better_fix:
Take the proposed fix and make three additions.

1. Put `t` (f64 bit pattern) in a declared per-event envelope next to `seq` and `prev`, and name it in Q2's canonical encoding. That way V-CHAIN covers every event kind, not only deposit and attention, and `retention` / sleep-pass events can carry the reducer's `now` as well. Add a V-CHAIN sabotage that edits only `t`.

2. Say that this is a new journal dependency. v1's reducer ignores per-entry timestamps (attention_log.py:127-131, ecs.py:214), so the per-event fold's use of `t_event` departs from v1 in the same way as the step-order change at :274-279. Record it in the same place.

3. Choosing between unconditional `t_last ← t_event` and `t_last ← max(t_last, t_event)` changes the anchors, so put that choice in the same Round 4 E3 / O7 item as the per-batch versus per-event ruling. Don't settle it locally. Add the backward-clock-step case to V-ORACLE-FOLD's corpus, with the sabotage "one implementation uses max, the other doesn't".

verdicts.reason: The finding stands. In the G1 node table (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:133-134), `deposit` carries record id, H(payload), vector digest, scope and protected floor, and `attention` carries {record id: weight} and gen. Neither row has a time field. No common per-event envelope is declared anywhere else. Q2 (:583) defines the canonical bytes only abstractly (sorted keys, floats as bit patterns, payload digest) and names no time field. Yet the paper's own fold needs time from the journal. :282 uses `t_event` and sets `t_last ← t_event`. fold_recall (:558) takes `t0` and `until_t`. EvalBuf attention runs (:556) carry `(t f64, w f64, gen u32)`. G2-1 (:228) and P6 (:439) say time is an argument and no read touches a clock, so time can only be pure in the journal prefix if the events carry it. The paper itself notes at :341 that v1 attention entries carry `(entity_id, weight, timestamp)` (attention_log.py:73), but the G1 row drops that field. The clock source is also never stated. v1 stamps with wall-clock `time.time()` (api.py:429-432). decay.py:65-67 clamps a negative Δt to 0, and with `t_last ← t_event` that moves t_last backward, so the backward-step scenario is real and is not covered by any listed V-ORACLE-FOLD case (:284 names only the per-event vs per-batch case). Open question 1 at :686 asks about "the clock source" but doesn't resolve it, which confirms the gap rather than closing it. Severity minor is fair: this is a missing field and a missing declaration, not a design contradiction.
verdicts.better_fix: The proposed fix is correct. Three tightenings: (1) Put `t` (f64 bit pattern) in a declared common event envelope `{seq, kind, t, prev}` that Q2's canonical bytes cover, rather than adding it row by row. Then retention, seal, govern and the other events are timed too, and V-CHAIN's re-serialization sabotage covers an edit to t. (2) Pick one option and state it in G3 next to :282. Either (a) the substrate enforces t non-decreasing in seq at append (clamp to max(t, t_prev), with a verify Fail kind if it is violated), or (b) the fold uses `t_last ← max(t_last, t_event)`. Option (a) is stronger because it makes the journal itself monotone and the fold needs no special case. Also state that `t0` is the deposit event's t and that `until_t` is a caller argument per P6. (3) Add the backward-clock-step fixture to V-ORACLE-FOLD, and if option (a) is chosen, add an append-time sabotage to V-CHAIN/V-STATE. Also add a row to §… v1 deltas noting that v1 used unclamped wall time.

all.title: V-POOL demands exact top-k equality with a read path whose default scan is only δ-exact and environment-dependent
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:517 (V-POOL), :552 (scan δ by default), :525 (V-ORACLE-SCAN), :434 (P1 input list)
all.claim: The paper makes the scan the one seam where δ is the default, because arm P (numpy) sums in BLAS order. BLAS summation order also varies with library (MKL or OpenBLAS), CPU dispatch and thread count, and neither G1 nor the QueryRecord captures any of these. If arm P is the live read path, the returned ids a QueryRecord logs at a near-tie on the k boundary depend on that float environment, not only on P1's six inputs. V-POOL nevertheless requires the referee's top k to equal the read path's exactly, while the referee works from builder-computed cos f64 rows. These two conditions contradict each other whenever two pool scores lie within δ at rank k.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:552 'Arm P (numpy) sums dot products in BLAS order ... V-ORACLE-SCAN states its pass condition under δ from the start'; :517 V-POOL exact equality; :525; src/moneta/vector_index.py:160-162 (left-to-right loop in v1).
all.proposed_fix: Either keep the read path's cosine on the left-to-right oracle order, with the scan accelerating only candidate generation followed by an exact rescore of the top k plus a δ margin, or restate V-POOL with the same 'except pairs within δ, ordered by the total order' clause and record the BLAS environment in the echo.

verdicts.reason: The finding holds against the paper. Line 552 makes δ the default for the scan, because arm P (numpy) sums dot products in BLAS order. Arm P is the live read path: line 467 (SM4) moves the scan to Rust only if arm P misses its gate, line 639 records arm P's p95 on the real store, and moneta-scan is "absent until gated" (line 559). V-POOL at line 517 still requires the referee's top k to equal the read path's exactly. The referee's pool rows carry a builder-computed `cos f64` (line 556). The QueryRecord (lines 247-253) logs the returned ids but nothing about the BLAS library, CPU dispatch or thread count. So at a near-tie on the k boundary, the logged ids can differ from the referee's exact top k, and V-POOL can fail at mile 3 (line 654) for reasons unrelated to the pool logic. The paper's own fix ledger, J1-8 at line 793, claims the δ clause was applied "wherever δ applies", but it lists only V-ORACLE-SCAN and V-EXP. V-POOL was missed, so the paper does not already handle this; it has an internal inconsistency. One qualifier: the exact-equality condition fails only when an arm-P cosine differs from the builder's, so the risk depends on how the builder computes cos. The paper does not specify that anywhere, which leaves the gap open. Severity minor is fair.
verdicts.better_fix: Make the smallest consistent edit: extend J1-8 to V-POOL. Restate V-POOL at line 517 as "the referee's top k equals the read path's except pairs whose oracle scores lie within δ, which must be ordered by the total order (P5)", and add V-POOL to the J1-8 row at line 793. Then choose one of two ways to settle the cosine source, and state it explicitly. (a) The builder recomputes cos with the same left-to-right oracle order the referee uses, and V-POOL compares the read path to the referee only under δ. (b) The QueryRecord also logs the per-returned-id scores, so a near-tie at rank k can be recognized from the log rather than from the environment. Recording BLAS, CPU-dispatch and thread-count details in the echo is optional diagnostics, not a correctness fix, because those details cannot be replayed. The exact-rescore alternative (scan generates candidates, then an oracle-order rescore of the top k plus a δ margin) is also sound. It goes beyond the scope of a minor fix, though, and it changes arm P's latency budget against the 50 ms SM4 gate, so it should not be the default recommendation.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute this finding. The paper never reconciles the two conditions it names.

V-POOL (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:517) requires the referee's top k to equal the read path's, with no δ clause. §6 consequence 2 (:552) says the scan is the one seam where δ is the default, because arm P (numpy) sums dot products in BLAS order rather than v1's left-to-right loop (src/moneta/vector_index.py:160-162). The scan seam's oracle is api.query's own clamped path, max(cos,0)×U (:559). That makes arm P the read-path scan whose p95 is measured (:639, :656, SM4 :467).

The referee does not rescan. It scores builder-supplied pool rows that carry `cos f64` (:556). The paper does not say how the builder computes that cos. If it uses left-to-right order or a different BLAS build or thread count from the live read path, two pool scores within δ at rank k can swap. V-POOL then fails on noise.

The J1-8 fix (:793) says pass conditions read "identical except pairs within δ, ordered by the total order" wherever δ applies. That clause was applied only to V-ORACLE-SCAN (:525) and V-EXP (:519), not to V-POOL, even though V-POOL inherits the scan's δ through its cos inputs.

P1 (:434) and the QueryRecord echo (:247-253) do not record the float environment. So the returned ids logged at a near-tie at rank k depend on more than P1's six inputs. The finding's claim holds. Severity minor is fair: the failure appears only at near-ties.

Related consequence the finding does not name: G3-5 / V-REBUILD (:296, :496) require the eval set, including its cos f64 rows, to rebuild byte-identically. That breaks across machines if the builder computes cos via BLAS. Open question 1 (:686) asks this kind of question but does not answer it.
verdicts.better_fix:
The direction is right, but the fix is offered as an either/or and one of its parts is weak.

1. Pin how the eval-set builder computes `cos f64` to the deterministic left-to-right oracle order (the semantics of vector_index.py:160-162, ported once). This keeps G3-5 and V-REBUILD byte-identical across machines, independent of the BLAS build.

2. Restate V-POOL using J1-8's wording: "top k identical except pairs whose oracle scores lie within δ, which must be ordered by the total order." Here the read path means arm P. Also extend J1-8's coverage note (:793) and Q5 (:586) to list V-POOL alongside V-ORACLE-SCAN.

3. Optional: give arm P an exact rescore of the top k plus a δ margin in oracle order. V-POOL could then stay exact, and the logged returned ids would depend only on P1's inputs.

Recording the BLAS environment in the echo is not enough on its own. It documents the nondeterminism without removing it, and the bytes it adds would still need to be added to P1's input list.

all.title: A proposal scored during probation can be promoted after rollback, carrying the rolled-back generation's attention into a signed pointer move
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md §2 G4-3 (line 327), G3-7 (line 298), G4-5 (lines 329-331), evidence edge (line 177), §3 tuning pass steps 4-7 (lines 413-416); V-LEAK (line 499), V-PENDING (line 501)
all.claim: This is the owner-signs-promote-after-a-verdict path, and it is a real feedback edge because nothing invalidates stale evidence. G4-3 allows one Promoted generation and one Proposed generation at the same time. G4-7 refuses new proposals only once the ceiling is reached. G3-7 cleans only eval sets built AFTER a rollback. Counterexample: (t0) the owner signs promote g, and SYNAPSE's echo attention gets stamped g. (t1) A tuning pass builds eval set E1 over a train window that contains g-stamped attention. That is legal, because probation attention goes to the eval builder (R4a; pass1_rulings_brief.md:298). The pass scores candidate g' against the head, which is g (line 413), gets verdict V1, and appends propose g' with evidence → V1. (t2) The owner signs rollback g. G4-5 excludes g's attention from retention and reseals, but nothing touches g', because withdraw fires only when a proposal is declined or replaced (line 152). (t3) Nothing is pending now, so V-PENDING passes, and the owner signs promote g' with evidence V1. The pointer moves on a verdict built from the rolled-back generation's attention, measured against a head (g) that is no longer live. V-LEAK passes, since E1 was built before the rollback. R4a's purpose (rollback is an undo) is defeated through the owner path.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:327 ('at most one is in {Promoted, Expired}, and at most one is Proposed'); :337 (proposals refused only at the ceiling); :298 (G3-7 limited to 'built after a rollback'); :152 (withdraw only when declined or replaced); :177 (evidence → verdict by hash); :413 (candidate vs the head); :499 V-LEAK; :501 V-PENDING; RULINGS.md:20 (R4a); pass1_rulings_brief.md:298
all.proposed_fix: Add to G4-5: a rollback of g is followed by a substrate withdraw of any Proposed generation whose evidence eval set's Prefix covers any seq in [promote(g), rollback(g)]. Or make promote refuse when the evidence verdict's eval-set Prefix lies before the latest rollback, or names a head other than the live one. Give V-LEAK the sabotage 'propose during probation, roll back, then promote the proposal'. Both are edits consistent with R4a, not new rulings.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute it. The paper does not cover this path, and every step of the counterexample is legal as written.

1. **Proposing during probation is legal.** G4-3 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:327) allows one generation in {Promoted, Expired} and one Proposed at the same time. G4-7 (:333-337) refuses new proposals only once the ceiling is reached. Tuning-pass step 6 (:415) checks only G4-3, and step 8 (:417) does not pause tuning during probation.
2. **The candidate is scored against the live head.** Step 4 (:413) scores it against the head, which during probation is g.
3. **G3-7 does not reach this case.** G3-7 (:298) and V-LEAK (:499) apply only to eval sets built after a rollback, so E1, built before the rollback, is untouched.
4. **Rollback does not withdraw the pending proposal.** G4-5 (:329-331) only changes the retention fold and reseals. Withdraw (:152) fires only when the owner declines a proposal or a newer one replaces it. No edge or invariant cancels an existing Proposed generation.
5. **Nothing at promote time binds the evidence to the current head.** The evidence edge (:177) points at verdict, eval-set and referee leaves by hash. V-PENDING (:501) checks only how many are pending. V-STATE (:500) checks the shape of transitions, not whether the evidence is still valid.

So once g is rolled back, Proposed → promote of g' is a legal G4 transition (:322-324), and it rests on a verdict that measured g' against g using g-stamped attention. R4a (RULINGS.md:20) says rollback must work as an undo. That intent is defeated through the owner-signed path.

**One mitigating point is weak.** The owner signs the promote, and that signature is a gate. But under R4d the owner sees only train scores and held-out pass/fail (:416). The paper gives them nothing that would show the verdict is stale. A signature is not informed consent to a stale comparison.

**One caveat that strengthens the finding.** R4c says "Only one generation may be pending at a time" (RULINGS.md:22). The paper reads that as one Promoted plus one Proposed. That is a permissive reading of the ruling, and the owner may not have intended it. The coexistence that enables this bug comes from the paper's reading, not from the ruling's text.
verdicts.better_fix:
The fix is directionally correct and stays within R4a. I would make three changes.

1. **Bind evidence to the head, not to the Prefix window.** The verdict leaf should record the head generation it was scored against, by the seq of its govern. Promote should then refuse if that head is not the current live pointer. Add this to G4-3 or G4-1, and add a V-STATE sabotage: promote g' after g is rolled back. A stale baseline is the root problem, and it exists even when the eval-set window misses g's attention, because the comparison is still g' versus a head that is no longer live. The Prefix-coverage criterion alone is weaker.

2. **Withdraw on rollback.** Rollback of g should be followed by a substrate withdraw of any Proposed generation whose evidence names g as head. Withdraw's meaning at :152 must then widen to include "invalidated by rollback of its head".

3. **Consider the simpler reading of R4c.** That reading forbids a propose while any generation is Promoted or Expired: "only one pending" would then cover Proposed as well. It removes the window entirely. But it re-reads a ruled item, so the owner should be told about it rather than the paper adopting it silently.

V-LEAK or V-PENDING should still gain the sabotage "propose during probation, roll back, then promote the proposal". If g' is a partial set layered over g's spec, also check that promoting g' after a rollback does not re-introduce g's values.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute it. Every step of the counterexample is legal under the paper as written.

(1) A proposal can exist during probation. G4-3 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:327) allows one generation in {Promoted, Expired} alongside one Proposed. G4-7 (:333-337) refuses new proposals only once the ceiling is reached. Tuning-pass step 6 (:415) checks only G4-3. Step 4 (:413) scores the candidate against "the head", and during probation the head is g.

(2) Probation attention can enter the train window. Line :110 states that probation attention is stamped and kept, and is excluded only from the retention fold. G3-7 (:298) and V-LEAK (:499) restrict only eval sets built AFTER a rollback.

(3) Rollback does not touch the Proposed generation. G4-5 (:329-331) changes only the retention fold and the reseal. `withdraw` fires only when the owner declines or a newer proposal replaces it (:152). The G4 diagram (:306-320) has no rollback-triggered withdraw.

(4) Promote after rollback is accepted. After the rollback nothing is pending, so G4-3 and V-PENDING (:501) pass. The signed body binds only the genesis hash and the seq of an of/restores target (:162). Promote has neither, only `evidence` edges to the verdict, eval-set and referee leaves (:177). Nothing ties the evidence to the live head or orders it after the latest rollback. V-STATE (:500), V-UNDO (:503) and V-HASHGATE (:497) do not cover this path. V-HASHGATE's "after the latest rollback" rule (:296, :390) applies to fold checkpoints, not to evidence leaves.

Result: the owner signs a pointer move whose evidence was measured against g, a generation that is no longer live, and possibly on g-stamped attention. This defeats R4a's purpose of making rollback an undo (RULINGS.md:20; pass1_rulings_brief.md:298, "without the patches below a rollback is not actually an undo").

Mitigations that do not close it:
- Owner review (:416) is not a guard, because the owner is shown train scores and pass/fail with no staleness indicator.
- G4-6 shadow mode (:332) only postpones the issue past mile 4 on real stores. Mile 4 runs the full cycle on test stores, where this sequence is reachable.

Severity: major is reasonable. needs_owner=false holds, since closing the gap enforces R4a and is not a new ruling.
verdicts.better_fix:
The direction is right. Of the two options offered, use the second, unconditional form. The first option, "withdraw if the eval set's Prefix covers [promote(g), rollback(g)]", is narrower than the defect. A proposal made during g's probation was scored against head g even when its eval window has no g-attention, so it is stale either way.

Recommended edits:

(a) Add a typed edge **scored_against**: `govern{propose|promote}` → the self `govern` (promote, genesis, rollback or roll-forward) that was the live head when the pass scored. Principle 6 (:102) applies here: the head comparison must be an edge, not a field inside a verdict leaf.

(b) Add G4-8 "Fresh evidence". Promote is refused unless both hold:
- its `scored_against` equals the live self head at append
- its eval-set `Prefix` seq follows the latest self rollback or roll-forward

(c) In G4-5, a rollback or roll-forward is followed by a substrate `withdraw` of any Proposed generation. Extend the `withdraw` row at :152 to cover "superseded by a pointer move". This keeps the G4 diagram honest, so no stale Proposed node lingers.

(d) Put the sabotage "propose during probation, roll back, then promote the stale proposal" under V-STATE or V-PENDING, plus a new V-FRESH row. Do not put it under V-LEAK. V-LEAK's property is about eval-set contents, and it would still pass in this scenario.

(e) Optionally, decide whether proposing during probation should be refused outright. That is simpler, but it narrows R4c's "one pending" and may need an owner nod. (b) and (c) do not.

all.title: G3-2 names the wrong host path; the dominant leaf→host→attention edge (recall anchors → query → SYNAPSE top-5) is unnamed, and 'one path exists' is false
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md §2 G3-2 (lines 288-293); derived leaves (lines 260-268)
all.claim: G3-2 says SYNAPSE reads snapshot.json and 'ranks with that utility', and that this is the only host-mediated path. The [V] evidence carried from v6 describes a different mechanism. SYNAPSE fills a 50-candidate pool from Moneta's query() and reranks it with its own reranker. After every search it signals attention on its own top five results, weighted by its reranker score. Utility enters through query's cos·utility ranking (api.py:414), which decides pool membership, not through a snapshot read. In v7, query ranks on the recall fold, and 'recall anchors' are a G3 derived leaf (line 263). So recall anchors (leaf) → query answer → SYNAPSE rerank → signal_attention is a leaf→host→attention edge by the paper's own definition. It is the edge v6 identified as the loop's indirect route to retention (v6:121, v6:520). The hold also does not bound this edge inside probation. Hold G4-4 covers only retention events, while the recall fold counts every non-excluded attention event at once (line 282). During probation, g's echo raises the recall utility of g's own results immediately, so g is evaluated in a self-reinforced state.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:288-293, :263 (recall anchors are a leaf), :282 (the recall fold skips only the excluded set), :328 (the hold covers retention events only); inputs/BLUEPRINT_v6.md:25 ('fill a 50-candidate pool that it reranks itself [V]'), :97 (top five reranked results after each vector search [V]), :121, :520; src/moneta/api.py:393-418 (rerank by max(cos,0)*utility)
all.proposed_fix: Replace the three-step paragraph with a list of every leaf → outside agent → G1 path and its bound: (1) recall anchors → query → host echo → attention; (2) verdict → tuner view (J3 train scores) → propose; (3) verdict → owner → promote/adopt/rollback; (4) snapshot.json → host (see the next finding). Say plainly that the hold bounds only (1)'s retention effect, and that the recall effect is live during probation.

verdicts.reason: The paper does not handle this, and the claim holds against the sources. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:288-293 says G3-2 has exactly one host-mediated path: snapshot.json → SYNAPSE "ranks with that utility" → signal_attention. The [V] evidence describes a different mechanism. SYNAPSE asks Moneta for max(3×limit, 50) results and reranks them with its own tag, keyword and text-match scorer, breaking ties by recency and then id (inputs/BLUEPRINT_v6.md:99). It then signals attention on its own top five reranked results, weighted by its reranker score (v6:97). Nothing in the sources says SYNAPSE ranks with snapshot utility. v6:132 only says SYNAPSE reads snapshot.json. Utility does enter through query: src/moneta/api.py:414 ranks by max(cos,0)*utility, and that ranking decides pool membership. v6:121 and the change log near v6:520 name exactly this route as the loop's indirect path ("a tuned policy changes what SYNAPSE shows, which changes its attention"). In v7, recall anchors are a derived G3 leaf (:261, :263). Probation rebuilds them (:417). The recall fold skips only the excluded set (:282). The hold G4-4 (:328) blocks only retention events. So recall anchors → query → SYNAPSE echo → attention is a leaf→host→G1 edge that G3-2 does not name. During probation that echo raises the recall utility of g's own results immediately. Nothing in the paper bounds that. O6 (:671) asks only whether the recall fold drops rolled-back attention after rollback. It does not cover the live self-reinforcement during probation. The paper's own G3-2 question (:687) already half-concedes that verdict → owner → promote is another path. So "one path exists" is false on the paper's own terms. Severity major is fair. The paper's main no-feedback invariant names the wrong path and leaves out the one v6 built the hold around.
verdicts.better_fix:
Accept the fix, with three refinements:

1. Tag the snapshot.json path [A]. Drop "ranks with that utility", because v6:99 says SYNAPSE's reranker uses its own scorer and no source shows a snapshot read feeding a rank.

2. For path (1), split the bound into two effects:
   - Retention effect: held by G4-4 and undone on rollback by G4-5.
   - Recall effect: live during probation and not bounded. Name its consequence. The verdict that informs adopt is computed while g's echo is inflating g's own recall anchors. Hold-out eval sets must therefore not depend on probation-window anchors. V-HOLDOUT/V-LEAK should get a sabotage that catches this.

3. Cross-reference O6. Add a probation-time variant, or a new open item, so the owner can decide whether the recall fold should exclude live-generation attention during probation.

For paths (2) and (3), say they create govern events, not attention events. Note that they fall under G3-2's "No G1 event's content is computed from a leaf" clause and the question at :687.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds. G3-2 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:288-293) says "One host-mediated path exists", and the path it names is snapshot.json → SYNAPSE ranks with that utility → signal_attention. The paper itself makes the query path a second one:
- Recall anchors are a derived leaf (:261, :263).
- Probation rebuilds them under the promoted generation (:417).
- v6, carried forward, says "Ranking uses the tuned recall half-life" (v6:130).
- query ranks by max(cos,0)*utility (src/moneta/api.py:393-418, line 414).
- SYNAPSE fills its 50-candidate pool from query and echoes attention on its own top five, weighted by its reranker score (v6:25, v6:97 [V]).

So the chain is recall-anchor leaf → query answer → host rerank → attention event. By the paper's definition at :293, that is a leaf → host → attention edge, and G3-2 never names it. v6 called this the loop's indirect route (v6:121, v6:520).

The bound G3-2 claims does not cover this path's recall side:
- The hold G4-4 (:328) stops only retention events.
- The recall fold skips only the excluded set (:282). Nothing is excluded during probation, so the echo raises g's recall utility immediately.
- O6 (:671) keeps rolled-back attention in the recall fold even after rollback.

Nothing in the paper handles this. The closest text is O6 and attack 3 (:293, :343), and both cover misattribution and rollback, not the self-reinforcement live during probation.

One overstatement in the finding: snapshot.json is not "the wrong path". v6:132 [V-carried] says SYNAPSE reads that export, so the path may exist. What is unsupported is step 2, "it ranks with that utility". Pool membership comes from query (v6:25), so that step should be marked [A] rather than deleted.
verdicts.better_fix:
Take the proposed list, with these refinements:

1. Change "One host-mediated path exists" to "these host-mediated paths exist". Make the recall-anchors → query → SYNAPSE top-5 echo → attention path the primary one, cited to v6:25, v6:97 and api.py:414.

2. Keep snapshot.json → host as a possible secondary path. Mark it [A]: SYNAPSE reads it (v6:132), but nothing shows its ranking uses it. Don't present it as false.

3. State each path's bound plainly:
   - The hold (G4-4) bounds only retention.
   - During probation the recall effect is live and self-reinforcing, because the anchors are rebuilt under g (:417) and the fold skips only the excluded set (:282).
   - After a rollback the recall effect persists unless O6 is ruled the other way. Cross-reference O6 (:671), and add "self-reinforcement during probation" as a consequence the owner should know when ruling O6. This leaves R4a untouched.

4. Keep the verdict → tuner → propose and verdict → owner → promote/adopt/rollback paths. Cross-reference :687, which already asks the owner question.

5. Add a V-NOFEEDBACK (:494) or attack-plan line. It should measure how far the probation echo inflates g's held-out score, for example by scoring g's eval on attention stamped before promote versus after. Otherwise the referee may evaluate g in the self-reinforced state.

all.title: snapshot.json is SYNAPSE's persistence and restore artifact, so it may be a leaf written back into the store, which neither the stamp nor the hold can see
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md §2 G3-2 (lines 288-293), G3-4 (line 295), V-NOFEEDBACK (line 494); §3 store layout (line 379)
all.claim: The paper treats snapshot.json as something SYNAPSE reads in order to rank. The repo's own integration record says SYNAPSE uses a 'wrapper-managed snapshot and restore' for persistence, and v6 times 'SYNAPSE's snapshot on every add'. In v1, restoring from that format calls hydrate. Hydrate writes utility, attended_count, last_evaluated and state verbatim into the ECS (durability.py:203-215 via ecs.hydrate_row, ecs.py:150-164), bypassing any event log. The v1 format has no gen field (durability.py:88-100). If the v7 facade keeps a restore entry point for SYNAPSE, a derived leaf becomes substrate state without a journal event, which violates G3-2 and G3-4. Rolled-back attention baked into an exported attended_count (exported after a later adopt, or from an earlier store) cannot be excluded by G4-5. A stale export restored after tombstones can also bring pruned rows back. V-NOFEEDBACK checks only 'no substrate append path reads derived/', so a restore that is not an append escapes it. The blueprint never says what the facade does on a SYNAPSE restore. SYNAPSE source is absent (line 13), so this is [A].
all.evidence: docs/synapse-loop.md:38 ('SYNAPSE's wrapper-managed snapshot and restore'); inputs/BLUEPRINT_v6.md:365 ('SYNAPSE's snapshot on every add'), :132; src/moneta/durability.py:83-100, :181-215; src/moneta/ecs.py:150-164; BLUEPRINT_v7.md:13 (SYNAPSE source absent), :494 (V-NOFEEDBACK scope)
all.proposed_fix: State that snapshot.json is export-only in v7, and that the facade refuses or ignores a hydrate from it: restore means replaying the journal. Add a V-check: 'no host restore sets utility, attended_count or state from a derived file', with the sabotage 'v1 hydrate from snapshot.json after a rollback'. Add a mile-3 step to verify SYNAPSE's restore path against the pinned commit (synapse-loop.md:13). If SYNAPSE needs restore-from-export, the owner must rule on it.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute the finding. Its factual claims check out, and the paper has a real gap here.

1. The paper treats snapshot.json only as something SYNAPSE reads. It is listed as a derived leaf (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:266, :379). The one named host path is read → rank → signal_attention (:288-293), and §10 attack 2 (:687) repeats that framing.
2. No section says what the v7 facade does on a SYNAPSE restore. Searching for restore/hydrate/facade in the blueprint finds only the govern `restores` edge (:171, :185) and the mile-3 migration line (:639).
3. The repo record calls this a "wrapper-managed snapshot and restore" (docs/synapse-loop.md:38). v6 times "SYNAPSE's snapshot on every add" (inputs/BLUEPRINT_v6.md:365).
4. In v1, Moneta.__init__ calls durability.hydrate (api.py:229). Hydrate writes utility, attended_count, last_evaluated and state verbatim (durability.py:203-215) through ecs.hydrate_row (ecs.py:150). The v1 row format carries no gen field (durability.py:85-100).
5. V-NOFEEDBACK (:494) covers only "append paths". V-HASHGATE (:493) covers only fold checkpoints. V-LEAF (:492) tests that deleting leaves changes nothing; it does not test that a leaf is never used as an open/restore source. So a v1-compatible hydrate from the export escapes every V-check.
6. G3-2 (:287) and G3-4 (:295) forbid this in principle. A spec property with no check and no stated facade behavior is still an open hole, so the paper does not already handle it.

The claim is conditional on the facade keeping a restore entry point, and SYNAPSE source is absent (:13). So "[A]" and "needs_owner" are correct.

One nuance: in v1 the snapshot is Moneta's own file. "Wrapper-managed" likely means SYNAPSE drives Moneta's snapshot_ecs/hydrate, not a SYNAPSE-authored format. That strengthens the finding, because the facade's v1-compatible open path is itself the risk.
verdicts.better_fix:
The fix is sound. Four refinements:

(a) Widen V-NOFEEDBACK at :494 from "no substrate append path" to "no substrate append or open/restore path reads derived/ content", rather than adding a separate V-check. Add the sabotage "v1-style hydrate from snapshot.json after a rollback revives rolled-back attended_count and pruned rows".

(b) State in §2 next to G3-2, or in the §3 layout note, that the v1-format snapshot.json is export-only. The facade's restore/open replays the journal (plus a hash-gated, post-rollback-sealed checkpoint per G3-3/G4-5). It never calls hydrate_row from an export.

(c) Fold the mile-3 SYNAPSE restore-path check into the existing mile-3 compatibility step at :639, rather than adding a new step. Verify against the pinned commit referenced at synapse-loop.md:13.

(d) Add this item to §10 attack 2 (:687) so pass 3 attacks the restore direction too.

The owner ruling is needed only if SYNAPSE in fact requires restore-from-export.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute this finding. The paper names only the read path. G3-2 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:288-293) gives the host-mediated loop as "SYNAPSE reads snapshot.json, ranks, calls signal_attention", and §3:379 lists snapshot.json as a derived export leaf. Nothing in v7 says what happens when a host restores from that file. I grepped the paper and RULINGS.md for "restore", "hydrat" and "facade": "restore" appears only as the govern `restores` edge (T4, V-RESTORE), and there is no ruling on the facade's open or restore path.

The v1 evidence holds up:
- In v1, snapshot.json is the restore source, not just an export. Moneta.__init__ calls durability.hydrate() (src/moneta/api.py:229). hydrate() loads utility, attended_count, last_evaluated and state verbatim through ecs.hydrate_row (durability.py:203-215, ecs.py:150-164).
- The format has no gen or produced_under field (durability.py:88-106).
- synapse-loop.md:38 qualifies "SYNAPSE's wrapper-managed snapshot and restore" as the persistence path. v6:132 says the v1-format snapshot.json is something SYNAPSE reads, and v6:365 times SYNAPSE's snapshot on every add.

So a v7 facade that keeps v1's open semantics would turn a derived leaf into substrate state. G4-5's exclusion only acts on attention events carrying produced_under, so rolled-back attention already folded into an exported attended_count escapes it. A stale export could also bring back rows that were pruned later.

The paper does partly cover this, though not by design for this case:
- G3-3 (line 294) says a leaf is read only if its hash matches one the journal names or one recomputed from its inputs. That would reject a stale or post-rollback export.
- G1 makes the journal the only authority (line 375).

But G3-3 is written as a rule for leaf consumers. No V-check exercises a host restore: V-NOFEEDBACK (line 494) covers substrate append paths, V-LEAF (line 493) covers resolvers, and V-HASHGATE (line 495) covers checkpoints. A fresh, hash-matching export restored after a later adopt would also pass G3-3.

Whether SYNAPSE's restore actually loads Moneta's snapshot.json is [A], because SYNAPSE source is absent (line 13). That fits needs_owner=true and a mile-3 verification step.
verdicts.better_fix:
Keep the proposed fix and tighten it in four ways.

1. Anchor the statement in G1 and G3-3, not as a new principle. In §3 or the facade section, say: "In v7, snapshot.json is export-only. The v7 facade's open/restore always rebuilds from the journal. v1's Durability.hydrate path (api.py:229, durability.py:181-215) is not carried forward. Any host restore request either replays the journal or is refused."

2. Do not add a separate check. Widen V-NOFEEDBACK's scope from "no substrate append path" to "no substrate append path or open/restore path reads derived/ content into substrate state". Add the sabotage "v1 hydrate_row from snapshot.json after a rollback, so the rolled-back generation's attended_count survives". Also extend V-HASHGATE to cover "open seeded from a snapshot.json export".

3. Add the hazard to G3-2's "not bounded" note next to attack 3.

4. Put a mile-3 step in §7 line 639 (SYNAPSE compatibility re-measure): inspect SYNAPSE's wrapper restore at the pinned commit 7d121ea1 (synapse-loop.md:13).

Leave an owner question in the open-questions list (near line 687/825): does SYNAPSE need restore-from-export? If it does, the restore must go through the journal (import as events) rather than set state.

all.title: The stamp and hold defer the host path but do not bound it; outside probation (all of real-store life through mile 4) the echo loop runs unchecked on the prune key
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md G3-2 line 293 ('bounded in two ways'), G4-4 (line 328), G4-6 (line 332)
all.claim: Both bounds act only while a generation is in {Promoted, Expired}. G4-6 says no real-store generation leaves Proposed through mile 4, so on the real store the hold never fires. Every stamp names the base generation, which cannot be rolled back. After any adopt, the deferred attention lands in one fold. In steady state the host echo raises attended_count by one per signal, with no decay (ecs.py:213). Any record echoed three times leaves the prune predicate attended_count < 3 permanently (consolidation.py:111-112), and its utility keeps it in the query pool (api.py:414). That is the rich-get-richer effect v6 tagged [U] at v6:97, and v7 now calls it bounded. The owner should also know a consequence of R4d: at adopt, the owner sees held-out pass/fail only, and nothing shows the retention and prune effect the adopt releases.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:293, :328, :332; src/moneta/ecs.py:213; src/moneta/consolidation.py:111-112; src/moneta/api.py:414; inputs/BLUEPRINT_v6.md:97 ('what ranks well may keep ranking well ... [U]'), :124; RULINGS.md:23 (R4d)
all.proposed_fix: Reword line 293 to say the hold defers a generation's incremental retention effect and makes it reversible, and does not bound the host loop. Name the steady-state echo loop as pre-existing v1 behavior outside G3-2's scope. Optionally show the owner, at adopt, the count of records whose prune status changes when the held attention is folded. That is information only and stays within R4d.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:293 says the host path is "bounded in two ways": the gen stamp and the G4 hold. Both only act while a generation is pending. G4-4 (:328) holds retention only while a generation is in {Promoted, Expired}. G4-6 (:332) says no real-store generation leaves Proposed through mile 4, so on the real store the hold never fires and every stamp names the base generation. That generation can't be rolled back, so G4-5's exclusion (:330) never applies to it.

v1 code confirms the steady-state loop. ecs.py:213 does `_attended[row] += count` with no decay. consolidation.py:111-112 prunes only when `utility < thr and attended_count < PRUNE_ATTENDED_THRESHOLD`, so once a record's count crosses the threshold, the prune branch can never fire for it. The paper names this mechanism itself at :110 and :503, but only in the rollback-undo context. It never tags the steady-state loop as unbounded. v6:97 keeps it as a [U] hypothesis.

The only partial acknowledgment is attack question 2 at :687 ("is the named host path ... bounded enough by the stamp and the hold?"). That is an open question, not a statement of scope, and :293 still asserts the bound. The only unboundedness the paper admits is the misattribution window (:293, :343), not the out-of-probation loop. So the paper does not already handle this, and the overstatement is real.

Two small nuances; neither refutes the finding:
- A record past the attended threshold can still leave VOLATILE through the stage branch (consolidation.py:114-117) once its utility decays below the stage threshold. "Never prunes" is accurate; "stays in the query pool" is looser.
- api.py:414 ranks every vector hit by cos×utility. Utility scales a record's rank but does not gate whether it is in the pool.

Severity minor is appropriate.
verdicts.better_fix:
Take the proposed rewording of :293 and add three things.

1. State the scope explicitly. Something like: "The stamp and hold make a pending generation's share of the echo deferrable and reversible. They do not bound the echo loop under an adopted or base generation. That is pre-existing v1 behavior (ecs.py:213, consolidation.py:111-112), and it stays [U] per v6:97." Then cross-reference attack question 2 at :687, so the attack is pointed at a stated limitation rather than at a claimed bound.

2. Make the precise claim "a record echoed past PRUNE_ATTENDED_THRESHOLD can no longer prune." Don't claim it "stays in the query pool," because the stage path still applies.

3. Optionally, show the owner at adopt how many records would change prune or stage status. Hedge this display: it reports a retention effect and reveals nothing about the held-out set, so it plausibly sits outside R4d's wear accounting. Whether it counts as a "disclosure" under R4d (RULINGS.md:23) is for the owner to confirm, not the paper to assert. Mark it [P] or as an open item rather than declaring it within R4d.

verdicts.reason: The claim holds against the paper and the code. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:293 says the host path "is bounded in two ways" (the stamp and the G4 hold). The only exception it names is the misattribution window. But G4-4 (:328) holds retention only while a generation is in {Promoted, Expired}. G4-6 (:332) keeps every real-store generation in Proposed through mile 4, so on the real store the hold never fires in that period. Attention is then stamped with the base or adopted generation. G4-5 (:329-331) excludes attention only for a RolledBack generation, and the base generation never enters Promoted, so its attention is never excluded. An Adopted generation that is later rolled back goes to Retired (diagram, :320), not RolledBack, so its attention is not excluded either. In v1 the retention fold adds every non-excluded event to attended_count with no decay (ecs.py:211-213). Prune requires utility < 0.1 AND attended_count < 3 (consolidation.py:54-55, :110-113), so after three echoes a record can never be pruned. Staged records go to CONSOLIDATED and stay in the ECS (consolidation.py:171-186), and query ranks every ECS record by cos*utility (api.py:408-414). The v6 [U] hypothesis at v6:97 ("what ranks well may keep ranking well") is therefore not bounded by anything in G3-2. In mitigation, the paper's attack list asks at §10 item 2 (:687) whether the path is "bounded enough by the stamp and the hold". That shows the question is open, but it does not remove the flat assertion at :293. One nuance: utility still decays, so the lasting part is prune immunity, not permanent high rank. The R4d point is fair as a consequence the owner should know: held-out pass/fail (RULINGS.md:23) does not show the retention effect the adopt releases. needs_owner=false is right, because no ruling is reopened.
verdicts.better_fix: Accept the fix with three changes. (1) Change :293 to: "The stamp and the hold make a probation generation's share of this path attributable, deferred, and reversible. They do not bound the loop. Outside probation (all real-store life through mile 4, per G4-6), host echoes reach retention directly, raise attended_count with no decay (ecs.py:213), and can make a record prune-immune after three echoes (consolidation.py:54-55, :111-112)." (2) Carry v6:97's rich-get-richer hypothesis forward as [U], marked as pre-existing v1 behavior outside G3-2's scope. Point §10 attack 2 (:687) at it so the attack question and the invariant text agree. (3) The optional adopt-time count of records whose prune or stage status the held attention would change is fine as information under R4d. It is computed on train/retention state, not held-out queries, so it does not count against window wear. State that explicitly so the next pass doesn't read it as a breach of R4d.

all.title: "Live at append" isn't pinned to the signal_attention call. If E3 is ruled against, all of a rolled-back generation's attention survives.
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:135, :174, :341 (stamp definition); G4-4 :328 / J7 :451 (hold); E3 fallback :631; V-GENTAG :504
all.claim: The paper defines the stamp as the self generation live 'at append' (:174, :341) but never says whether 'append' is the signal_attention call or the journal write. E3 is [A], and its stated fallback is that 'the journal and the attention log coexist' (:631). On that path v1's flow holds: signal_attention puts an entry in an in-memory buffer (api.py:431-437, attention_log.py:73), and the buffer is drained only at the top of a sleep pass (consolidation.py:154, attention_log.py:82,127). G4-4 holds sleep passes for the whole probation. Interleaving: seq m is the signed promote of g, which goes live. From m+1 to m+k the host calls signal_attention for g-ranked results k times; the entries sit in the buffer because no sleep pass may run. At seq r the owner signs rollback of g, so the live generation is now the rollback event. The first sleep pass after the rollback drains the buffer and journals the attention at seq >r. Each event is stamped produced_under = rollback(r), not g. G4-5 excludes nothing. Every probation-era attention event counts in utility and attended_count, so the undo is a no-op. The opposite case is symmetric: attention signaled under g0 just before the promote but drained later is stamped g and dropped. V-GENTAG ('stamp equals the generation live at its seq') passes in both cases, because the stamp does match the generation live at the journal seq.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:135 (attention source = signal_attention, gen stamp), :174, :328, :341, :417 ('retention is held'), :451, :504, :631; src/moneta/api.py:420-437; src/moneta/attention_log.py:71-83, :127-129; src/moneta/consolidation.py:153-156
all.proposed_fix: Define the stamp as captured inside signal_attention at call time: the in-memory AttentionEntry gains an internal gen field (api.py:433). This doesn't change the locked signature and doesn't need §9 or O14. Make this hold whatever E3's outcome. Add a V-GENTAG sabotage: 'stamp taken at drain/journal time rather than at the signal_attention call', with a fixture where promote → signal → rollback → sleep pass runs in that order.

verdicts.reason:
The paper doesn't handle this case. The only place it pins the write point is the G1 node table, where `attention` is "Written by `signal_attention`" (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:135). That holds only if E3 is ruled for, which makes the journal the attention log. If E3 is ruled against, the paper says only that the journal and the attention log "coexist; their relative order becomes an open risk" (:631). It never says which side writes the journal's `attention` event, or when the stamp is read.

In v1, `signal_attention` only pushes `(entity_id, weight, timestamp)` into an in-memory buffer and the WAL (api.py:431-437, attention_log.py:71-73). The buffer is drained only by `reduce_attention_log` at the top of a sleep pass (attention_log.py:127, consolidation.py:154). G4-4 / J7 forbids retention, and V-HOLD names "a sleep pass during probation" as the sabotage (:328, :451, :502). So on the coexist path, a stamp taken at drain or journal time would fall after the rollback for all of g's probation attention. G4-5 (:329-330) would then exclude nothing, and V-UNDO's guarantee (:503) would fail.

The paper's named "misattribution window" (:343) describes only a narrow edge: attention arriving "just after a promote or rollback." That understates this case, where the window is the whole probation. V-GENTAG (:504) checks the stamp against the generation live at its journal `seq`, and its only sabotage is "last *proposed* generation." So it would pass on a drain-time stamp, as the finding says.

Attack 3 (:688) invites exactly this interleaving, so the paper knows the area is open. But inviting the attack doesn't resolve it.

Two caveats on scope:
- The defect only appears if E3 is ruled against.
- In that branch the paper already flags ordering as an open risk.

That arguably makes the severity high rather than critical, but the claim is factually right and not handled.
verdicts.better_fix:
