The fix is right in direction but incomplete. Capture `gen` inside `signal_attention` at call time, as an internal field on `AttentionEntry` (api.py:433), and state that this holds whatever E3's outcome. This is internal, so the locked signature (ARCHITECTURE.md §2) is unchanged and neither §9 nor O14 is needed.

Add these:

1. **WAL.** The same `gen` must go into the WAL record (api.py:435-437, the `durability.wal_append(AttentionEntry(...))` call) and survive WAL replay. Otherwise a crash between signal and drain re-stamps the entry at recovery time, and the bug comes back.

2. **Stamp source.** State that the journal `attention` event copies its stamp from the entry and never reads the live generation at drain.

3. **:341 and :343.** Rewrite :341 so "at append" means "at the `signal_attention` call." Amend :343 so the residual window is only the host-latency edge, and note that without call-time capture the window would be the whole probation.

4. **V-GENTAG (:504).** Change the property to "the stamp equals the self generation live when `signal_attention` was called." Add sabotages: "stamp taken at drain/journal time" and "stamp lost or recomputed on WAL replay." Use fixtures in this order: (a) promote g → signal → rollback → sleep pass; (b) signal under g0 → promote g → … → sleep pass; (c) promote g → signal → crash → recover → rollback → sleep pass.

5. **E3 row (:631).** In the ruled-against column, name call-time stamping as the requirement that keeps G4-5 sound.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute it. The paper never says what "append" means for an attention event. G1 :135 says the event is written by `signal_attention`. :174 and :341 say the stamp is the generation "live at append". :504 (V-GENTAG) checks the stamp against the generation live at its own `seq`. None of these ties the `seq` or the stamp to the moment of the call. The ruled-for path (E3, one ordered journal) is fine, because there `signal_attention` writes the journal directly. On the ruled-against path, :631 says only that "the journal and the attention log coexist; their relative order becomes an open risk". In v1 code, `signal_attention` appends to the in-memory buffer and the WAL (api.py:431-437, attention_log.py:71-73). The buffer is drained only at the top of a sleep pass (consolidation.py:153-156, attention_log.py:127). G4-4/J7 (:328, :451) hold sleep passes for the whole probation. So if the journal write happens at drain, every attention event from probation is stamped with the rollback generation. G4-5 (:330) then excludes nothing, and R4a (RULINGS.md:20) is silently defeated.

The misattribution window named at :343 does not cover this. It is about host-side lag "just after a promote or rollback", for results shown just before it, and it is short. This hole spans the whole probation and comes from the substrate's own buffering. V-GENTAG would pass, as the finding says, because it is checked against the journal seq.

On severity: the paper doesn't state that the journal write happens at drain. It leaves the timing unspecified, so this is a spec gap that makes the failure possible rather than a defect the paper asserts. It is still serious enough to rate high or critical, since it can nullify a ruled item (R4a/J8).
verdicts.better_fix:
Keep the proposed fix, with three additions.

(1) Say in G1 :174 and :341 that the stamp is captured when `signal_attention` accepts the call, under the same single writer that orders `govern` appends. That way a promote or rollback can't interleave between the generation read and the buffer append. Then state that the journal `seq` of a drained attention event can be later than its stamp, and that the stamp, not the `seq`, decides G4-5 exclusion.

(2) The stamp must also go into the WAL entry (durability.wal_append, api.py:436), not only the in-memory AttentionEntry. Otherwise a crash-replay during probation would re-stamp the entries at recovery. Note that the WAL record format changes. That is internal, so no §9.

(3) Restate V-GENTAG as "every attention stamp equals the self generation live when `signal_attention` returned". Keep its existing sabotage, and add "stamp taken at drain/journal time" with the fixture promote → signal → rollback → sleep pass → assert excluded. Also add a WAL-replay variant: promote → signal → crash → recover → rollback → sleep pass.

Also add one line under E3 "if ruled against" (:631) saying the stamp-at-call rule holds whatever the ruling.

all.title: The host path the paper names (G3-2) doesn't depend on g, yet all of its attention during probation is stamped g. The window covers the whole probation, not the moments just after promote.
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md G3-2 :288-293; misattribution paragraph :343; O14 :679
all.claim: Line 293 says the stamp and the hold bound the snapshot.json → SYNAPSE → signal_attention path. They don't. The self tier may set only recallHalfLife (G2-4, :231). The recall fold writes nothing back to retention (G2-8 :235, V-EVAL3). V-UNDO treats 'a tunable that also feeds retention' as sabotage (:503). snapshot.json reports retention utility (:289), and retention is frozen during probation (G4-4). So nothing SYNAPSE ranks on during probation was produced by g. Interleaving: seq m, promote g. For seq m+1 through m+N (up to the 14-day ceiling, :333, and beyond while Expired), SYNAPSE ranks from the same retention utility that existed before the promote and calls signal_attention. Every event is stamped g. At seq r, rollback(g), and G4-5 drops all N events. If g had instead been adopted, the same events would have been credited to g in eval sets. For this path the 'window the stamp misattributes' (:293) is the entire probation, not 'just after a promote or rollback' (:343). This is a consequence of R4a combined with stamp-at-append. R4a itself isn't reopened here. It is the 'material harm' that O14 (:679) says should reopen the echo question.
all.proposed_fix: Correct :293 and :343 to say that for host paths which read retention-derived leaves, the misattribution is the whole probation. Size it in the paper as all attention on that path for the ceiling duration. Bring it to the owner under O14 as material harm. Alternatives within the substrate that keep the signature: mark attention from a declared host-path source as gen-neutral, or have SYNAPSE read a leaf that is explicitly stamped (both [P]).

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute it. Each premise checks out in BLUEPRINT_v7.md:
- G2-4 (:231) lets the self tier set only recallHalfLife.
- G2-8 (:235) says the recall fold writes nothing back to retention.
- :289 says snapshot.json reports retention utility.
- G4-4 (:328) appends no retention event while a generation is Promoted or Expired.
- The V-UNDO sabotage (:503) treats 'a tunable that also feeds retention' as a fault.

So on the named path (snapshot.json -> SYNAPSE -> signal_attention), the ranking input during probation is the pre-promote retention state and does not depend on g. The stamp is taken at append (:341), so every event on that path from promote until adopt or rollback carries g. At rollback, G4-5 (:329) and RULINGS R4(a) drop all of it from utility and attended_count. If g is adopted instead, G3-7 and V-LEAK credit it to g in eval sets. That is wrong attribution over the whole probation, not only 'just after a promote or rollback' (:343).

The paper does not handle this anywhere. :293 says the path is 'bounded' by the stamp and the hold, and gives only the transition window as the gap. Attack 2 at :687 asks whether that path is 'bounded enough', but it is an open prompt, not an answer. O14 (:679) waits for attack 3 to 'show material harm', and this is that harm. The window is longer than the 14-day ceiling (:333): after `expire` the hold stays and the pointer does not move until the owner signs (G4-7), so the window runs until adopt or rollback.

Two minor caveats. The finding is limited to the snapshot.json path; a host path that ranks via query() would read recall anchors under g's half-life and is not g-independent (compare :653 'SYNAPSE as it consumes recall today'). And whether dropping g-independent attention counts as 'harm' is the owner's call, since R4(a) is ruled. Neither caveat weakens the core claim that :293 and :343 overstate the bound.
verdicts.better_fix:
The core fix is right:
- Rewrite :293 so the stamp and hold bound *substrate* reach, and say that for host paths ranking on retention-derived leaves, every event in probation is stamped g but not caused by g.
- Widen :343 to name a second, whole-probation window for those paths, next to the transition window.
- Size the window as all attention on the path from promote until adopt or rollback. That is not 'ceiling duration', because Expired keeps the hold with no deadline (G4-7).
- Route the result to the owner as O14's material-harm evidence. Also link O6, since the recall fold keeps this attention while retention drops it.

Both [P] alternatives are weaker than stated and should be marked as such:
- 'Gen-neutral by declared host-path source' cannot be told apart under the locked signature `(entity_id, weight, timestamp)` (attention_log.py:73; api.py:420). It would need a side channel such as a per-caller registration, which itself needs justifying. It also narrows R4(a)'s exclusion, so it is an owner decision, not a substrate choice.
- 'SYNAPSE reads a stamped leaf' changes nothing unless the stamp travels back on signal_attention. That is the O14 echo itself, which needs §9.

A third option that stays inside the substrate: flag in the paper that rolling back drops g-independent attention, and have V-UNDO's fixture include a host that reads snapshot.json, so the size of the loss is measured.

verdicts.reason:
I couldn't refute this. The paper doesn't handle it, and the factual chain holds against the text.

1. **g can't touch what SYNAPSE ranks on.** The self tier may set only recallHalfLife (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:231, G2-4). The recall fold is a pure view that writes nothing back to retention (:235 G2-8, V-EVAL3 :492). V-UNDO treats "a tunable that also feeds retention" as sabotage (:503). snapshot.json reports retention utility (:289). G4-4 (:328) appends no retention event while g is Promoted or Expired. So for the whole probation, SYNAPSE ranks from retention state that g could not have produced.

2. **The stamp still lands on g.** The stamp is the generation live at append (:341, checked by V-GENTAG :504). Every signal_attention through this path is therefore stamped g, for the whole probation: up to the 14-day ceiling (:333) and on through Expired, which has no time limit (:322).

3. **Consequences of the existing rulings.**
   - On rollback, R4(a) (RULINGS.md R4a; G4-5 :330) drops all of that attention from retention utility and attended_count.
   - V-LEAK (:497) also drops it from eval sets.
   - On adopt, the same events are credited to g in eval sets.

4. **What the paper says instead.** :293 calls the path "bounded" by the stamp and the hold. :343 says the misattribution window is only attention "just after a promote or rollback." For this path that sizing is wrong: the window is the entire probation. Nothing in §10 attack 3 (:688), O6 (:671) or O14 (:679) covers the source-independence case.

**Nuance.** If SYNAPSE also uses `query` results, which g does influence through the recall anchors, that share is correctly attributed. The finding holds for the snapshot.json path the paper itself names. R4a isn't reopened. This is a consequence the owner should know about, and it's the kind of material harm O14 asks for.
verdicts.better_fix:
The fix is right in substance: correct :293 and :343, size the harm in the paper, and raise it under O14. Three refinements:

1. **Gen-neutral marking can't travel through signal_attention.**
   - Its signature is locked (:341; ARCHITECTURE §2), and a new entry point would be a fifth op, which is forbidden.
   - So any "declared host-path source" has to be configuration outside the call, such as a per-handle or per-process setting, and must be tagged [P].
   - The paper should also say plainly that this splits the stamp semantics R4a was ruled on. That makes it an owner question, not a local change.

2. **Size the harm on two axes.**
   - **Rollback:** all of the path's attention for the probation, across the ceiling plus Expired with no time limit (:322), is lost from retention utility, attended_count and eval sets. Read the attended_count loss against the prune key (consolidation.py:54-55, 111-112).
   - **Adopt:** g receives eval-set credit for signal it didn't cause. That biases the next verdict toward g.

3. **Add a fixture and cross-reference O6.**
   - Add a V-GENTAG/V-LEAK fixture with a retention-ranked host during probation, so the effect is measured rather than argued.
   - Note in O6 (:671) that the recall fold keeps this attention while retention drops it. After a rollback, recall and retention then diverge for the whole probation.

all.title: Sizing on the prune key: after a held probation, attended_count alone decides delete vs consolidate, and one misattributed call can flip up to `limit` records. No V-check can detect it.
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md :343, V-UNDO :503, V-GENTAG :504, V-EXCL :524; consolidation.py:54-55, :110-119
all.claim:
Default protected_floor is 0.0 (api.py:332), and the maximum half-life is 24h (decay.py:34). Utility falls below 0.1 after log2(10) ≈ 3.32 half-lives, which is at most 3.3 days. With a 14-day ceiling, every unprotected record not attended in roughly the last 3.3 half-lives before the first post-rollback pass has u < 0.1. For those records the prune/stage split (consolidation.py:110-119) reduces to attended_count < 3 → delete from the ECS and vector index (:167-169), and ≥ 3 → stage to USD and become CONSOLIDATED (:174-186). One signal_attention call carries up to `limit` records (default 5, api.py:380; loop at :431).

Drop direction: R has c = 2 under g0. Seq m, host query under g0 returns R. Seq m+1, owner signs promote(g). Seq m+2, signal_attention({R: w}) is stamped g. Seq r, rollback(g) excludes it. At the first pass, c = 2 and u < 0.1, so R is pruned. A never-promoted run would have c = 3 and stage R.

Survive direction: during probation, g's recall surfaces R′ (c = 2) at seq r−1. Seq r, rollback(g). Seq r+1, the attention is stamped rollback(r) and kept. Now c = 3, and w also lifts u, so R′ stays volatile or is staged instead of pruned.

V-UNDO's pass condition, 'the same attention minus g's' (:503), V-GENTAG (:504) and V-EXCL (:524) all define 'g's attention' by the stamp, so all three pass on both interleavings. The paper names the window but no check sizes or catches it.
all.proposed_fix: Add a fixture, V-MISATTR, that injects late signals at ±δ around promote and rollback and reports how many records cross c = 3 and u = 0.1 against a ground truth tagged with the result's generation. State the expected flip count in the paper. Also consider a tagging rule ([P], no signature change): stamp = the generation live at (call time − δ_host), with δ declared in the constitution. This is a tagging-rule choice and doesn't change R4a.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute it. The code facts check out. deposit has protected_floor=0.0 (api.py:332). query has limit=5 (api.py:380). signal_attention appends one entry per weight in a loop (api.py:430-432). MAX_HALF_LIFE is 24h (decay.py:35, not :34). The prune and stage split is u<0.1 with c<3 to prune, and u<0.3 with c>=3 to stage (consolidation.py:54-57, 110-119). Prune is a hard ecs.remove plus vector_index.delete (:166-169). So for any record that has decayed below 0.1, attended_count alone decides delete versus consolidate, and a one-count shift flips the outcome. The 14-day ceiling (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:333) and the G4-4 hold (:328) let utility decay a long way before the first pass after rollback.

The paper names the window qualitatively (:343, :293) but never sizes it. Attack 3 (:688) explicitly asks for that sizing: "Size the effect on the prune key (consolidation.py:54-55, 111-112)." No answer is given anywhere. V-UNDO (:503), V-GENTAG (:504), V-EXCL (:524) and V-LEAK (:499) all define g's attention by the stamp. So both interleavings pass every listed check, as the finding says.

Two minor caveats. First, E4 (:56, :632) may turn prune into a tombstone, which makes the drop direction recoverable rather than a permanent delete. Second, the survive direction also needs w to lift u, which is true for any positive weight. Neither caveat removes the finding. "Major" is defensible because it is the undo guarantee (G4-5) that silently misses.
verdicts.better_fix:
Keep the V-MISATTR fixture: late signals at ±δ around promote and rollback, measured against a test-only ground truth tagged with the result's generation, reporting how many records cross c=3 at u<0.1 and u=0.1. State the bound in the paper alongside attack 3 (:688): at most `limit` records per call (api.py:380) times the number of host calls that land inside the window. Also say which direction is the irreversible one under v1 prune (drop) versus under E4 tombstones.

Drop the "stamp = generation live at (call time − δ_host)" proposal, or demote it to an open item. It does not close the window. It shifts the window: attention for results shown after the switch but sent within δ now gets the old generation. It also contradicts the fixed resolution J1-14 ("live at append", :799) and the V-GENTAG pass condition (:504), so it would reopen a settled row.

A cheaper mitigation that stays inside the rules and changes no signature: during the δ window after any rollback, the first post-rollback pass treats records whose attended_count was within ±1 of the threshold across the rollback seq as "hold, don't prune" for one pass. Alternatively, record it as a consequence the owner should know under R4a or O14, since the host echo is the only complete fix and that is a §9 escalation.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds. The paper names the window at BLUEPRINT_v7.md:343 and :293, and parks the echo as O14 (:679), which is gated "only if attack 3 shows material harm". It never sizes the window, though. §10 attack 3 (:688) asks for exactly this: "Construct an interleaving ... Size the effect on the prune key (consolidation.py:54-55, 111-112)." The finding is a direct answer to that open attack, not something the paper already handles.

Facts checked:
- `protected_floor` defaults to 0.0 (api.py:332).
- The maximum half-life is 24 h (decay.py:34). log2(10) ≈ 3.32 half-lives is about 3.3 days, well inside the 14-day ceiling (G4-7, :336).
- The prune and stage thresholds are u<0.1 / c<3 and u<0.3 / c≥3 (consolidation.py:54-57, :110-119). Prune deletes from both the ECS and the vector index (:167-169).
- In both interleavings, V-UNDO (:503), V-GENTAG (:504) and V-EXCL (:524) define "g's attention" by the stamp, so all three pass. That claim is correct.

One imprecision: "one signal_attention call carries up to `limit` records" is a host convention, not a code bound. `signal_attention(weights: Dict)` (api.py:420-437) loops over an unbounded dict. `limit=5` (api.py:380) bounds a query's results, not an attention call. So the per-call flip count can exceed `limit`, which makes the problem worse, not better. Severity major is reasonable. The flips are limited to records sitting exactly at the c=2/3 boundary with u<0.1, but a flip in the drop direction is an irreversible delete.
verdicts.better_fix:
The first half of the fix is right. Add V-MISATTR to the §5 table, with its target set to attack 3 / O14 and G4-5. It should inject attention at ±δ around promote and rollback, compare against a ground truth tagged with the generation of the served result, and report the number of records that cross c=3 at u<0.1 in each direction. Then state the expected flip bound in the paper, near :343. The bound is roughly the number of distinct entity_ids attended inside the window whose c is within 1 of 3 and whose u is below 0.1 at the first pass. Measure the window by entity_ids per signal_attention call, not by `limit`, since the dict is unbounded (api.py:431). That result is the evidence O14 is waiting on (:679).

The second half, the δ_host tagging rule, should not be offered as a drop-in [P] with no other changes:
(a) It only moves the window. Attention for results served just after promote, arriving within δ, now gets the old generation, so a mirrored misattribution remains.
(b) It puts a wall-clock lookup into seq-ordered stamping. That brings in the clock-source dependence attack 1 already raises (:686) and breaks the deterministic replay V-REPLAY relies on.
(c) It changes V-GENTAG's pass condition (:504, "live at its seq"), so it isn't a pure tagging-rule change.

If a mitigation is wanted short of the §9 echo, two options:
- Mark attention appended within a declared δ after any promote or rollback as ambiguous, and keep the G4-4 hold until the first post-rollback pass has resolved it.
- Make the drop direction non-destructive: during the first pass after a rollback, a record at c=2 with u<0.1 that the exclusion touched is kept volatile for one more pass instead of pruned.

Both choices belong to the owner and should be listed as options under O14, not adopted as [P].

all.title: Roll-forward is a signed pointer move that isn't in the G4 machine. Its attention can't be excluded and isn't held, and rolling back an Adopted generation doesn't exclude either.
all.claim: Exact contradiction. Roll-forward is a signed, pointer-moving self govern (:155, G4-2 :326) and a valid produced_under target (:174). But the G4 diagram has no roll-forward arrow, RolledBack has no exit (:317), and G4-1 says 'Only the arrows above exist' (:325). Either roll-forward is illegal, contradicting :155/:171/:174/:326, or it moves the pointer outside G4. In the second case: seq a, promote(g); seq b, rollback(g), so g is RolledBack; seq c, roll-forward restoring g's spec. No generation is in {Promoted, Expired}, so no hold applies (G4-4) and retention runs on the new attention. Attention is stamped roll-forward(c). If the owner later signs a rollback at seq d, G4-5 excludes only attention whose produced_under 'points to g' in state RolledBack (:330). roll-forward(c) is not a generation with a G4 state, so its attention survives. Separately, rolling back an Adopted g moves it to Retired (:319), not RolledBack, so G4-5 never fires. Yet J8 says unconditionally 'After rollback, the retention fold excludes that generation's attention' (:452).
all.proposed_fix: Bring roll-forward into G4 as a transition into Promoted (so the hold and probation apply), or define it as a new generation with its own machine. State that J8/G4-5 exclusion applies only to RolledBack, not to Retired, and change J8's wording to match. Both depend on O9.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute this finding. The paper contradicts itself in exactly the ways claimed.

**Roll-forward is in the signed set but not in G4.**
- It is a signed, pointer-moving self `govern` (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:155) and appears in G4-2's list of pointer-moving edges (:326).
- It is the source of a `restores` edge (:171) and a legal `produced_under` target (:174).
- Yet the G4 diagram (:307-319) has no roll-forward arrow, RolledBack has no exit (:317), and G4-1 says "Only the arrows above exist" (:325).

**A roll-forward generation can't be rolled back or excluded.**
- The `of` edge allows only promote or propose as the target of a rollback (:172), so a later rollback cannot target a roll-forward event.
- G4-5 excludes attention only when `produced_under` points to a generation in state RolledBack (:329-330). Attention stamped with a roll-forward event is never excluded.
- G4-4's hold covers only {Promoted, Expired} (:328), so it never applies to a roll-forward either.
- O9 (:674) only asks whether roll-forward belongs in the signed set. It says nothing about its lifecycle, so it does not cover this gap.

**Rolling back an Adopted generation excludes nothing.**
- Rolling back an Adopted generation leads to Retired (:319), not RolledBack, so G4-5 never fires.
- J8 (:452) and RULINGS.md:20 (R4a, "On rollback, the retention fold excludes attention tagged with the rolled-back generation") are both unconditional.
- So for an Adopted target, the paper as drawn falls short of the literal ruling.

**Where the proposed fix goes wrong.** The first half is sound: put roll-forward into G4, or model it as a new generation. The second half is not. Narrowing J8 and G4-5 to RolledBack only would take a side against R4a's literal wording. That is reopening a ruled item, which pass rules forbid. The paper should show the consequence and leave the choice to the owner.
verdicts.better_fix:
1. Bring roll-forward into G4. Either:
   - model it as a transition that creates a new generation entering Promoted, so G4-3 (one pending), G4-4 (hold), G4-7 (ceiling) and probation all apply; or
   - give its target its own row in the machine.

   Then widen the `of` edge (:172) so a later rollback can target a roll-forward. Without that, its attention can never be excluded.

2. Do not edit J8 to exclude Retired on the paper's own authority. R4a (RULINGS.md:20) applies on any rollback, so rolling back an Adopted generation is inside the ruling's literal text. Either:
   - redraw the Adopted→rollback arrow so it also triggers G4-5 exclusion and the reseal (after an adopt, the generation's attention is already in retention, so this undoes adopted effects); or
   - if exclusion is not wanted for Adopted targets, raise it as an open item to the owner, showing the consequence that R4a's literal wording is not met.

3. Add to V-UNDO and V-EXCL:
   - a fixture: promote, rollback, roll-forward, then rollback again;
   - a fixture: adopt, then rollback;
   - a sabotage: roll-forward attention survives the later rollback.

Steps 1 and 2 depend on O9 and on the owner's reading of R4a.

verdicts.reason: The finding holds against the text. Roll-forward is a signed, pointer-moving self govern in four places: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:155, :171 (restores), :174 (produced_under target) and G4-2 :326. But the G4 diagram (:307-320) has no roll-forward arrow, and RolledBack has no outgoing edge (:317). G4-1 (:325) says "Only the arrows above exist", so the paper contradicts itself. The paper never says which G4 state, if any, a roll-forward or a rollback event occupies when it acts as a produced_under target. G4-4's hold (:328) applies only to {Promoted, Expired}, and G4-5's exclusion (:329-331) only to a generation g in RolledBack. So attention stamped to a roll-forward event is neither held nor excludable. O9 (:674) covers only whether roll-forward is signed, not its place in the state machine, and T4 (:430) covers only byte-identical restore. Neither resolves this. The Adopted-to-Retired branch is also real: the arrow at :319 sends "a rollback (signed)" to Retired, not RolledBack, so G4-5 never fires. Meanwhile J8 (:452) and RULINGS.md:20 (R4a) say without condition that rollback excludes the rolled-back generation's attention. One more point the finding does not make: the same gap applies to attention stamped to a plain rollback or genesis event (:174), since neither is a G4 generation either.
verdicts.better_fix: Part 1 of the fix is sound: bring roll-forward into G4. That can be an edge RolledBack → Promoted, so the hold (G4-4) and the ceiling (G4-7) apply again. Or roll-forward can create a new generation g′ with its own machine, entered at Promoted. Either way, also state which G4 state a rollback event and a genesis event occupy when used as produced_under targets (:174). Part 2 should not be adopted as written. Narrowing J8 to RolledBack-only would quietly narrow ruling R4a (RULINGS.md:20), and R4a does not distinguish Adopted from Promoted. Instead, put the choice to the owner as a consequence of R4a, with two options. (a) Rolling back an Adopted g also triggers G4-5 exclusion and a reseal. Its attention already reached retention after adopt, so this needs a refold from the last seal before g's promote. (b) R4a is read as covering only pre-adopt rollback, and J8 is reworded to match. Until the owner decides, mark J8 and G4-5 as open on this point and cross-reference O9.

all.title: One pending generation bounds how many are in probation at once, not how long or how often. The excluded mass is unbounded while Expired.
all.claim: G4-3 limits {Promoted, Expired} to one generation. It doesn't bound how long attention accumulates under one stamp. At the ceiling, G4-7 appends expire, keeps retention held, and leaves Expired with signed exits only (:322, :335). If the owner is offline for T days after the ceiling, all attention for 14 + T days is stamped g, and a later rollback drops all of it from attended_count. At the first pass this mass-prunes every record whose third or later signal came in that span (see the prune-key sizing finding). The hold also blocks v1's pressure trigger, ecs.n ≥ MAX_ENTITIES = 10000 (consolidation.py:49, :89), so the volatile set grows without limit. Frequency isn't bounded either: nothing requires a cooldown between rollback and the next propose/promote, so N cycles open 2N boundary windows. The answer to the attack's question is no: one pending generation isn't enough.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:322, :327-339, :670; src/moneta/consolidation.py:49, :87-95
all.proposed_fix: Bound the Expired dwell time, or the attention mass under one stamp. Options: a hard second ceiling after which the O5 alternative applies, or excluded attention beyond the ceiling kept as gen-neutral. Add a minimum interval between rollback and the next promote. Decide whether the MAX_ENTITIES pressure pass may run prune-free during the hold. These are owner calls under O5.

verdicts.reason:
The paper does not already cover this, and the claim holds against the sources. G4-3 (:327) only limits how many generations can sit in {Promoted, Expired} at once. G4-7 (:333-339) appends `expire`, keeps retention held and raises an alarm. Expired has only signed exits (:322), so how long a generation stays Expired has no limit. Every attention event in that time is stamped with g (:341). G4-5 (:329-331) and V-UNDO (:503) then drop all of it from utility and `attended_count` on rollback. That `attended_count` feeds the v1 prune key (`consolidation.py:55`, `:111-112`), so the prune consequence is real. The size of the mass depends on how long the hold lasts.

Nothing in the paper mentions the size-pressure trigger, ECS growth or the volatile set during the hold. A grep for volatile, unbounded, MAX_ENTITIES and pressure finds nothing. J7 (:451) holds all sleep passes, while v1's `should_run` fires on `ecs.n >= max_entities` (`consolidation.py:49`, `:89`). That gap is real and unaddressed.

Nothing requires a cooldown between a rollback and the next propose/promote. The paper names the misattribution window at each boundary (:343) but never bounds how many boundaries can occur.

There is a partial counterpoint. O5 (:670) names auto-rollback as an alternative way to end probation, and pass1_rulings_brief.md:272 already flagged that the hold is "held without limit". So the indefinite hold is a known default choice, not a blind spot. But neither source states the consequences above, and RULINGS.md:22 (R4c) only requires a ceiling with a default. These are consequences the owner should know about, not a reopening of R4c.

The frequency point is the weakest part. Each promote is owner-signed (G4-2 :326), so how often cycles happen is already up to the owner. The 2N-windows argument is about exposure, not about losing control.
verdicts.better_fix:
Keep the fix scoped as consequences the owner should know under O5, without reopening R4c. Concretely:
(1) In G4-7 and O5, state that under hold-plus-alarm the time spent Expired has no limit. A rollback then drops every attention event stamped with g over the whole 14 + T days from `attended_count`. Give the owner bounded options: a second hard ceiling that falls back to auto-rollback, a cap on attention events stamped g, or treating attention after the ceiling as gen-neutral. Note that the gen-neutral option weakens G3-7 and V-LEAK.
(2) Add a line to J7/G4-4 saying what the `MAX_ENTITIES` pressure trigger (`consolidation.py:89`) does during the hold. Either the ECS grows without limit, or a prune-free pass that only stages may run. Either way it should be an X1 code ceiling with an alarm.
(3) Treat the cooldown as optional, and name it as limiting how many misattribution windows (:343) can open, not as a safety bound, because promote is already signed.
(4) Add a V-row covering a long Expired hold followed by rollback, so the prune delta is measured on a test store at mile 4.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute the finding. The paper raises these exact questions and leaves them open. Attack 3 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:688) asks "Is one pending generation enough to bound it?", and attack 7 (:692) asks how an indefinite Expired hold interacts with §15.2. Nothing in the paper answers either one.

What the paper says:
- G4-3 (:327) bounds how many generations can be pending at once. It sets no bound on time or on how often.
- G4-7 (:333-339) keeps the hold at the ceiling, with no second deadline.
- Expired has only owner-signed exits (:322).
- The `gen` stamp is "the generation live at append" (:341), so every attention event during Promoted and Expired is stamped g.
- G4-5 (:330) excludes all g-stamped attention from both utility and `attended_count` on rollback.
- The hold blocks whole sleep passes, not just retention events: J7 (:451) says "Sleep passes are held", and the V-HOLD fault is "a sleep pass during probation" (:502).
- So v1's pressure trigger `ecs.n >= self._max_entities` (consolidation.py:89, DEFAULT_MAX_ENTITIES=10000 at :49, ruling #5 / MONETA §2.6) cannot fire while a generation is held. That is a real collision with a locked v1 value, and the paper doesn't name it.
- Re-promotion is limited only by the ceiling refusal (:337) and the owner's signature. Nothing sets a cooldown after a rollback.

Two parts are overstated, but neither changes the conclusion:
1. "Mass-prunes every record whose third or later signal came in that span" is too strong. Prune needs both `utility < 0.1` AND `attended_count < 3` (consolidation.py:110-113), and applies only to VOLATILE rows (:108). Records still above 0.1 from earlier attention survive, and how many cross the line depends on λ. The direction of the effect is correct; the size is not established.
2. "Frequency isn't bounded" is true structurally, but every cycle needs an owner signature (G4-2, :326). So frequency is limited by the owner, not by the substrate. The 2N boundary windows still follow.

Severity major is justified. The hold blocking the pressure trigger is the strongest part of the finding and should be stated as a lock consequence, not left inside the prune argument.
verdicts.better_fix:
The direction is right and it correctly goes to the owner under O5. Four sharpenings:

(1) Report the MAX_ENTITIES collision as a consequence of a ruling. J7/G4-4 makes the locked pressure trigger (consolidation.py:89, ruling #5, MONETA §2.6) unable to fire during probation. Either list it in the lock-collision table (like E1-E4) for owner or §9 handling, or add a bounded relief valve to G4-4 and V-HOLD. One option: a pressure pass that stages but never prunes, and appends no retention event. That relief valve itself contradicts V-HOLD's fault definition (:502), so the owner has to rule on it rather than the paper adding it quietly.

(2) Don't propose making post-ceiling attention "gen-neutral". That rewrites R4a's "excludes every attention stamped g" (G4-5, :330), which is a ruled item. Instead, give attention appended while g is Expired its own stamp, (g, expired). Rollback excludes it by default, which keeps R4a literal, and the owner's signed rollback can choose to readmit it. This bounds the excluded mass under the plain g stamp to the ceiling window without reopening R4a.

(3) For dwell, use a hard second ceiling (for example, the X1 maximum) after which the O5 auto-rollback applies. Record it as an O5 sub-option, not a new mechanism.

(4) Add a rollback-to-promote cooldown to the constitution's `const` bounds (the G2 tier at :211 already holds the ceiling). Add a V-CEILING-style check for it.

Also fix the finding's prune wording: affected records are those that become `attended < 3` AND fall below `utility < 0.1` after exclusion. Do not say "every record".

all.title: Recall fold exclusion: the oracle order and the kernel seam skip excluded attention, but O6 says only retention excludes
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:282, :558 vs O6 :671
all.claim: Exact contradiction. The recall-fold oracle order says 'Attention whose produced_under generation is in the excluded set is skipped' (:282), and the fold_recall seam takes excluded_gens (:558). O6's default is 'retention only, as ruled' (:671). After a rollback, recall anchors and retention would then disagree on the same misattributed events, and the attack-3 window affects ranking or doesn't depending on which text an implementer follows.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:282, :558, :671; RULINGS.md R4(a)
all.proposed_fix: Make :282 and :558 conditional on O6, or change O6's default to 'both' and say so in the paper.

verdicts.reason:
The tension is real, but it is narrower than "exact contradiction." BLUEPRINT_v7.md:282 says, with no condition, that recall-fold attention whose produced_under generation is in "the excluded set" is skipped. The paper never says what that set holds for the live recall path. O6 (:671) defaults the recall fold to "retention only, as ruled", meaning live recall does not drop rolled-back attention. RULINGS.md R4(a) (RULINGS.md:20) covers the retention fold only. A reader of :282 alone would implement exclusion in live recall ranking, and that contradicts the O6 default.

Two points weaken the finding. First, the seam at :558 takes `excluded_gens` as a parameter, so it does not contradict O6 by itself: an empty set satisfies O6's default. Second, the paper has a separate reason to exclude in some fold calls. The referee "calls the fold oracle, because features carry raw attention" (:557). G3-7 (:298) and V-LEAK (:499) require that eval sets built after a rollback carry no attention stamped with the rolled-back generation. So the same fold oracle must exclude when the referee or eval builder calls it, and under the O6 default must not exclude when it computes live recall anchors. The paper never states this per-caller split. That gap is the real defect, and minor severity fits.

Nothing in the paper already resolves it: neither :282, :283, :524 (V-EXCL) nor :671 defines the recall-path excluded set.
verdicts.better_fix: The first half of the proposed fix (make :282 conditional on O6) points the right way but is incomplete. The second half (change O6's default to "both") would have Claude settle a decision the paper routes to the owner after attack 3 (:671), so drop it. Instead, edit :282 to say that `excluded_gens` is supplied by the caller. For the referee and eval-set builder, it is the set of rolled-back generations (required by G3-7 and V-LEAK, :298 and :499). For live recall anchors and ranking, it is empty under O6's default and becomes the rolled-back set only if the owner rules "both" on O6. Keep the `excluded_gens` parameter on the :558 seam and note there that it is caller-supplied. Add one line to O6 (:671) noting that, under the default, recall ranking and the eval and referee features disagree on the same misattributed events during the attack-3 window. The owner should know this when ruling. V-EXCL (:524) then tests the fold with the parameter set.

verdicts.reason: The contradiction is real, and nothing in the paper resolves it. At BLUEPRINT_v7.md:282 the recall-fold oracle order says, with no condition: "Attention whose produced_under generation is in the excluded set is skipped." The open-decisions table at :671 (O6) sets the default to "retention only, as ruled". That default matches RULINGS.md R4(a) (RULINGS.md:20), which binds only the retention fold. Nowhere does the paper say that recall's excluded set is empty under the O6 default. The fold_recall seam at :558 also lists V-UNDO and V-EXCL among its checks. V-EXCL (:524) asserts that "a fold with g excluded equals a fold of a journal in which g's attention was never written". Read with :558, that makes exclusion in the recall fold a tested behaviour, which contradicts O6's default. G3-7 and V-LEAK (:298, :499) cover only eval sets, so they don't settle the question. The attack-3 window text (:293, :343) also doesn't say which fold drops the attention. An implementer reading :282 would build exclusion into recall, and one reading :671 would not. One partial weakness in the finding: the excluded_gens parameter at :558 is not a contradiction by itself, because a caller can pass an empty set. The conflict comes from :282's unconditional wording plus the V-EXCL and V-UNDO checks listed for that seam. Severity minor is fair, and needs_owner=false is right because O6 already belongs to the owner. The fix only has to make the text agree with the default.
verdicts.better_fix: The first option (keep the default and make the text conditional) is right. The second option (change O6's default to "both") would quietly decide an owner-open item and goes past R4(a), so drop it. Concretely: (1) Change :282 to "Attention whose produced_under generation is in the recall excluded set is skipped. Under O6's default (retention only), that set is empty, so the recall fold sees rolled-back attention; only the retention fold (:283) and eval sets (G3-7) drop it." (2) Keep the excluded_gens parameter at :558, and note there that it receives the empty set unless O6 is ruled 'both'. (3) Mark V-EXCL's use on the fold_recall seam as conditional on O6. Note in the checks column at :558 that V-UNDO and V-EXCL there test the parameter's mechanics, and the retention fold's exclusion, not recall policy. Otherwise, move V-EXCL's recall instance to "if O6 = both".

all.title: A slot selection is resolved as a value but must obey authorization, and no rule decides which wins when they conflict
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md §G2, 'Two resolution rules' lines 223-225; G2-5 line 232; edges lines 219-220; C1/C4 lines 440,443; V-NARROW line 489
all.claim: Line 224 resolves slot selections by strength: the first opinion along stronger_than wins, and an ancestor's opinion is inherited when the child has none. Line 225 and G2-5 resolve scopes and exclusions by intersection, so a child only narrows. A slot selection names which claim (record) wins a slot (v6:74, v6:540). That makes it a value whose content must also satisfy an authorization. Counterexample 1, inherited leak: record r2 is in scope `private`. owner@P admits {public, private} and selects r2 as the winner of slot S. owner@C (parent P) narrows scopes to {public} and states nothing about S. By strength, Resolved(C).S = r2 (line 219: owner@C > owner@P). By intersection, r2 is not admissible in C. So Resolved(C) holds a value field that names a record its own authorization field excludes. Counterexample 2, re-admission by slot: owner@P excludes r3. owner@C selects r3 for S. Strength says C's selection wins. G2-5 says exclusions(C) ⊇ {r3}. G2-5 constrains only the scope and exclusion sets, not slot selections, so no invariant refuses this reload, and V-NARROW (line 489) tests only scopes. The paper never says whether the read returns r2/r3 (which leaks past C4), drops the slot, or falls back to another candidate. A fallback would be a third, filter-then-choose rule that is neither strength nor intersection. A write-time refusal can't fully work either: in Counterexample 1 the conflicting opinion is authored by the parent, and refusing the parent's reload because of a child's narrowing would invert the narrows edge.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:224 ('Values (recallHalfLife, slot selections, other scalars) resolve by strength'); :225 (authorization by intersection; 'A child can only remove what its parent admits'); :232 (G2-5 covers scopes and exclusions only); :219 (stronger_than order); :489 (V-NARROW sabotage covers only 'scopes resolved by strength'). inputs/BLUEPRINT_v6.md:74 ('which claim wins a slot'); :540 (Slot definition). src/moneta/ has no scopes, slots or contexts (a grep for scope|slot|context finds only unrelated hits in usd_target.py:9,19,295,311, decay.py:9,84, api.py:1,70,81,117,181,202), so all slot semantics are v5 [A]. Line 224 carries no tag.
all.proposed_fix: Make slot selections a third, explicit kind, a 'constrained value': a strength-resolved, ordered preference list whose effective winner is the first entry admitted by the context's intersected authorization (scopes(c), minus exclusions(c)), with a fallback stated in P5 order when no entry is admitted. Add G2-9: 'no Resolved slot winner lies outside the admitted set of its context.' Add V-SLOT with both counterexamples as sabotages (a slot inherited by strength past a child's narrowing; a child slot re-admitting a parent exclusion). Tag the slot semantics [A] (v5).

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds, and the paper does not resolve it. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:224 puts slot selections under strength resolution. Line 225 and G2-5 (:232) put scopes and exclusions under intersection. Nothing says how a strength-won slot selection interacts with the intersected admitted set. V-NARROW (:489) tests only scopes. RULINGS.md never mentions slots, narrowing or intersection, so no owner ruling covers this.

The paper only flags the question. §10 attack item 4 (:689) asks: "Is every policy field cleanly a value or an authorization? Slot selections depend on the caller's scopes (v6: [A])." That is an open invitation to attack, not a handling of the problem. This finding is a direct answer to it, which supports keeping it.

Two corrections to the claim:
(a) Calling the fallback "a third rule that is neither strength nor intersection" overstates the novelty. v6:95 (inputs/BLUEPRINT_v6.md:95) records that v5 already filters before it chooses: "records the caller may not see are removed before a slot's winner is picked [V, v5 code]". So filter-then-choose is v5 behaviour for caller scopes. The real gap is that v7's G2 never states this rule, and never extends it to context scopes and exclusions.
(b) Both counterexamples assume an owner's slot selection names a specific record id. The sources leave that open. v6:74 and :540 say only "which claim wins a slot", and pass1_rulings_brief.md:89 says "If slot selections ever list record ids". If a selection is a rule or ranking rather than a pinned id, Counterexample 1 is weaker, though Counterexample 2 still arises whenever a selection can name an excluded record.
Severity of major is reasonable: as written, a read could leak past C4 (:443).
verdicts.better_fix:
The direction is right, but the fix should be restated in four ways.

1. Do not call it a new third kind. State it as a composition of the two existing rules, applied at read time: the slot selection resolves by strength (G2 values), then the winner is chosen from candidates filtered by Admitted(c) ∩ caller scopes, minus exclusions(c). Cite v6:95 (v5 already does filter-then-choose for caller scopes) as [A; v6: V], and mark the extension to context authorization as [P].

2. Do not invent a P5-order fallback. State that when no admitted candidate exists, the slot resolves to empty or no-winner, unless v5 does something else, which is [A] and should go to the owner. Any "next candidate" ordering is a v5 behaviour question, not something to settle locally.

3. Add G2-9: "a read never returns a slot winner outside Admitted(c) ∩ caller scopes". Add V-SLOT with both counterexamples as sabotages.

4. Before choosing between a "preference list" and a "pinned id" model, ask the owner which shape a v5 slot selection has (record id, ordered list, or rule). That answers §10 item 4 (:689) and decides whether G2-7 (:234) byte-equality applies to the selection value, to the filtered winner, or to both. Keep needs_owner = true. The finding is the answer to attack item 4, so record it against :689 as well.

verdicts.reason:
The finding stands. The paper raises this exact question but never answers it. §10 'What to attack' item 4 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:689) asks: "Is every policy field cleanly a value or an authorization? Slot selections depend on the caller's scopes (v6: [A])." That is an open question, not a resolution. Line 224 still puts slot selections under strength, and nothing reconciles them with line 225 or G2-5 (line 232).

The other places the finding cites also leave it open:
- G2-5 constrains only scope and exclusion sets.
- V-NARROW (line 489) tests only scopes.
- C2/V-SELF (lines 441, 487) only stop the self tier from authoring slots. They say nothing about the owner-on-owner conflict in Counterexamples 1 and 2.
- RULINGS.md has no entry on slots, intersection or authorization, so no owner ruling is being reopened.

Both counterexamples follow mechanically from lines 219, 224, 225 and 232. Counterexample 1 is the stronger one: the parent authored the conflicting opinion, so a write-time refusal does not work.

One weakness: the finding presents filter-then-choose as a new 'third rule'. The paper's own primary source says v5 already does this for caller scopes. BLUEPRINT_v6.md:95 says "records the caller may not see are removed before a slot's winner is picked [V, v5 code]". So filtering before choosing is v5's existing read-time behavior, not an invention. That supports the finding's direction but changes how the fix should be framed.

Counterexample 1 also assumes a slot selection names a record id. Nothing in src/moneta/ can confirm or refute that. pass1_rulings_brief.md:89 ("if slot selections ever list record ids at scale") treats it as possible. Owner input is needed.
verdicts.better_fix:
Keep the fix's core: slot selections become a third kind, a strength-resolved preference with filter-then-choose at read time. Five amendments:

(1) Ground it in v5 rather than presenting it as new. Cite BLUEPRINT_v6.md:95 (v5 removes caller-invisible records before picking a slot winner, [V, v5 code] per v6). The context's intersected authorization, scopes(c) minus exclusions(c), is then filtered in exactly the way caller scopes already are. Tag whether v5 also filters by context scopes as [A].

(2) The admitted set must also intersect the caller's scopes from the QueryRecord (G3, line 249). The effective winner is therefore a read-time function of (Resolved(c,n), caller scopes), not a field of Resolved(c,n). Word G2-9 as: "the effective slot winner returned by a read lies in scopes(c) ∩ callerScopes, minus exclusions(c)". Do not word it as a property of Resolved alone.

(3) State the consequence for G2-7/C3 (line 234). USD may carry the strength-resolved preference as a value field, but the effective winner depends on the intersected authorization. Like authorization itself, it is computed only by the plain resolver and only displayed by USD (O3). Otherwise slots reintroduce the LIVRPS-cannot-intersect problem that line 225 removed.

(4) Fallback: when no preferred entry is admitted, the winner is the top admitted candidate under P5's total order (score desc, seq asc, record_id asc), which matches v5's pick-after-filter. If no candidate is admitted at all, the slot is empty. Say this explicitly.

(5) Add V-SLOT with both counterexamples as sabotages, plus a third: the caller-scope filter applied after choosing. Mark §10 item 4 (line 689) as answered by this change, pending owner confirmation of whether a slot selection names a record id or a rule.

all.title: A slot outcome depends on caller scopes, so it can't be a field of the prefix-pure Resolved(c,n), and G2-7 checks the wrong object
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md G2-1 line 228; line 224; G2-7 line 234; QueryRecord echo lines 247-249; P1 line 434; attack item 4 line 689
all.claim: v6 records that 'the caller's scopes even change slot outcomes, because records the caller may not see are removed before a slot's winner is picked' (v6:95). Caller scopes are a per-query input (P1, QueryRecord line 249), not journal content. G2-1 says Resolved(c, n) depends only on the journal prefix. So the slot winner a reader actually gets can't be a field of Resolved(c, n). Only an uncommitted preference can be, yet line 224 lists 'slot selections' as resolved value fields. Concrete case: context c, slot S, preference [r1 (scope A), r2 (scope B)]. Caller X (scopes {A, B}) gets r1. Caller Y (scopes {B}) gets r2. Both carry the same echo policy fingerprint (line 248). The plain and USD resolvers can be byte-identical on S (G2-7, V-C3 line 491) while the answers differ, so C3's agreement says nothing about the slot outcome readers receive. The USD layer 'displays' a winner (line 225) that is the answer for no caller in particular. Neither resolution rule computes the effective winner; it is computed by an unstated read-time step. So slot selection is 'both' in the attack's terms: a value in its storage and an authorization-dependent filter in its effect.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:228 (G2-1: 'depends only on the journal prefix to n'); :224; :234 (G2-7 'byte-identical value fields'); :247-249 (QueryRecord holds the echo {seq, time, context, policy fingerprint} and, separately, the caller's scopes); :434 (P1 lists scopes as a read input); :689 (the paper itself flags 'Slot selections depend on the caller's scopes (v6: [A])' but resolves nothing). inputs/BLUEPRINT_v6.md:95. pass1_rulings_brief.md:75 ('Caller scopes and context policy change slot outcomes and candidate pools').
all.proposed_fix: State in G2 that Resolved(c, n) holds slot preferences only. Define the effective winner as a pure read-time function winner(Resolved(c, n), scopes(c) ∩ callerScopes, P5 order), placed with the read (P1), not with policy resolution. Restrict G2-7/C3's claim to preferences, and add a replay check that the effective winner reproduces from QueryRecord's caller scopes. Fold this into the same G2-9 / V-SLOT as the previous finding.

verdicts.reason: The paper does not handle this, and the claim holds against the sources. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:224 lists "slot selections" as a Value field that resolves by strength. G2-1 (:228) makes Resolved(c, n) depend only on the journal prefix. G2-7 (:234) and V-C3 (:491) claim byte-identical value fields across the plain and USD resolvers. v6:95 says the caller's scopes change slot outcomes, because records the caller may not see are removed before the winner is picked. The paper treats that v5 fact as [A], which is correct since v5 code is unavailable. pass1_rulings_brief.md:75 repeats it. The caller's scopes are a per-read input (P1 :434; QueryRecord :249), not journal content. So the slot winner a caller actually receives is not a prefix-pure field of Resolved(c, n), and nothing in G2 or P1 names the read-time step that computes it. The only places slots appear are :224, :231 and C2 :441 (self can't author slots), V-SELF :487, and attack item 4 at :689. Item 4 raises the question but does not answer it, so the gap is open, not handled. No ruling in RULINGS.md covers slots. Agreement under C3 therefore leaves the effective winner unverified. Two callers with different scopes can get different winners under the same echo fingerprint (:248), while the USD display (:225) shows a winner that belongs to no particular caller. One caveat: the finding assumes a slot selection is an ordered preference list. The paper never defines its shape (see also pass1 brief :89, "if slot selections ever list record ids at scale"). Even if it is a single record id, the outcome is still caller-dependent (that id, or no winner), so the defect stands either way.
verdicts.better_fix: Accept the direction, with three adjustments. (1) Don't assume the preference-list shape. Have G2 define the stored slot field explicitly, as an ordered list of candidate record ids, and say what happens when no candidate is visible: an empty slot, or fall back to normal ranking. (2) Define winner(Resolved(c,n).slotPref, visibleTo(Resolved(c,n).scopes ∩ callerScopes, exclusions), P5 order) as a pure read-time step under P1. P1 already lists scopes as an input, so purity of the read is preserved, and G2-1 stays true because Resolved holds only the preference. (3) Restrict G2-7/V-C3 to preferences. Note at :225 that the USD layer shows the preference, not a winner. Add the replay assertion to the existing P2/V-REPLAY path, which already logs caller scopes in QueryRecord, rather than creating a new seam. Then mark attack item 4 (:689) as addressed by the new G2 clause, and point to v6:95 as the source of the scope-filter-before-pick order ([A], from v5).

verdicts.reason: I couldn't refute it. The paper doesn't handle this. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:224 puts "slot selections" among the value fields that resolve by strength, and G2-1 (:228) makes Resolved(c, n) depend only on the journal prefix. G2-7 (:234) and V-C3 (:491) check only that the two resolvers agree byte for byte on those fields. Meanwhile v6:95 says the caller's scopes "change slot outcomes, because records the caller may not see are removed before a slot's winner is picked". The pass-1 brief repeats that at pass1_rulings_brief.md:75. P1 (:434) and QueryRecord (:249) treat caller scopes as a per-query input that lives outside the journal. So the winner a reader actually gets is not in Resolved(c, n), and no G2 rule computes it. The paper's only response is to list the problem as open attack item 4 (:689), with no resolution. No ruling covers slot semantics: RULINGS.md has no slot entries, and the brief's :89 mention concerns only spec size. Three caveats on how the finding is put. First, the paper never says what a "slot selection" is. If it means the stored preference or opinion, which is the natural reading of v6:74, v6:157 and the glossary at v6:540, then line 224 is not wrong as written. In that case the defect is that the read-time winner step is unstated and untested, not a contradiction with G2-1. Second, line 225 says USD "displays" authorization, not a slot winner, so the finding misattributes "displays a winner" to that line. Third, the filtering semantics come from v5 and are tagged [A] in v6:95's lineage. Neither caveat removes the gap: G2-7/C3 agreement still says nothing about what readers receive, so the finding stands, though "major" may be one notch high for what is mainly an unspecified step rather than a contradiction.
verdicts.better_fix: Take the proposed fix with three adjustments. (1) Before restricting G2-7, define the term: in G2 or the glossary, say that a slot selection is a strength-resolved preference over candidate records. (2) Tag the filter step [A] (v5 semantics, v6:95), not [P]. Write the winner as winner(pref from Resolved(c, n), visible = records admitted by flattened scopes(c) ∩ QueryRecord.callerScopes and not excluded, tie-break P5). Name it as a P1 read-time step, and add it to G2-1's attack list: the winner is prefix-pure only given the caller's scopes. (3) Don't create a separate V-SLOT check. Extend V-REPLAY and P2 with a case where two callers with different scopes share one echo fingerprint and get different slot winners, each of which must reproduce from its QueryRecord. Seed the sabotage by computing the winner before scope filtering. Then mark attack item 4 (:689) as answered for slots.

all.title: G2-4 and C2 treat slot selections as authorization, contradicting line 224's value classification
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md G2-4 line 231; C2 line 441; V-SELF line 487; vs line 224
all.claim: G2-4 is titled 'Self can't author authorization' and lists 'scopes, exclusions or slot selections' as what self can't author. C2 and V-SELF ('a self proposal carrying a scope, exclusion, slot or non-open key is refused') group slots with the authorization fields. Line 224 puts slot selections under Values, and C1 says values are what self participates in (weakest). The paper therefore classifies the same field as a value in the resolution rule and as authorization in the self-tier rule. If slots were cleanly values, the open-names list would be the only thing keeping them from self, and adding a slot name to `rules`' open list would be legal. The paper itself treats exactly that kind of open-list widening as a sabotage (line 487, 'the open-names list extended to a scope key').
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:224, :231, :440, :441, :487; inputs/BLUEPRINT_v6.md:116 ('read-time values only'), :295 (C2).
all.proposed_fix: Rename G2-4 to 'Self authors open read-time scalars only'. State that slot selections are a constrained value (see the first finding), barred from self because they select among records, not because of the open list. Add 'a slot name on the open list' to V-SELF's sabotages.

verdicts.reason:
The textual inconsistency is real. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:224 puts "slot selections" under Values, which resolve by strength. G2-4 at :231 is titled "Self can't author authorization" and lists slot selections among the things self can't author. C2 (:441) and V-SELF (:487) group slots with scopes and exclusions. The paper does not resolve this tension anywhere. The closest it comes is §10 "What to attack" item 4 (:689), which asks whether every policy field is cleanly a value or an authorization and notes that slot outcomes depend on caller scopes (v6:95). That flags the classification as open, but it does not fix G2-4's title. The title is also loose in a second way: it lists "records" under authorization, and records are neither values nor authorization (v6:116 "read-time values only"; v6:295 C2 has no "authorization" framing at all). So the mislabel is new in v7.

The open-list point holds as well. G2-4's operative sentence says "may set only the names on the open list". Under :224's classification, that list is the only mechanism keeping slots away from self. V-SELF's sabotage column covers only "open-names list extended to a scope key" and not a slot name. RULINGS.md has no ruling on slots or the open list, so nothing already ruled is being reopened. Severity minor is correct.
verdicts.better_fix:
Keep the rename and the V-SELF addition. Do not settle how slot selections are classified in G2-4. The paper lists that classification as an open attack item (:689, §10 item 4), and the proposed fix depends on a separate finding ("see the first finding") that may not survive.

Concrete edits:
1. Retitle G2-4 to "Self authors only open-list values". Keep its body. Add one sentence: slot selections are excluded from self because they are not on the open list, and their value-versus-authorization status is open under §10 item 4.
2. In V-SELF (:487), extend the sabotage cell to: "the open-names list extended to a scope key or a slot name".
3. Optionally, add a parenthetical "(classification open, §10.4)" after "slot selections" on line 224, so the Values rule does not state the classification as settled.

If the owner later rules that slots are constrained or authorization-like, update :224 and G2-4 together at that point.

verdicts.reason:
The core inconsistency holds. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:224 lists "slot selections" under **Values** (resolved by strength), and :225 defines **Authorization** as "scopes, exclusions" only. But G2-4 at :231 is titled "Self can't author authorization" and puts slot selections in its forbidden list. C2 (:441) and V-SELF (:487) group slots with scopes and exclusions in the same way. So the paper calls one field a value in the resolution rule and authorization in the self-tier rule. v6 never made that classification: v6 C2 (inputs/BLUEPRINT_v6.md:295) forbids slot selections without calling them authorization. The "authorization" label is new in v7 and is not covered by any ruling.

Part of the finding overreaches. It says the open-names list would be "the only thing keeping them from self". That is not quite right. G2-4's second sentence is an explicit denylist ("can't author records, scopes, exclusions or slot selections"), and that sentence holds even if the open list is widened. So the self-authorship gap is not real today. What is real:
- **The title mislabels slots.**
- **V-SELF's sabotage covers only one case.** Its only sabotage, at :487, is "the open-names list extended to a scope key", so nothing tests the slot or exclusion case.

Severity "minor" is right.
verdicts.better_fix:
The rename and the added sabotage are right. Two other parts of the fix should not be adopted:
- **The phrase "constrained value (see the first finding)".** It depends on a different finding that may not be accepted.
- **The claim that slots are barred "not because of the open list".** The paper already bars them with G2-4's denylist, so the fix only needs to say that the denylist applies whatever the open list holds.

Minimal fix:
1. Retitle G2-4 (:231) to "Self authors only open read-time scalars."
2. Keep its denylist, and add: "This holds whatever the open list contains. Slot selections are values (line 224), but self can't author them because they choose among records."
3. Leave C2's wording at :441 as it is, since it matches v6 C2.
4. Extend V-SELF's sabotage column at :487 to: "the open-names list extended to a scope, exclusion or slot key."

all.title: The retention half-life and retention policy are a policy field that is neither a value, an authorization, a bound nor a pin
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md G2 tier table line 211; C5 line 444; G2-8 line 235
all.claim: The const row cites v6:114 for 'retention policy' and declares that const contributes 'no values', only bounds and pins checked at write. C5 repeats this. But v6:114 puts 'the retention policy and its half-life' in the constitution, and v6:118 says 'the thresholds and the retention half-life decide what a sleep pass tombstones'. Those are scalar values the retention fold consumes at the three evaluation points (G2-8), not bounds on some other tier's value. Under v7's taxonomy the retention half-life enters no Resolved, is not authorization, and is not a bound or pin. So it is a policy field that is 'neither', its resolution rule is unstated, and so is whether it is per-context or global. v1 keeps it as a single global DecayConfig (decay.py:34-35, 92). Without a stated rule, nothing says whether an owner@c layer may override it. If one can, it would be a value outside self's reach but resolved by strength, and it would change what is tombstoned, which is not pointer-reversible (v6:107-119).
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:211, :235, :444; inputs/BLUEPRINT_v6.md:114, :118-119; src/moneta/decay.py:34-35,92 (cited by the blueprint at :233).
all.proposed_fix: Add a fourth category to the G2 table and C5: 'const global write-time values (retention half-life, prune thresholds): one global value, no context layering, never in Resolved, changed only by a signed amend.' Add a check that no owner@c or self layer names a retention field.

verdicts.reason:
The finding stands. In the G2 table at BLUEPRINT_v7.md:211, `const` contributes "no values", only bounds and pins checked at write. C5 at :444 says the same thing: "`const` contributes bounds and pins, not values". The same :211 row lists "retention policy" as `const` content and cites BLUEPRINT_v6.md:114. That line puts "the retention policy and its half-life" in the constitution, and v6:118 says the thresholds and the retention half-life "decide what a sleep pass tombstones". A half-life is a scalar that the retention fold consumes. It is not a bound on another tier's value.

v7 does consume it as a value. At :283 the retention fold runs "under the owner's λ", and that phrase is itself ambiguous: it could mean an owner@c layer or a `const` amendment. Nothing in G2 says where that λ resolves. The values rule at :222 covers only the `stronger_than` chain (owner@c > … > self). The table also says owner@c contributes "values and authorization" (:213), and no invariant excludes retention fields from owner@c. G2-4 at :232 restricts only self. G2-6 at :233 covers only the recall-half-life bounds. G2-8 at :235 fixes when retention utility is evaluated, not where its λ comes from.

So the paper does not handle the case. A per-context owner λ would change what gets tombstoned, which v6:118-119 says is not pointer-reversible. The finding's description of v1 is accurate: λ is one global value set through `DecayConfig` (src/moneta/decay.py:34-35, 92). Severity "minor" fits, because this is a gap in the taxonomy, not a broken mechanism.
verdicts.better_fix:
The fix is mostly right, with one error. Grouping the "prune thresholds" with the half-life as `const` values "changed only by a signed amend" conflicts with the locked thresholds. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:632 and :737 cite consolidation.py:53-55: 0.1 and 3, "Locked Round 2". Making them owner-amendable would quietly reopen a Round 2 decision, which CLAUDE.md treats as a MONETA.md §9 trigger. It would also contradict E4's framing.

Revised fix:
(1) Add a fourth row or category to the G2 table at :211 and to C5 at :444: "`const` retention values: the retention half-life (λ_retention). One global value with no context layering. It never enters `Resolved(c, n)`, is consumed only by the retention fold at the three evaluation points (G2-8), and changes only by an owner-signed amendment. Changing it is not pointer-reversible and stays outside the loop (§4 the line)."
(2) State that the prune thresholds remain locked code constants (`consolidation.py:53-55`, Round 2), not `const` content. If v7 wants them amendable, list that as an open item for Round 4. Do not grant it implicitly.
(3) Replace "the owner's λ" at :283 with "the constitution's retention λ".
(4) Add an invariant, for example G2-9, and a check with a sabotage: no owner@c or self layer may name a retention field, and a `reload` that does so is refused before it is journaled. The sabotage is an owner@c layer that sets the retention half-life.
(5) Optionally, cross-check against G2-6: the recall-half-life bounds are decoupled from `DecayConfig`, but nothing says whether λ_retention keeps `DecayConfig`'s 60 s to 24 h range (decay.py:34-35). Say which it does.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute this. The finding holds as stated.

- **The const row contradicts its own source.** BLUEPRINT_v7.md:211 says const contributes "no values", only bounds and pins checked at write, and C5 at :444 repeats it. Yet the same row lists "retention policy" and cites BLUEPRINT_v6.md:114, which puts "the retention policy and its half-life" in the constitution. v6:118 says "the thresholds and the retention half-life decide what a sleep pass tombstones". Those are scalars the retention fold consumes. They are not bounds on another tier's value.
- **The paper names the scalar but never places it.** Line :283 says the retention fold runs "under the owner's λ". That phrase is ambiguous: it could mean a const value or an owner@c context value.
- **No rule says which.** The values rule at :224 resolves scalars by strength over owner@c and self. G2-4 at :231 stops only self from touching non-open names. G2-6 at :233 says only that "every self or owner value lies inside the constitution's bounds". Nothing forbids an owner@c layer from naming a retention λ or threshold, and nothing says the retention value is global rather than per context.
- **The sleep pass is global in v1.** It uses one DecayConfig (src/moneta/decay.py:30-35, :91-105) and module-level thresholds (src/moneta/consolidation.py:53-57). A per-context retention λ would therefore have no defined meaning for a store-wide sleep pass. It would also change which records are tombstoned, which a pointer move cannot undo (v6:118-119).
- **Nothing else covers it.** G2-8 (:235) and V-EVAL3 (:492) govern evaluation points only. V-BOUNDS (:488) checks only the recall λ.
- **Severity.** Minor is fair. It is an under-specification, not a contradiction in mechanism.
verdicts.better_fix:
The direction is right, but the fix needs four corrections.

1. **The prune and stage thresholds are not amendable.** They are locked Round 2 values: ARCHITECTURE.md §6 and src/moneta/consolidation.py:53-57 ("Locked Round 2 selection thresholds"). CLAUDE.md also bars re-opening Round 2 decisions. So "changed only by a signed amend" cannot apply to them. Split the new category as follows:
   - (a) the retention half-life / λ: one global const value, changeable only by a signed `amend`, and bounded by X1. The paper must also say whether v1's 60 s to 24 h DecayConfig range (decay.py:34-35) still bounds it. G2-6 decoupled that range only for the recall λ.
   - (b) the prune and stage thresholds: locked spec constants, recorded in the constitution as pins. Changing them needs a MONETA.md §9 escalation, not an `amend`.
2. **Reword the existing text, not just append to it.** The const cell at :211 and C5 at :444 should read: "no read-time values; bounds, pins and global write-time retention values". Also change :283 from "under the owner's λ" to "under the constitution's retention λ (global, never in `Resolved`)".
3. **Make the check a gate with a sabotage.** Extend G2-4/G2-6 into a new invariant: no owner@c or self layer may name a retention field, and a `reload` that does is refused at write. Add it to V-BOUNDS or a new V-RETAIN gate, with this sabotage: "an owner@c layer sets a retention λ and a sleep pass reads it".
4. **Flag the λ change itself as history-rewriting.** Under the v5 half-life call (O1), changing the retention λ by amend reinterprets past utility. It must therefore count as a held, journal-writing change that a pointer move cannot undo, not a read-time change.

all.title: Vectors have no authoritative home: they are neither in the journal nor in payloads/, yet the vector index is a disposable leaf
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md G1 node table L134; G3 derived leaves L262; G3-4 L296; §3 layout L375-378; V-LEAF L493
all.claim: `deposit` carries only a "vector digest" (L134). The layout names the journal as "the only authority" (L375). `payloads/` holds "record payloads" (L376), and `blobs/` holds referee, eval and label sets only (L377). The vector index is a derived G3 leaf (L262, L378). G3-4 and V-LEAF say that deleting every derived file changes no answer once the leaves are rebuilt. Counterexample: deposit 10k records, then `rm -r derived/`. The journal holds 10k vector digests and no vectors, so the index can't be rebuilt and every query loses its similarity term. v1 confirms that vectors live only in the index: USD deliberately doesn't store them (usd_target.py:78-82), and the only other copy is the snapshot (durability.py:91), which v7 demotes to a derived export leaf (L266). So either G3-4/V-LEAF are false, or the vector is a payload and the paper never says so. Attack 5's own question (L690) is left unanswered.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:134, :262, :266, :296, :375-378, :493, :690; src/moneta/usd_target.py:78-82; src/moneta/durability.py:89-91; src/moneta/api.py:328-331 (deposit takes payload and embedding)
all.proposed_fix: Declare the vector payload-class. Store its canonical bytes in `payloads/`, with a Q2 vector encoding (dim, f32 or f64 bit patterns, endianness) fixed so the digest is reproducible. Add a `commits` edge for the vector. Make V-LEAF's sabotage include "vector index rebuilt from a derived file rather than committed vectors". Then the erase, dedup, open and revector findings below apply to vectors too.

verdicts.reason:
I couldn't refute it. I checked every citation and each one holds.

**What the paper says**
- The `deposit` node carries only "record id, `H(payload)`, vector digest, scope, protected floor" (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:134).
- The only **commits** edge is `deposit` → `payloads/<sha>`, described as "the payload, by digest" (:178).
- G1-6 talks only about payloads (:191).
- The layout gives `payloads/` "record payloads" and `blobs/` only the referee, eval sets and label sets (:376-377). The vector index is a leaf under `derived/` (:262, :378).
- G3-4 (:296) and V-LEAF (:493) promise that deleting every derived file changes no answer once leaves are rebuilt.

**Where vectors appear elsewhere**
- The paper mentions vectors in only three other kinds of place:
  - the query-side "exact f64 embedding" in the host's `QueryRecord` (:250), which is a query vector, not a record vector;
  - `revector`, deferred "as in v5" (:138);
  - attack 5's unanswered "Is a vector a payload?" (:690).
- E1 (:301, :629) only moves authority from the index to the journal. It never says where the vectors themselves are kept.
- RULINGS.md and pass1_rulings_brief.md say nothing about record vectors.
- v6 defines a record as "payload, vector and provenance" (BLUEPRINT_v6.md:538). v7 committed the payload and left the vector out.

**v1 code**
- `usd_target.py:78-82`: USD deliberately doesn't store `semantic_vector`; the vector index is authoritative.
- `durability.py:91`: the snapshot holds the only other copy.
- `api.py:328-331`: `deposit` takes both a payload and an embedding.

**The gap.** The journal holds a digest of each vector and nothing anywhere holds the vector itself. So after `rm -r derived/`, the index can't be rebuilt from authorities, and G3-4 and V-LEAF are false as written. Severity critical stands, because this is the central disposability invariant.
verdicts.better_fix:
The fix points the right way: make the vector payload-class, give it a fixed Q2 encoding, add a commits edge, and extend the V-LEAF sabotage. It needs five additions.

1. **Revector.** A `revector` event (:138, :173) must also carry a new vector digest and its own **commits** edge. Otherwise the index still can't be rebuilt after an embedder swap.

2. **Embedder identity.** Put the embedder id and version and the vector dim in the digest's canonical input, or on `genesis`/`revector`. That way a rebuild can refuse vectors of mixed dimension.

3. **Erase.** State whether erase also removes the vector. Embeddings can be inverted to recover the text they came from, so the default should be yes. That means the `erase` event (:136) names the erased vector digest as well, and V-ERASE (:481) checks that both files are gone.

4. **Open cost.** Answer attack 5's open-cost question (:690). 10k separate vector files at open is the cost already listed at :197. Name a packing option, such as content-addressed segment packs, or accept the cost explicitly.

5. **The alternative.** The other option is to carry the vector inline in the `deposit` event. That keeps open fast, but then erase can't remove the vector without breaking the chain, which is the same trade-off that moved payloads out. The paper should say why it chose one over the other.

If E1 is ruled against, the index becomes a second authority (:301) and the problem disappears. Either way, add a G3 note that the index is built only from committed vector bytes.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:134 gives `deposit` only a "vector digest". The only content-commitment edge is **commits** (L177), which goes `deposit` → `payloads/<sha>` and is described as "the payload, by digest". G1-6 (L189) covers only "payload". The §3 layout gives no home for vectors: the journal is "the only authority" (L375), `payloads/` holds "record payloads" (L376), `blobs/` holds referee, eval and label sets (L377), and the vector index is listed under `derived/` (L378, also L262). The only place the paper stores an exact embedding is the host-owned QueryRecord (L250), and that is the query vector, not the deposited one. `revector` is left "as in v5 [A]" (L138), so the paper never says whether it carries vector bytes.
