It only adds an alarm and refuses new proposals. v6's explicit cost line ('memory grows without retention for as long as probation lasts', BLUEPRINT_v6.md:126) has no counterpart in v7's G4 or J7 (:451). X1 (:461) lists no ceiling on hot-tier size, journal tail or hold duration.

The paper does partially see the problem. Attack 7 (:692) asks 'How does an indefinite Expired hold interact with §15.2's rotation at 50k prims?' So it knows the Expired hold is indefinite, but it leaves this as an open question for reviewers. It states no cost and says nothing about the v1 pressure trigger. That weakens the finding's 'v7 has no counterpart' wording only slightly and does not refute it.

Two factual corrections to the finding:
1. v1's MAX_ENTITIES is a sleep-pass trigger, not a hard cap. `should_run` returns True at ecs.n >= 10000 (consolidation.py:87-90), and api.py contains no deposit refusal. So under a hold, deposits continue and the pressure trigger becomes a pass that is due but forbidden. Nothing forces a choice among refusing deposits, exceeding the cap or breaking the hold. The real problem is that the trigger is silently overridden with no defined behavior.
2. v7 carries attention as journal events, so the claim that the held pass is the only path draining the attention log is v1-specific. Hot-tier growth, the missing prune/stage, the WAL snapshot (api.py:466-469) and the growing unattested tail remain real.

Severity should probably be high rather than critical, since attack 7 shows the paper is aware of the indefinite hold. It still needs the owner's attention: R4c's ruled intent (pass1_rulings_brief.md:272, :300) was to fix 'held without limit', and the O5 default does not do that.
verdicts.better_fix:
Items 1, 2 and 4 of the proposed fix are right. Item 3 needs changing.

1. Restore v6's cost line in G4-4/G4-7. State that under the O5 default the ceiling is an alarm, not a bound, and that the hold lasts as long as the owner is absent. Add this to O5's row (:670) as the consequence the owner must weigh. R4c's intent (brief:272) is not met by the hold-plus-alarm default.

2. Do not adopt an auto-rollback X1 action unilaterally. O5 is explicitly reserved for the owner, and auto-rollback breaks J6 unless the owner carves it out. Instead, add an X1 resource ceiling: a maximum held wall time, hot-tier count or unattested-tail length. Give it a [U] value. Its action should be one the owner chooses in O5 from these three:
   (a) auto-rollback, carved out of J6
   (b) a held pass that only reduces attention and stages, never prunes. This is admissible only if it is shown to write no `retention` event, so G4-4 and V-HOLD still pass. Note that staging feeds §15.2's 50k sublayer rotation.
   (c) refusing `deposit` at the ceiling. This must be checked against X3: the deposit signature stays the same, but a new refusal mode may be a §9 issue.

3. In G4-4, state that the v1 pressure trigger (consolidation.py:87-90, MAX_ENTITIES = 10000) is overridden by the hold. Make that override visible as an alarm, not silent.

4. Add a V-check whose sabotage is 'hot tier grows past the X1 hold ceiling while Expired with no defined action', instead of the finding's 'deposits continue past the pressure cap'. MAX_ENTITIES is not a cap.

5. Fold attack 7 (:692) into this, so the 50k rotation interaction is answered alongside it.

all.title: Releasing the hold drains the backlog in one sleep pass, breaking §15.2 #2 and #3, and G3-8 claims the envelope with no check
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:299 (G3-8), :613 (§15.2 'Untouched'), :503 (V-UNDO 'first sleep pass after rollback'), :657 (mile 5)
all.claim: §15.2 #3 reads 'Maximum batch size per consolidation pass: 500 prims … at accumulated ≤ 50k' (ARCHITECTURE.md:273). #2 confines consolidation to idle windows over 5 s (:272). v1's pass loops every 500-prim batch inside one pass (consolidation.py:181-183), and that was tolerable with a steady drip of passes. A hold of 14 days or more turns the first pass after adopt or rollback into a bulk operation. It reduces 14 or more days of attention, classifies the whole accumulated volatile set, and stages every candidate in one pass. Counterexample: 6,000 stage candidates build up over a 20-day Expired hold. The release pass then makes 12 consecutive commit_staging calls, each with the planned ~131 ms p95 reader stall (ARCHITECTURE.md §15.2 #5), so about 1.6 s of stall in one pass. That is 12× the literal per-pass cap. The pass runs past the idle window into inference. Every prim also routes to the release day's `cortex_YYYY_MM_DD` sublayer (usd_target.py:157-160, :273-279), so 20 days of content lands in one daily layer and stays under 50k only by luck of volume. Rotation still fires per prim count (usd_target.py:276-279, :335), so the 50k cap itself holds; the batch and idle-window constraints are what break. G3-8 asserts the envelope `[V]`, but §5 has no V-check citing G3-8, so no harness would catch this. V-UNDO and mile 5 require exactly this post-release pass to run on a real store.
all.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:271-276; src/moneta/consolidation.py:172-185; src/moneta/usd_target.py:157-160, :267-282, :335; BLUEPRINT_v7.md:299, :503, :613, :657; grep of BLUEPRINT_v7.md for 'G3-8' finds only :299
all.proposed_fix: 1. Require the post-hold release to drain in passes of at most 500 prims each, every pass in its own idle window, so stage candidates carry over between passes (v1's dry-run path already leaves unstaged entities VOLATILE). 2. Add a V-ENVELOPE check citing G3-8. Its sabotage: a release pass after a held backlog authors more than 500 prims, or runs outside an idle window. 3. If the multi-pass drain changes which records prune, because utility keeps decaying between passes, list it with O7.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds, though one sub-claim needs a narrower wording.

Confirmed:
1. G4-4 / J7 hold all sleep passes while a generation is Promoted or Expired (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:328, :451).
2. G4-7 sets the ceiling at 14 days, and Expired can last indefinitely (:333).
3. v1 run_pass commits every stage_id in one pass, in a loop of 500-prim commits (consolidation.py:172-185).
4. The stage rule is utility < 0.3 and attended_count >= 3 (consolidation.py:115-119). Decay keeps running lazily during a hold, so stage candidates pile up. They also can never fall into the prune set, since prune needs attended < 3.
5. Routing uses the authored_at date of the release pass (usd_target.py:157-160, :273-279). Rotation still caps each layer at 50k.
6. A grep finds G3-8 only at :299, and no §5 V-check cites it, so its [V] tag has no harness behind it.
7. The paper does not handle this. Q7 (:692) only asks reviewers how an Expired hold interacts with rotation at 50k. It says nothing about the 500 batch or the idle window, and it is a question, not a mechanism.

Narrower wording needed:
- The '12x the literal per-pass cap' claim is overstated as a v7 regression. v1 already reads §15.2 #3 as a cap on each commit, not each pass. Its comment at consolidation.py:172 says so, and it already makes several commits in one pass whenever stage_ids > 500.
- What the hold adds is that this case becomes systematic and large. The idle-window break (#2) and the stall sum are the real consequences. A bigger stall budget inside one pass is the real exposure.
- The finding also misses that v1's should_run pressure trigger (MAX_ENTITIES, consolidation.py:88-95) is blocked by the hold. The ECS can therefore grow without bound during a long Expired hold. That makes the backlog worse.
verdicts.better_fix:
Keep the multi-pass drain and V-ENVELOPE, with these changes:

(a) State the cap per pass: at most 500 staged prims per pass, one pass per idle window. Keep the per-commit batching as it is. Prune stays uncapped, because it has no USD side (consolidation.py:166-169).

(b) Reword V-UNDO (:503) and the mile-5 exit (:657). They currently pin 'the first sleep pass after the rollback'. They should compare the whole post-release drain (or the classify output at the release time) with a never-promoted run. With a multi-pass drain, the first pass writes only a subset, so V-UNDO as written would fail or need a carve-out.

(c) Name what the hold does to the pressure trigger (MAX_ENTITIES, consolidation.py:88-95). Either allow prune-only passes during the hold, or record ECS growth as a bound under O7/Q7. Allowing prune-only passes is a G4-4/J7 matter, which is ruled, so it goes to the owner as a consequence and is not reopened here.

(d) Add to Q7 that a held backlog lands in the release day's cortex_YYYY_MM_DD layer (usd_target.py:157-160). Rotation still bounds that layer, but its date no longer tells you when the content was authored.

(e) The O7 note on drain order is minor. Carried-over stage candidates cannot become prune candidates (attended_count >= 3), so draining in several passes changes only when and in what order the USD writes happen, not which records prune.

verdicts.reason:
The paper does not handle this. The only nearby text is reviewer question 7 at BLUEPRINT_v7.md:692, which asks how an indefinite Expired hold interacts with §15.2's 50k rotation. It says nothing about the 500-prim batch or the >5 s idle window. Every other mention is an assertion with no check behind it: G3-8 at :299 and "Untouched" at :613. A grep finds G3-8 only at :299, and no §5 row cites it (V-HOLD at :502 and V-UNDO at :503 cover retention, not envelope). G4-4 at :328 and G4-7 at :333-337, with a 14-day default and an indefinite Expired state, hold every retention event, so the backlog and the single release pass are real. V-UNDO at :503 and mile 5 at :657 require that post-rollback pass on a real store.

Two caveats weaken the counterexample but do not refute it.
(a) v1 itself reads §15.2 #3 as a cap per `commit_staging` batch, not per pass. Its comment at consolidation.py:172 ties #3 to the inner loop at :181-183, so "12× the per-pass cap" is the literal ARCHITECTURE.md:273 reading, not v1's operative one. The stall-budget and idle-window breach still holds: 12 × ~131 ms runs well past a 5 s idle trigger's slack.
(b) v1 already breaks the idle-only rule through the pressure trigger. `should_run` fires on `ecs.n >= MAX_ENTITIES` (10k) regardless of idle (consolidation.py:88-90). The hold makes this worse: volatile entities keep building past 10k while every pressure-triggered pass is held. That is a second consequence the finding misses, namely ECS growth past MAX_ENTITIES during the hold.

The rotation-per-prim-count point (cap holds, content concentrates in one daily layer) is accurate and fits question 7.
verdicts.better_fix:
Keep all three parts, with these refinements.
(1) State which reading of §15.2 #3 v7 adopts: per commit batch, as v1 does at consolidation.py:172-183, or per pass, as ARCHITECTURE.md:273 literally says. If per commit batch, express the bound as a per-pass stall budget instead: at most N commit batches per idle window, with N derived from the ~131 ms p95 (§15.2 #5) and the idle slack. A literal 500-prims-per-pass rule is not something v1 meets either.
(2) The drained release must also cover the held pressure trigger. Add a G4-4 or G3-8 clause that says what happens when `ecs.n` exceeds MAX_ENTITIES under a hold: either deposits are still admitted and the overshoot is bounded under X1, or the overflow is named as an O-item. The release drain must run only in idle windows even when pressure is set. Otherwise the pressure trigger lets the drain run outside idle windows.
(3) Write V-ENVELOPE (citing G3-8 and G4-4) with two sabotages: a release pass that commits more than the per-pass budget, and a release pass that starts on the pressure trigger outside an idle window. Run it at mile 4 on a test store with a synthetic held backlog (for example, 6k stage candidates).
(4) Extend reviewer question 7 at :692 so it covers batch, idle and per-day-layer concentration, not only rotation.
(5) Under O7, note that the multi-pass drain plus continued decay between passes changes the prune set. V-UNDO's "exactly the retention events a never-promoted run would write" (:503) must then name the drain schedule as part of the pinned comparison. Otherwise V-UNDO becomes ill-defined.

all.title: `adopt` rests on no evidence, so the loop 'finishes' only by an unconditioned signature or by timeout
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:177 (evidence edge), :154 (adopt), :417 (step 8), :102 (principle 6), :333 (14-day default)
all.claim: Attack 7 asks whether the loop ever finishes anything. Mechanically it can, because nothing sets a minimum probation, so the owner may sign `adopt` one second after `promote`. But the paper defines nothing that probation measures. The **evidence** edge exists only on `propose` and `promote` (:177). Step 8 says only that 'the owner later signs adopt or rollback' (:417). No verdict leaf, tripwire or V-check feeds adopt. By principle 6, 'if it isn't an edge, it isn't enforced' (:102), so v7 cannot claim that adopt means anything. A solo owner therefore has two consistent behaviors, and both defeat the design. (a) Adopt at once, so probation is about 0 and the hold protects no window except the stamp-misattribution window (attack 3). R4a's undo then covers almost nothing. (b) Wait for an undefined signal until the ceiling, which leads into the unbounded Expired hold of finding 1. The 14-day value is `[P; value U]` and is derived from no measurement window, so the paper gives no reason to pick 14 days over 1. Throughput is bounded too: one Promoted-or-Expired at a time (G4-3), so at most one adoption per owner review-and-probation cycle. Mile 6 needs 'one proposer change promoted on held-out evidence' (:658) behind the same serial gate.
all.proposed_fix: 1. Define what probation measures, for example the recall verdict on queries logged under g's stamp against a counterfactual replay of the restored head. 2. Add an **evidence** edge from `adopt` to that verdict leaf. 3. Set a minimum probation (or minimum query count) alongside the ceiling, and derive the ceiling from the time needed to gather that evidence. 4. If no such measurement is wanted, say plainly that adopt is an owner judgement with no typed basis, and drop the probation-evidence framing.

verdicts.reason:
The core claim holds against the text. The `adopt` row (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:154) says only "It ends probation". The **evidence** edge is scoped to `govern{propose | promote}` (:177), and **of** is adopt's only edge (:172). Step 8 (:417) says only "The owner later signs `adopt` or `rollback`". G4-7 (:333) sets a 14-day ceiling `[P; value U]` but no minimum and no measurement window. Nothing anywhere names a verdict, tripwire or V-check that is gathered during probation or that feeds `adopt`. J5 (:449) says tripwires are never shown. V-STATE, V-HOLD and V-CEILING (:500-505) check only the structure of the transitions. Principle 6 (:102) is quoted correctly, and under it the paper can't claim that `adopt` rests on anything. Attack 7 (:692) explicitly asks whether the loop finishes anything, and the paper never answers it. RULINGS R4(b)/(c) require a signed adopt and a ceiling with a default. They don't say what probation measures, so the finding doesn't reopen a ruling. The pass-1 brief (pass1_rulings_brief.md:272) already flagged that "how long probation can safely last is [U]", and v7 still doesn't derive it.

Two parts are overstated, and neither refutes the finding. (1) Mile 6 (:658) promotes a *proposer* change in the rules tier. Per the govern.why table (:157), the rules tier changes through `amend`, not through the self-tier G4 machine. So the "same serial gate" throughput claim for mile 6 isn't shown. G4-3's one-pending limit applies only to self generations. (2) The two-behaviour dilemma assumes the owner has no out-of-band judgement. The real defect is narrower: the paper gives that judgement no typed basis and no stated window.
verdicts.better_fix:
Options 1 to 3 are the right shape but add a new mechanism (counterfactual replay of the restored head). That needs its own oracle and V-check, and it widens pass-2 scope. The minimal correct fix has three parts.

(a) Add **evidence** to adopt: `govern{adopt}` → a probation verdict leaf. Define that leaf as the G3 verdict recomputed on the held-out window over queries whose **produced_under** is g, compared with the pre-promote verdict already named by promote's evidence edge. This reuses the existing referee and eval-set builder, with no counterfactual replay.

(b) Add a minimum-evidence floor (a minimum query count under g, `[P; value U]`) next to the ceiling. Add a V-check: an adopt with no probation-verdict evidence edge, or one below the floor, is refused.

(c) If the owner declines (a) and (b), state in G4 and step 8 that adopt is untyped owner judgement, per principle 6. Answer attack 7 explicitly in that case.

Either way, take the mile-6 throughput point out of the finding, or rephrase it. Mile 6 goes through `amend` on the rules tier, not through G4.

verdicts.reason: The core claim holds. In BLUEPRINT_v7.md the **evidence** edge exists only on govern{propose|promote} (:177). Probation step 8 says only "the owner later signs adopt or rollback" (:417). The adopt row says only "It ends probation" (:154). G4-7 sets a 14-day default tagged [P; value U] with no derivation (:333), and no minimum probation appears anywhere: grep for minimum/probation turns up nothing. No V-check gives adopt a basis. V-STATE (:500), V-SIGSET (:483) and V-CEILING (:505) check only legality, signature and the ceiling. So the paper does not answer what probation measures. Three parts of the finding are overstated. (1) Principle 6 (:102) is not violated. v7 never claims that adopt rests on evidence, and that principle only stops it from making such a claim. The gap is an unstated purpose, not a broken invariant. (2) The source frames adopt as an owner act, not a measured verdict. BLUEPRINT_v6.md:124 says "Adoption is the owner's act, so retention effects after it fall on the owner's side of the line." BLUEPRINT_v6.md:520 says the hold exists so that loop-induced attention cannot reach retention without the owner's act. Under that framing an immediate adopt does not "defeat the design": it moves responsibility to the owner, as intended. What v7 lacks is any statement of this rationale, or of what the owner should look at before adopting. (3) The throughput point is a consequence of R4c (RULINGS.md:22, G4-3 :327), which is ruled. Mile 6 (:658) requires a proposer change "promoted on held-out evidence", and promote already carries evidence. Mile 6 does not require adopt, so the serial gate slows mile 6 but does not block it. Severity is closer to moderate than major. It still needs the owner, because the paper should say whether probation is a measurement window or a liability-transfer hold. Note that v6 itself flagged the probation length as unknown (BLUEPRINT_v6.md:126, :494).
verdicts.better_fix: Steps 1–3 of the proposed fix overreach. A counterfactual replay of the restored head on probation queries amounts to a new eval channel. It would wear the held-out window under R4(d) (RULINGS.md:23), and it reverses v6's framing of adopt as an owner act (BLUEPRINT_v6.md:124). Step 4 is closest to right, but it should not drop the probation framing. Recommended fix: (a) In G4/step 8 (:417) and the adopt row (:154), state that adopt is an owner judgement whose purpose is to transfer responsibility for retention effects (citing BLUEPRINT_v6.md:124 and :520), and that it has no typed evidence basis by design. (b) Add an optional **evidence** edge from adopt to the probation tripwire leaves and to the `disclose` events the owner viewed, so that what the owner saw is recorded under principle 6 (:102) without becoming a gate. Any held-out figure shown stays pass/fail under R4(d). (c) Derive the ceiling default from what probation actually costs, which is memory growth with retention held (BLUEPRINT_v6.md:126, :494). Do not derive it from a measurement window. Record the 14-day value as unjustified pending that measurement. (d) Make a minimum probation an explicit constitution value, which may be 0, and send it to the owner as a new open item next to O5 (:670). Also record that one pending generation (R4c) caps adoptions at one per review cycle. That cap is a known consequence of the ruling and is not to be reopened.

all.title: A Proposed generation scored against a Promoted head can be promoted after that head is rolled back, on stale margin evidence
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:327 (G4-3), :413-416 (tuning steps 4-7), :162 (signed body binds genesis + `of` seq only)
all.claim: G4-3 lets one generation be Proposed while another is Promoted. The tuning pass scores 'the candidate and the head' (:413), and while g1 is Promoted the head is g1's values. The promote signature binds the genesis hash and the `of` seq of the proposal (:162). No invariant requires that the pointer at promote time equal the head the evidence was scored against. Counterexample: g1 is Promoted. The tuner proposes g2 and gets a margin against g1. The owner rolls back g1, which restores the pre-g1 values. The owner then signs promote of g2. The evidence edge points to a verdict comparing g2 against values no longer live, so the margin rule (step 5) was never checked against the actual head. V-STATE, V-PENDING and V-SIGSET all pass. This is the normal path for a solo owner who batches reviews: rollback and promote in one sitting.
all.proposed_fix: 1. Add the head generation to the `propose` evidence. 2. Refuse `promote` when the current pointer differs from that head. 3. Alternatively, make any pointer move (rollback, adopt or roll-forward) auto-`withdraw` an outstanding Proposed. 4. Add a V-PENDING or V-STATE sabotage: promote a proposal scored against a rolled-back head.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds against the paper. G4-3 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:327) allows one Proposed alongside one generation in {Promoted, Expired}. The only refusal of new proposals is at the ceiling (G4-7, :331-337). Tuning step 4 (:413) scores 'the candidate and the head', and step 6 (:415) checks only G4-3. V-PENDING (:501) refuses a second promote while one is pending. So to promote g2 the owner is forced to end g1 first, by adopt or rollback. Adopt leaves the values unchanged (the table at :155 says adopt does not move the pointer). Rollback and roll-forward do change them (:156). Nothing makes a pointer move invalidate an outstanding Proposed:
- `withdraw` exists only for 'declined or replaced by a newer proposal' (:152).
- The `of` edge (:172) and the signed body (:162) bind the proposal's own seq and the genesis hash, not the head it was scored against.
- The `evidence` edge (:177) names the verdict leaf, but no invariant compares that verdict's baseline with the live self generation at promote time.
- V-STATE (:500), V-PENDING (:501) and V-GENTAG (:504) have no sabotage covering this.

It is worse than stale margin evidence. The tuner's output is `{"tier":"self","set":{name:number}}` (:412), a set of named values. If it is not a full spec, then promoting it over the rolled-back head yields a resolved policy that was never scored at all. Nothing in RULINGS.md or pass1_rulings_brief.md addresses this, and the J-ledger fixes (:791, :806) cover withdraw-as-edge and stale checkpoints, not stale proposals. So refuted=false.

Fix: points 1, 2 and 4 are right. Point 3 has a factual slip. It lists `adopt` as a pointer move, but :155 says adopt moves nothing. Auto-withdrawing on adopt would also throw away valid evidence, since the head's values are unchanged. Also, binding the head only in the unsigned `propose` evidence leaves the owner's signature not covering the baseline the owner reviewed.
verdicts.better_fix:
1. Add a `base` edge from `govern{propose}` to the self `govern` (promote, genesis, rollback or roll-forward) live at propose time. This is the generation the referee scored as 'the head' in step 4. Also record the base seq in the verdict leaf's `built_from`.
2. Put the base seq in the signed `promote` body next to the genesis hash and the `of` seq (:162), so the owner's signature covers the comparison the owner reviewed.
3. Add a G4 invariant (e.g. G4-8 'Fresh base'): the substrate refuses `promote` unless the live self generation at that seq equals the proposal's `base`.
4. Also, on rollback or roll-forward only (not adopt, which leaves the values unchanged per :155), have the substrate append an unsigned `withdraw` of any outstanding Proposed, with `of` pointing at it. Widen the `withdraw` description at :152 to cover 'its base was displaced', and note in V-WRITE (:484) that this withdraw is substrate-appended.
5. Add a sabotage to V-STATE: promote a proposal whose base was rolled back between propose and promote. Add a sabotage to V-GENTAG or the new invariant's check: the base taken from the last proposed generation rather than the live one.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute the finding. The paper does not handle the case and the claim is accurate.

(1) G4-3 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:327) allows one Proposed alongside one in {Promoted, Expired}. V-CEILING (:509) refuses proposals only at Expired, not while Promoted. So the tuning pass can propose g2 while g1 is Promoted.

(2) Step 4 (:413) scores "the candidate and the head", and while g1 is Promoted the head is g1. Nothing records which generation was the head. The evidence edge (:177) points only to the verdict, eval-set and referee leaves.

(3) The signed body binds only the genesis hash and the `of`/`restores` seq (:162). That makes it replay-proof but not proof against a stale baseline.

(4) V-PENDING (:500) refuses a second promote only while a generation is in {Promoted, Expired}. That actually forces the scenario: g2 can be promoted only after g1 is adopted or rolled back. Adopt is harmless because the head values are unchanged. Rollback is the failing path: the margin from step 5 was measured against g1, not against the restored pre-g1 values.

(5) It gets worse. The tuner returns a sparse `{"set":{name:number}}` (:412). If promote applies that to whatever head is live, the config that goes live after a rollback is not the config the referee scored. The margin is stale, and so is the candidate.

(6) Nothing in RULINGS.md R4 (lines 18-23) addresses this, so the finding does not reopen a ruled item. It strengthens R4(c) "one pending".

Neither V-STATE, V-PENDING nor V-SIGSET catches it. Severity "major" is fair: it is the normal path for a solo owner who reviews in batches.
verdicts.better_fix:
Use fix 1 plus fix 2 as the main fix, and tighten them.

(a) Put `base: seq of the self govern live at scoring` inside the canonical `propose` body, as a typed edge (e.g. `scored_against` → promote/genesis/rollback/roll-forward). Also record the full resolved spec the referee scored, not the sparse delta. Then promote installs exactly that spec.

(b) Copy `base` into the signed `promote` body. The owner's signature then covers it, and the review in step 7 shows it.

(c) Refuse `promote` when the live self generation's seq differs from `base`. Comparing seqs rather than values is fine: after an adopt the live seq is unchanged, so an adopt does not falsely block.

(d) Make fix 3 targeted rather than blanket. On rollback or roll-forward, the substrate appends `withdraw` for any Proposed whose `base` is no longer live. Adopt does not trigger it. This keeps G4-3's "Proposed alongside Promoted" useful.

(e) Add sabotages:
- V-STATE: a promote whose `base` ≠ live head after a rollback.
- V-STATE: a promote that applies a sparse set over a different head.
- G1-3: `base` must target a self govern of a lower seq.

Note the effect on G1's edge table at :170-180, which gains the new edge.

all.title: V-POOL demands exact top-k equality against a read path the paper itself says agrees only within delta
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:517 (V-POOL), :519 (V-EXP), :551-552 (Two consequences), :556 (referee EvalBuf carries precomputed `cos f64`), :559 (arm P is the default scan)
all.claim: V-POOL passes only if, for random in-bounds values, the referee's top k equals the read path's exactly. The referee scores from a `cos f64` frozen in its EvalBuf (:556). The v7 read path scores with arm P (numpy), and Consequence 2 (:552) says arm P 'sums dot products in BLAS order, which differs from v1's left-to-right loop', so δ is the default there. Consequence 1 (:551) also says only that the read path 'should' call the kernel exp, and v1's read path uses `math.exp` (decay.py:68). Counterexample: two pool records with equal stored utility whose cosines differ by 1 ulp under the loop order (the one the EvalBuf was built with) and tie or reverse under BLAS order. The referee and arm P then rank them differently, so V-POOL fails even though no bug exists. The same happens when one record's utility differs by 1 ulp between the kernel exp and `math.exp`. V-ORACLE-SCAN (:525) already handles exactly this case with a 'within δ → total order' clause. V-POOL does not, so the two checks contradict each other on the same pair of paths.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:517 'the referee's top k equals the read path's'; :552 'Arm P (numpy) sums dot products in BLAS order ... V-ORACLE-SCAN states its pass condition under δ from the start'; :556 pool rows '(record_seq, cos f64, ...)'; :551 'The read path should call the same kernel exp'; src/moneta/decay.py:68 `math.exp`; src/moneta/vector_index.py:160-162 left-to-right loop; src/moneta/api.py:414 `max(cos,0) × U`
all.proposed_fix: Pick one of two. (a) Make V-POOL compare the referee with a read-path oracle that uses the same `cos` bits as the EvalBuf (the stored cosines) and the kernel exp. Then exact equality is legitimate. (b) Give V-POOL the same pass condition as V-ORACLE-SCAN: top-k identical except pairs whose scores lie within δ, which are ordered by Q1. Separately, change 'should' at :551 to 'must', or V-EXP (:519) cannot be met by a read path that still calls `math.exp`.

verdicts.reason: The paper does not handle this. V-POOL (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:517) requires the referee's top k to equal the read path's exactly, with no δ clause. The referee scores from a frozen `cos f64` in the EvalBuf pool rows (:556). The paper never says where those cosine bits come from, or which scan (the v1 loop, arm P/numpy, or moneta-scan) the comparison read path uses. Meanwhile :552 says arm P's BLAS-order sums differ from v1's left-to-right loop (vector_index.py:160-162), and makes δ the default for exactly this seam. V-ORACLE-SCAN (:525) carries a 'within δ → total order' clause. V-POOL compares against the same read path and carries none. So a 1-ulp cosine difference between near-equal records can flip an order and fail V-POOL when there is no bug, and the two checks are inconsistent. The exp half of the finding is weaker but still right. V-EXP (:519) already demands bit-equal utilities by default, so an exp mismatch would also fail V-EXP; V-POOL would not be the only check to catch it. Even so, :551 says only 'should' while V-EXP assumes 'must', and v1's read path uses math.exp (decay.py:68). Those two statements do conflict. The finding is factually correct, and nothing in the paper, RULINGS.md or the pass-1 rulings brief resolves it.
verdicts.better_fix: Use (a) first. Judging by its mutants (bounds taken at one corner, the clamp removed; :517), V-POOL exists to test pool coverage under candidate values, not scan arithmetic. Running the read-path side over the same frozen cosine bits isolates that property, and V-ORACLE-SCAN already covers the scan's rounding. (a) also needs one added sentence: the EvalBuf `cos f64` is the value the logged read path actually computed at build time (logged under P2), not a recomputation. Without that sentence the bit identity behind (a) is still unspecified. If (a) is rejected, (b) works, but its δ must be the X1 δ and the clause should be worded exactly as V-ORACLE-SCAN's. Separately, change 'should' to 'must' at :551, or else state that V-EXP compares the referee against the kernel-exp read path only, so the v1 math.exp path is never measured.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute this. V-POOL (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:517) still requires exact top-k equality: "the referee's top k equals the read path's". Nothing in it covers ties within δ.

The paper's own premises create the conflict:
- The referee ranks from cosines frozen in EvalBuf pool rows (`cos f64`, :556).
- The read path's scan is arm P (numpy) by default (:559, SM4 :467). Consequence 2 (:552) says arm P sums in BLAS order, unlike v1's left-to-right loop (vector_index.py:160-162), and makes δ "the default" for the scan.
- Two records with equal stored utility whose cosines differ by about 1 ulp between the two summation orders can therefore swap rank. V-POOL fails with no bug present.

V-ORACLE-SCAN (:525) covers exactly this case with "identical except pairs within δ, ordered by the total order".

The change log shows the omission was not deliberate. J1-8 (:793) says the δ clause was applied "wherever δ applies" and lists only V-ORACLE-SCAN and V-EXP. V-POOL compares the same scan output and was missed.

The exp half of the finding is weaker but still holds. V-EXP (:519) already requires bit-exact utilities between the referee and the read path, which in effect forces the kernel exp. Still, :551 says only "should", and v1 uses `math.exp` (decay.py:68). Tightening "should" to "must" is a consistency fix, not a new requirement.

No ruling I saw closes this. pass1_rulings_brief.md:394 only keeps the scan under D1 with arm P first, which supports the finding's premise.
verdicts.better_fix:
Use option (b) only: give V-POOL the same pass condition as V-ORACLE-SCAN and J1-8, "top k identical except pairs whose scores lie within δ, which must be ordered by the total order `(seq, record_id)`". Add V-POOL to J1-8's list at :793.

Reject option (a). V-POOL exists to show that the referee ranks the way the real read path ranks (P2). An oracle that reuses the EvalBuf cosine bits would test the referee against itself and could no longer catch a real divergence in the read path.

Separately, change "should" to "must" at :551 so it matches V-EXP's bit-exact default, and say that the read path's utility comes from the kernel exp port, not `math.exp`. If the utility half of V-POOL should stay bit-exact, state that the δ exemption applies only to the cosine factor, not to U.

all.title: 'Identical f64 bits' fails on non-finite results: NaN sign and payload depend on how the NaN arose and on the runtime
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:556 ('A non-finite result means reject'; gate: 'two runtimes on Windows and Linux return the same f64 bits'), :521 (V-ORACLE-REF), :516 (V-REPLAY), :583 (Q2 floats as IEEE-754 bit patterns), :558 (fold oracle ports decay.py:66-69)
all.claim: The paper allows a non-finite score ('means reject') but compares raw `f64` bits across the Python oracle, native and wasm32, and across Windows and Linux runtimes. Measured on this machine (CPython, x86-64): `float('inf')*0.0` and `inf-inf` give 0xfff8000000000000, but `float('nan')` gives 0x7ff8000000000000. So the Python oracle's NaN bits depend on how the NaN was produced. On aarch64 hosts, hardware default NaNs are positive (0x7ff8...). The wasm spec makes the sign and payload of arithmetic NaNs nondeterministic unless the runtime canonicalizes them (Cranelift NaN canonicalization is opt-in). So V-ORACLE-REF, the mile-4 two-runtime gate, and V-REPLAY ('bit for bit'), if the verdict leaf records the score, can each fail or flake on any fixture that drives the score non-finite. The mutation-style fixtures need exactly those inputs. Inputs have a related gap: Q2 serializes floats as bit patterns, so NaN or inf timestamps and utilities are representable in the journal, and the paper sets no policy for them in the fold. decay.py:66-69 maps a NaN dt to `protected_floor`, because `NaN < 0.0` and `NaN > floor` are both false. The idiomatic Rust `dt.max(0.0)` maps NaN dt to 0, so `exp(0)=1` and the result is `utility`. One natural line of the port diverges from the oracle, and only a NaN fixture would catch it.
all.evidence: Local run: `struct.pack('>d', float('inf')*0.0).hex()` = fff8000000000000; `float('nan')` = 7ff8000000000000. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:556, :521, :516, :583; src/moneta/decay.py:65-69
all.proposed_fix: Make the comparison domain explicit. Seams canonicalize every non-finite output to one class code before return, or before journaling, for example a reject tag rather than raw NaN bits. Bit-equality is required only on finite results. Enable NaN canonicalization in the wasm runtime config. Have the G1 codec reject non-finite floats at append, or else define the fold's handling of NaN and inf. Add NaN, ±inf and -0.0 inputs to the shared fixtures, so a `max`/`min` idiom in the Rust port that differs from decay.py:66-69 fails V-ORACLE-FOLD.

verdicts.better_fix:
The proposed fix is right in substance. I would tighten its order and scope as follows:

1. **Reject at append.** The G1 codec and L2 should refuse any non-finite float in every journaled float field: attention t and w, floor, u0, and bounds. Do this at append, alongside the existing L2 "finite" rule, so the fold never sees NaN or inf from the journal.

2. **One rule at every float-returning seam.** In Rust (native and wasm) and in the Python oracle, map any non-finite result to a single canonical reject code before return. One way is a fixed sentinel bit pattern; better is a separate verdict tag. The bit-for-bit clauses in V-ORACLE-REF, V-EXP, V-ORACLE-FOLD and the mile-4 two-runtime gate then apply only to finite outputs, plus reject-code equality. V-REPLAY compares the verdict class, not the NaN bits. This rule alone settles the cross-runtime problem.

3. **Also turn on Wasmtime's cranelift_nan_canonicalization.** It is defense in depth, not the primary fix. It does not help the Python side, whose NaN bits depend on how the NaN arose.

4. **Fix the fold semantics for Q3 time arguments.** Specify that a non-finite `now` or `t` is rejected at the seam boundary. Do not leave it to whichever `max`/`min` idiom each implementation happens to use.

5. **Add fixtures.** Include NaN, ±inf, -0.0 and subnormal inputs, plus a 0/0 metric case, in the shared `fixtures/<sha>` set. Expect seam rejection, not oracle-specific values. That way a `dt.max(0.0)` port is caught whichever policy is chosen.

6. **Wording.** The phrase at :556 should read "a non-finite result is canonicalized to the reject code".

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:556 makes a non-finite `score` mean reject, but nothing defines which bits a non-finite result has. V-ORACLE-REF (:521) and the mile-4 gate at :556 compare raw `f64` bits across the Python oracle, wasm and two runtimes. SM3 (:534) asks for bit-for-bit agreement, and V-REPLAY (:516) asks for bit-for-bit verdicts.

I reproduced the Python half on this machine: `inf*0.0` packs to fff8000000000000 and `float('nan')` packs to 7ff8000000000000. The wasm half is standard wasm semantics: the sign and payload of an arithmetic NaN are nondeterministic.

The input side is also open. The only finiteness rule in the paper is L2 (:459), which covers proposal values. Q2 (:583) encodes floats as raw bit patterns, so NaN and inf can be journaled. Neither RULINGS.md nor pass1_rulings_brief.md mentions NaN or non-finite values.

The decay.py claim is correct (src/moneta/decay.py:65-69). A NaN `dt` fails the `<0` test, `exp` gives NaN, `NaN > floor` is false, and the function returns `protected_floor`. Rust's `f64::max(NaN, 0.0)` returns 0.0, so the result is `utility`, which diverges. The V-POOL sabotage named at :517 (clamp removed) would not catch this.

Two overstatements, neither of which saves the paper:
1. "The mutation-style fixtures need exactly those inputs" is wrong. The mutation corpus belongs to V-ORACLE-VERIFY (:522), which is byte- and integer-exact (:557). It is not a float-scoring seam.
2. aarch64 is not one of the named gate platforms. Wasm NaN nondeterminism is enough to break bit-equality anyway.

Severity "major" is defensible because the conformance gate the paper relies on is undefined on non-finite values. needs_owner=false is right: this is a spec gap, not a reopened ruling.
verdicts.better_fix:
The fix is sound. I would tighten it in five places:

1. **Codec.** Make the G1/Q2 codec reject non-finite floats at append. This sits next to L2's existing finiteness rule. It is cleaner than defining fold semantics for NaN or inf, and it removes the input-side gap at the source.
2. **`-0.0`.** Q2 should canonicalize `-0.0` to `+0.0`, or reject it. The two have different bit patterns but compare equal, so otherwise two logically equal events hash differently.
3. **`score` contract.** Define the return value in seam terms: either one canonical NaN constant (for example 0x7ff8000000000000), or a separate verdict tag with the f64 meaningful only when the result is finite. Then V-ORACLE-REF, SM3 and V-REPLAY compare (tag, finite bits). This holds even if the runtime does not canonicalize NaN, so treat canonicalization in Wasmtime/Cranelift as defense in depth, not the guarantee.
4. **Fixtures.** Add NaN, ±inf and -0.0 cases to the fold and referee fixtures. Add a V-ORACLE-FOLD sabotage row: "clamp written as `dt.max(0.0)`". Also add a sentence to the fold-oracle row at :558 saying the oracle's behaviour on non-finite inputs is either unreachable (the codec rejects them) or exactly that of decay.py:66-69.
5. **Scope.** Drop the claim about the mutation corpus. It belongs to the byte-exact verifier seam.

all.title: The subnormal band is reachable in normal operation, but no fixture covers it, and native and in-process paths depend on the process FP environment
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:539-543 (Exactness), :556 (fixtures), :233 (G2-6 bounds decoupled from DecayConfig), decay.py:68-69
all.claim: `utility*exp(-λΔt)` reaches subnormals at realistic ages. At the v1 minimum half-life of 60 s, exp itself is subnormal for Δt between about 17.0 h and 17.9 h (measured: λΔt=708.4 at 17.03 h). At the 24 h maximum, that happens at about 2.8 years. A utility below 1 widens the window. Because G2-6 decouples bounds from DecayConfig, the band moves wherever the constitution puts λ. In that band the libm port runs its special scaling path (k < -1021), and the floor branch at decay.py:69 keeps a subnormal (`decayed > 0.0` is true) instead of returning the floor. That path is where any FTZ/DAZ setting changes the answer. Wasm mandates gradual underflow. The native kernel runs in-process through pyo3 (`moneta-py`) and inherits the thread's MXCSR, as does the pure-Python oracle's own arithmetic, so a process with FTZ/DAZ set returns +0.0 → floor where wasm returns a subnormal. I tested hython 21.0.773 on its main thread, with pxr and hou imported, and it does NOT flush: `DBL_MIN/2` stays subnormal. So this is a hazard, not an observed failure. The trigger would be an extension built with -Ofast/crtfastmath that sets FTZ at load, or a worker thread with flags set. The paper's bit-exact argument (:543) names only FMA contraction and never names the FP environment as an input, which conflicts with SM1's 'a function of input bytes only'.
all.evidence: Local run: `math.log(2)/60` gives subnormal onset at 17.03 h; at the 24 h half-life, 2.80 years. hython3.11 (Houdini 21.0.773): `2.2250738585072014e-308/2` = 1.11e-308 before and after `import pxr, hou`. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:543 mentions FMA only; src/moneta/decay.py:68-69; :34-35
all.proposed_fix: Add fixtures that land in the subnormal and full-underflow bands for both exp and `utility*exp` (for example λ=ln2/60, Δt=61,500 s and 64,000 s), and fixtures where the floor branch compares against a subnormal. In the native entry points (moneta-py and the Python oracle harness), assert that MXCSR FTZ/DAZ are clear, or fail closed, and list the FP environment among the conditions at :543 alongside FMA.

verdicts.reason:
The paper raises the topic but does not deal with it. §10 item 8 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:693) asks attackers to "look at subnormals and at the floor branch (decay.py:69)". That is an open invitation, with no fixture, no condition and no ruling behind it. The Exactness paragraph (:539-543) names only FMA contraction as a reason the targets could diverge, and SM1 (:464, :532) says a seam is "a function of input bytes only". The FP environment (FTZ/DAZ in MXCSR) is never named. Nothing in RULINGS covers it.

The finding's numbers are right. With λ=ln2/60, exp(-λΔt) turns subnormal at Δt≈61,320 s (17.03 h) and underflows to zero at Δt≈64,500 s (17.9 h). decay.py:68-69 does keep a subnormal `decayed` whenever the floor is 0 or a smaller subnormal (`decayed > protected_floor`).

G2-6 (:233) decouples the half-life bounds from DecayConfig (decay.py:34-35), so the band moves with whatever λ the constitution sets. The claim that the in-process pyo3 kernel and the CPython oracle inherit the thread's MXCSR while wasm mandates gradual underflow is accurate. The finding correctly calls this a hazard, not an observed failure.

What the paper already has: Q8 points at the right place, so this finding is best read as a concrete answer to §10.8 rather than a fresh gap. That lowers its novelty but does not refute it. It adds the FP-environment input, the missing fixtures, and the conflict with SM1.
verdicts.better_fix:
The direction is right, but one fixture value is wrong. At λ=ln2/60, Δt=64,000 s gives exp≈7.95e-322, which is still subnormal, not full underflow. The full-underflow fixture needs Δt beyond about 64,500 s, for example 65,000 s. Keep 61,500 s for the subnormal band (exp≈2.78e-309), and add a value right at the onset (about 61,320 s) to exercise the libm port's k < -1021 scaling path.

Add the floor-branch fixtures as proposed: floor=0 against a subnormal decayed value, and a subnormal floor against a subnormal decayed value. Because G2-6 lets λ come from the constitution, derive the fixture Δt values from λ at the X1 bounds rather than hard-coding the v1 range.

For the guard, a runtime probe in each native and oracle entry point is simpler and more portable than reading MXCSR. For example, check that `2.2250738585072014e-308 / 2 != 0.0` and that `5e-324 * 1.0 != 0.0` (this one tests DAZ). Fail closed if either check fails, both at load and on any worker thread that calls the kernel.

Name the FP environment (FTZ/DAZ, rounding mode) explicitly at :543 alongside FMA, and treat it as an implicit input that SM1 must exclude. Cross-reference §10 item 8 (:693) so the fix closes that question.

verdicts.reason: I could not refute this finding. The paper does not handle it. It flags it as an open question: §10 item 8 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:693) asks reviewers to "look at subnormals and at the floor branch (decay.py:69)", and this finding answers that question. The Exactness paragraph (:539-543) names only FMA contraction as the condition for the bit-exact claim, and it is tagged [U]. Nothing in V-EXP (:519), SM3 (:534) or the fixtures line (:572) names the subnormal band or the FP environment. The numbers check out. With λ=ln2/60, exp(-λΔt) falls below DBL_MIN between 17.03 h and 17.90 h; I recomputed both. MIN_HALF_LIFE_SECONDS=60 at decay.py:34. Because G2-6 (:233) decouples the bounds from DecayConfig, the band moves wherever the constitution puts λ. The floor branch claim also holds. At decay.py:69, `decayed if decayed > protected_floor else protected_floor` returns the subnormal when protected_floor is 0.0. Under FTZ it returns +0.0, which has different bits, so SM1's "a function of input bytes only" is broken by an input the paper never declares. One limit on scope: when protected_floor is above zero, the floor wins either way and FTZ changes nothing. The hazard is limited to records whose floor is zero (or below the subnormal), and any effect on ranking is negligible. What it breaks is bit-equality checks (V-EXP, V-REPLAY, the referee's same-f64-bits gate at :556), not retrieval quality. Rating it minor is right, and the finding itself honestly calls it a hazard rather than an observed failure.
verdicts.better_fix: The fix is mostly right, with three refinements. (1) Pure Python has no stdlib way to read MXCSR, so "assert MXCSR clear" cannot be done in the oracle as written. Use a behavioural probe in both the oracle harness and the moneta-py entry point instead. To detect FTZ, check `sys.float_info.min / 2 > 0.0`. To detect DAZ, check that a stored subnormal operand survives arithmetic, for example `5e-324 * 1.0 == 5e-324` and `5e-324 > 0.0`. Fail closed if either probe fails. On the Rust native side, run the same probe at the pyo3 entry, so the check also covers aarch64 FPCR.FZ and is not tied to x86. Run the probe per call or per thread, not once at import, because the FP flags are per-thread. (2) Fixtures should cover all of these: exp landing in the subnormal band (λ=ln2/60, Δt≈61,500 s), exp underflowing fully to zero (Δt≈64,500 s, since the threshold is about 17.9 h, about 64,440 s), utility<1 times a normal exp producing a subnormal product, and the floor branch with protected_floor=0.0 against a subnormal decayed value, checking the exact bits (subnormal vs +0.0). Add one case with protected_floor>0 to document that the floor masks the hazard there. (3) At :543, list "the FP environment (FTZ/DAZ, rounding mode = nearest-even)" next to FMA as a declared precondition of SM1, and mention it in §10 item 8's answer. Rounding mode is the same class of hidden input the finding leaves out.

all.title: Open's offline fallback picks a checkpoint containing an earlier rolled-back generation's attention; the verifier takes the start seal as an input and the harness tests only one rollback
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:390 (§3 Open step 2), :294 (G3-3), :329-331 (G4-5), :495 (V-HASHGATE), :503 (V-UNDO), :557 (moneta-verify signature)
all.claim:
There is an exact contradiction, and it leads to a missed sabotage. Open step 2 (:390) says that when the post-rollback reseal is unattested, open loads 'the checkpoint of the latest attested seal before the rolled-back promote'. That checkpoint was sealed before the latest rollback. G3-3 (:294) requires a checkpoint to be 'named by a seal after the latest rollback', and V-HASHGATE's pass condition (:495) says 'open never uses a checkpoint sealed before the latest rollback'. All three can't hold. The fallback's only exclusion is 'never use a checkpoint sealed while *the* rolled-back generation was Promoted', which names one generation.

Counterexample with two rollbacks:
- seal S_b is written and attested while g1 is Promoted, so its retention checkpoint has g1's attention in utility and `attended_count`
- g1 is rolled back at r1, and its reseal S_c is never attested (owner offline)
- g2 is promoted at p2 and rolled back at r2, and its reseal S_d is never attested
- at open, no attested seal follows r2, so the fallback takes the latest attested seal before p2, which is S_b
- S_b wasn't sealed while g2 was Promoted, so it passes the stated rule
- the tail fold from S_b excludes g1 and g2 events in the tail, but g1's attention before S_b is already baked into the checkpoint

The next sleep pass prunes on an `attended_count` inflated by g1. Example: a VOLATILE record with 2 clean attentions, 1 g1 attention and utility 0.08 should prune under `consolidation.py:111-112` (utility < 0.1 and count < 3). It survives with count 3.

Neither layer catches this, because each assumes the other does:
- **Verifier.** `verify(..., start: Option<SealRef>)` (:557) receives the start seal as an argument and checks only that the seal's checkpoint hash matches, so S_b passes. It does not fold and does not choose the checkpoint.
- **Harness.** V-UNDO (:503) and the mile-5 drill (:657) cover one promote → rollback → first sleep pass with no restart. V-HASHGATE's sabotage, 'open from a pre-rollback checkpoint', can't be enforced as written, because the design's own offline path does exactly that. Whoever implements it has to relax the check, and the relaxed check admits S_b.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:390 ("load the checkpoint of the latest attested seal before the rolled-back promote … Never use a checkpoint sealed while the rolled-back generation was Promoted"); :294 ("must also be named by a seal after the latest rollback"); :495 ("open never uses a checkpoint sealed before the latest rollback"); :331 (rollback reseals, but attest is separate, :164); :557 (start seal is a verify() input; checks are only 'seal-to-checkpoint hashes'); :503 and :657 (single rollback, first pass); src/moneta/consolidation.py:53-55,111-112 (prune key); src/moneta/ecs.py:213 (attended_count increments per signal).
all.proposed_fix:
Restate the rule over every generation:
- **Usable checkpoint.** Its seal seq lies outside the [promote, rollback] interval of every generation that is RolledBack at head, and it is attested.
- **G3-3 and V-HASHGATE.** Rewrite both to that rule, which removes the contradiction with Open step 2.
- **Verifier.** Make the verifier choose the start seal, not receive it. Add `usable_checkpoint_seq` to `Verdict` so V-ORACLE-VERIFY covers the choice.
- **New sabotage for V-HASHGATE or V-UNDO.** Two rollbacks, both reseals unattested, a seal attested during the first probation, then reopen and run a sleep pass. The retention events must equal those of a run in which neither generation was promoted.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute it.

**The contradiction is real.** Open step 2 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:390) loads the checkpoint of "the latest attested seal before the rolled-back promote" when the reseal is unattested. That seal precedes the latest rollback. G3-3 (:294) requires a checkpoint "named by a seal after the latest rollback", and V-HASHGATE's pass condition (:495) says "open never uses a checkpoint sealed before the latest rollback". Its sabotage also lists "open from a pre-rollback checkpoint". All three cannot hold at once. Line :806 records this sabotage as the fix for J2-3, so the paper believes it is closed, and :390 reopens it.

**The fallback names one generation.** Its exclusion at :390, "never use a checkpoint sealed while the rolled-back generation was Promoted", covers a single generation. Nothing in G4-3 (:327) stops a second promote and rollback while g1's reseal is still unattested: g1 is RolledBack, so it is not pending. Attest is a separate event (:141, :164). Nothing I found makes promote, or open, wait on attestation; O12 (:677) only bounds the window as a tripwire. So S_b, attested during g1's probation, is a legal fallback start for g2's rollback.

**The paper treats probation-era checkpoints as contaminated.** G4-5 (:331) rebuilds from "the last seal before g's promote", and :390 forbids sealed-while-Promoted checkpoints. On the paper's own model, S_b carries g1's attention, so the fold exclusion at G4-5 (:330) cannot remove it from the tail.

**The prune example checks out against v1.** `consolidation.py:53-54` sets the thresholds at 0.1 and 3, and `:111-112` applies them. `ecs.py:213` increments `attended_count` per signal. A record with 2 clean attentions and 1 from g1 reaches a count of 3 and escapes pruning.

**Neither the verifier nor the harness catches it.** `verify` (:557) takes `start: Option<SealRef>` as an input. It checks seal-to-checkpoint hashes and G4 legality, not which checkpoint is usable. V-UNDO (:503) and the mile-5 drill (:657) exercise one promote → rollback → sleep pass. No check covers two rollbacks, an unattested reseal, or a reopen.

**Caveat.** The paper does not say outright whether a checkpoint sealed during the G4-4 hold (:328) already folds held attention into retention state. The finding follows the paper's own stated treatment (:331, :390), so this does not weaken it.

Severity "critical" is defensible: a silent retention divergence after rollback breaks R4a / J8.
verdicts.better_fix:
Take the proposed fix, with four additions.

1. **Interval bounds.** Define the excluded interval for each RolledBack generation g as `[seq(promote_g), seq(rollback_g))`, so it includes any Expired span. An Adopted generation's probation span is not excluded.
2. **Fallback when nothing qualifies.** When no attested seal lies outside every interval, open folds from genesis. It never falls back to an unattested reseal.
3. **The chosen start seal must be covered by attestation.** Its seq must be ≤ `signed_through_seq`.
4. **Wording.** Rewrite G4-5's second bullet (:331), "the latest seal therefore always follows the latest rollback", which is true only of written seals, not attested ones. Update the J2-3 row at :806 so it reflects the corrected rule.

The verifier can choose the start seal without folding, because the rule needs only G4 state, which verify already derives for its legality check. Expose the choice as `start_seq` in `Verdict`, so V-ORACLE-VERIFY covers it. The new two-rollback sabotage belongs in V-HASHGATE at mile 4 on a test store, and in the mile-5 drill.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds up against the paper.

1. **The contradiction is verbatim.**
   - BLUEPRINT_v7.md:390 (Open step 2) tells open to load "the checkpoint of the latest attested seal before the rolled-back promote" when the reseal is unattested. That checkpoint predates the latest rollback.
   - :294 (G3-3) requires a fold checkpoint to be "named by a seal after the latest rollback".
   - :495 (V-HASHGATE) has the pass condition "open never uses a checkpoint sealed before the latest rollback" and lists "open from a pre-rollback checkpoint" as a sabotage.
   - The design's own offline path therefore trips its own sabotage.

2. **The two-rollback counterexample is valid under the paper's rules.**
   - Seals are written on the loop machine whatever the G4 state, and attestation is a separate later event (:164). A seal S_b attested while g1 is Promoted is legal.
   - The G4-4 hold (:333) blocks only `retention` events, not seals.
   - G4-5 (:336-337) defines the exclusion inside the fold over attention events. A checkpoint of fold state taken during g1's probation therefore carries g1's attention. The paper's own "never use a checkpoint sealed while the rolled-back generation was Promoted" (:390) only makes sense if such checkpoints are contaminated.
   - G4-5's reseal rule rebuilds from "the last seal before g's promote". For r2 that is S_c, which is clean, so the online path is fine. Only the attested-only fallback reaches back to S_b.
   - The fallback's guard names one generation ("the rolled-back generation"), so S_b passes it.
   - The scenario needs no rule to break. Owner signatures on r1, p2 and r2 don't require attesting S_c or S_d, since attest is separate (:164).

3. **Neither layer catches it.**
   - `verify()` takes `start: Option<SealRef>` as an input and checks only seal-to-checkpoint hashes (:557).
   - V-UNDO (:503) and mile 5 (:657) exercise one promote → rollback → sleep pass, with no reopen and no second rollback.
   - The prune key is real: `consolidation.py` prunes on utility < 0.1 and count < 3, and `ecs.py:213` counts each signal. An inflated `attended_count` changes prune decisions.

4. **Severity.** "Critical" could be argued down to high, because the scenario needs two unattested reseals and a seal attested mid-probation. It is still a silent retention corruption that passes every listed check. Nothing in the paper handles it, so I did not refute it.
verdicts.better_fix:
The proposed fix is correct and sufficient. Four sharpenings:

(a) **Define the exclusion window concretely.** For each RolledBack generation g, the window is [seq of g's promote, seq of g's rollback]. A generation that went Expired → rollback uses its rollback seq too. A usable checkpoint's seal seq lies outside every such window. Choose the latest attested seal that meets this, and state it once as a single rule shared by G3-3 and Open step 2.

(b) **Define G4-5's reseal source by the same predicate.** Replace "the last seal before g's promote" with "the latest seal outside every RolledBack window". The online path is correct today only because each earlier rollback resealed, and this change makes that explicit.

(c) **Choosing the start seal is not folding.** Having `verify()` pick the start seal and report `usable_checkpoint_seq` in `Verdict` keeps it purely structural, which is consistent with "does not fold". `oracle/verify.py` must compute the same choice bit-exactly under V-ORACLE-VERIFY.

(d) **Make the new sabotage a reopen test.** Run two rollbacks with both reseals unattested and a seal attested during g1's probation. Close, reopen, then run a sleep pass. The retention events must equal those of a never-promoted run.
- Also add the one-rollback case where the only attested pre-promote seal falls inside an earlier window.
- Assign the test to V-HASHGATE, and rewrite its pass condition to the window rule so the sabotage is enforceable as written.

all.title: Nothing checks the excluded-generation set or the retention events after the first post-rollback sleep pass: verify omits the set, fold takes it as given, and V-UNDO checks one pass
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:557 (Verdict), :558 (fold_recall excluded_gens input), :503 (V-UNDO), :524 (V-EXCL), :395 (Audit), :136 (retention event)
all.claim:
The set of rolled-back generations is what makes J8 work. No checked component produces it:
- `Verdict = Ok{head_seq, head_hash, signed_through_seq, pending_gen}` (:557) has no excluded set.
- `fold_recall(..., excluded_gens)` (:558) takes it as an argument.
- V-EXCL (:524) and V-ORACLE-FOLD test the fold given a correct set.
- The set is computed by Python glue in Open step 5 or in the sleep pass, and no check names it.

V-UNDO (:503) constrains only 'the first sleep pass after the rollback'.

Sabotage both layers miss: the glue builds the excluded set from rollbacks since the last `retention` event, or from rollbacks in the folded tail only. A streaming fold that adds g to the set only when it reaches the rollback is another variant. Exclusion has to look forward: attention at seq k is dropped because of a rollback at m > k (attack 6).
- The first post-rollback pass is correct, so V-UNDO is green.
- The second pass counts g's attention again.
- Concrete case: a record with 2 clean attentions and 1 g attention has utility 0.15 at pass 1 (no prune either way) and 0.08 at pass 2. A never-promoted run prunes it at pass 2 (count 2 < 3). The sabotaged run keeps it (count 3), per `consolidation.py:111-112`.
- The verifier passes, because a `retention` event is a structurally valid unsigned event (:136).
- The audit misses it too: it 'rebuilds every leaf and compares hashes' (:395). Retention events are G1 authority, not leaves, so the wrong decision is replayed as fact, and every later checkpoint rebuilds consistently around it.

The result is that J8/R4a ('after you roll back, the next sleep pass tombstones by attention the rolled-back generation shaped', pass1_rulings_brief.md:268) is enforced for one pass only.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:557, :558, :503 ("the first sleep pass after the rollback"), :524, :395, :136, :329-330 (G4-5 says the exclusion holds "once g is RolledBack", which has no pass limit); docs/v7/pass1_rulings_brief.md:268, :298 (R4a); src/moneta/consolidation.py:53-55,111-112; src/moneta/ecs.py:213.
all.proposed_fix:
1. Add `rolled_back_gens` to `Verdict`, derived in the same G1 walk that already checks G4 legality, so V-ORACLE-VERIFY covers it. Make the fold's `excluded_gens` come only from that field.
2. Extend V-UNDO to every sleep pass, or at least the first N, after a rollback and after a reopen, compared with a never-promoted run.
3. Add an audit check (V-RETAIN): refold each prefix and confirm that every journaled `retention` event equals the decisions the retention fold computes at its seq.
4. Add the sabotage 'excluded set reset after the first post-rollback pass / computed from the tail only'.

verdicts.reason:
The finding stands. The paper states the rule but nothing checks it.

What the paper says:
- G4-5 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:329-330) says the exclusion holds "once g is RolledBack", with no pass limit.
- Open step 5 (:390) says the fold derives "the G4 state of every generation ... from the folded journal, never from a derived file". On paper that rules out the "since last retention" and "tail only" sabotages.

What is not checked, confirmed against the paper:
- `Verdict` (:557) carries only `head_seq`, `head_hash`, `signed_through_seq` and `pending_gen`. No rolled-back set.
- `fold_recall` (:558) takes `excluded_gens` as an argument. The fold order at :282-283 says only "in the excluded set". V-EXCL (:524) and V-ORACLE-FOLD (:523) take that set as given.
- V-UNDO (:503) checks only "the first sleep pass after the rollback".
- Audit (:395) "rebuilds every leaf and compares hashes". `retention` is a G1 event (:136), not a leaf (:261), so nothing recomputes it against the fold.

The paper also lists this as unsolved. It names it as open attacks: #6 "Retention that depends on later rollbacks" (:691) and #9 "a sabotage both miss because each assumes the other covers it" (:693). The finding answers #9 with a concrete case. It does not duplicate an existing check.

The numbers check out against v1:
- Prune is `utility < 0.1 AND attended_count < 3` (src/moneta/consolidation.py:54-55, :111-112).
- `attended_count` grows with every signal (src/moneta/ecs.py:213).
- A record at count 2 vs 3 with utility 0.08 is pruned by the clean run and kept or staged by the sabotaged run.
- R4a's intent (pass1_rulings_brief.md:268, :298) is the exclusion in general, not first-pass-only.
verdicts.better_fix:
The fix is right in direction. Four refinements:

1. **Fix 1 (`rolled_back_gens` in `Verdict`).** Keep it, but add a pinning rule: the fold may build its excluded set only from that field. Then V-ORACLE-VERIFY's mutation corpus (event deletion, truncation) covers it automatically.

2. **Fix 2 (V-UNDO).** Drop "first N passes". Use a property test: for every sleep pass after a rollback, up to the run's end and across a reopen, the retention events equal a never-promoted run fed the same non-g attention. Also add the attack-6 crash case from :691: a crash between the rollback and its reseal, then a reopen, then two sleep passes.

3. **Fix 3 (V-RETAIN).** The prefix refold must use the rollbacks known at the retention event's own seq, not the `Verdict` head set. Tombstones written before a later rollback at m > r are legitimately final (pass1 brief :268, "cannot be reversed"). V-RETAIN should check that the decisions at r match the fold of prefix [0, r) under the G4 states as of r. That needs the G4 walk to expose per-seq state, not only head state. Also say which gate owns V-RETAIN. It recomputes a fold, so it is a harness check, not the verifier's. Naming the owner closes attack #9.

4. **Sabotage list.** Add these sabotages:
   - "excluded set reset after the first post-rollback pass"
   - "excluded set built from the folded tail only"
   - "excluded set built by a streaming fold that adds g only when it reaches the rollback event"

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute it. Each cited line says what the finding says it does.

**Where the excluded set comes from**
- `Verdict = Ok{head_seq, head_hash, signed_through_seq, pending_gen}` (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:557) carries no RolledBack set, even though the same walk "checks G4 legality".
- `fold_recall` takes `excluded_gens` as an input (:558).
- V-EXCL (:524) and V-ORACLE-FOLD (:523) only compare folds that are given the same set.
- Open step 5 (:396) says to "derive the G4 state of every generation", so the set is specified. No check covers the derivation. V-STATE (:500) and V-PENDING (:501) check transitions and the pending count, not the RolledBack set that reaches the fold.

**How many passes are checked**
- V-UNDO (:503) explicitly limits itself to "the first sleep pass after the rollback".
- G4-5 (:329-330) has no pass limit ("Once g is RolledBack").
- R4a's purpose (pass1_rulings_brief.md:266-268) is that the next sleep pass must not tombstone by the rolled-back generation's attention. Nothing makes that hold beyond pass one.

**Why the audit misses it**
- Audit (:398) "rebuilds every leaf and compares hashes".
- `retention` is a G1 event (:136), not one of the derived leaves listed at :260-268. Nothing re-derives a journaled retention decision from the fold.

**The paper names the gap but does not close it**
- Red-team question 9 (:694) asks whether a sabotage slips past both the verifier and the harness. Question 6 (:691) asks about a rollback at m changing how attention before m counts.
- Both are open questions, not mechanisms that handle the case.

**The numbers check out**
- Prune requires `utility < 0.1 and attended_count < 3` (src/moneta/consolidation.py:54-55, 111-112).
- The count increments per signal regardless of decay (src/moneta/ecs.py:213).
- So a record with 2 clean attentions plus 1 attention from g is pruned with g excluded and kept when g is counted, as claimed.

**The streaming-fold variant is real**
- G4-4 (:328) means g's attention always comes before the rollback seq m, while retention events come only after m.
- A fold that adds g to the set only when it reaches m has already counted g's attention by then. V-EXCL cannot see this, because it hands the set in up front.

No ruled item is reopened. This is a gap in how R4a's checks are wired.
verdicts.better_fix:
The direction is right, with these refinements.

1. **Define the set.** State it in G4-5: `excluded(k) = {g : g is RolledBack in the journal prefix up to k}`. It is computed from the whole prefix before folding, never by a streaming fold.
   - Add `rolled_back_gens` to `Verdict`, so V-ORACLE-VERIFY covers it.
   - `fold_recall`, the retention fold and the eval builder (V-LEAK, G3-7) should take the set only from that field.

2. **Make V-RETAIN the main check, not the third item.** It replaces "first N passes" in V-UNDO, which only moves the blind spot to pass N+1.
   - For every journaled `retention` event at seq k, refold the prefix at k using `excluded(k)`, the policy and thresholds resolved at k, and the event's own time.
   - Require exact equality with the event's tombstone and stage decisions.
   - Run it in audit, and over the tail at Open. A wrong retention event is then caught even after later checkpoints have been rebuilt around it.
   - Note in the paper that V-RETAIN's fold order depends on O7/E3 (:283, :672).

3. **Have V-UNDO cover a multi-pass history.** Keep its current statement, and add a check that the complete retention event sequence over at least 2 passes, with a close and reopen between them (including the attack-6 crash between the rollback and its reseal), equals a never-promoted run's sequence.

4. **Add the sabotages** to V-RETAIN and V-UNDO:
   - the set is reset after the first post-rollback pass
   - the set is computed from the tail only, or from rollbacks since the last `retention` event
   - a streaming fold adds g at the rollback seq

5. **Add a back-reference in §8 attack 9** to the new check.

all.title: fold_recall is labeled conditional, but the always-built WASM referee needs it
all.location: BLUEPRINT_v7.md §6 crate table, lines 556, 558, 566-567; §8 mile 4 (655) and mile 4b (656); R2-flip row (633)
all.claim: Line 558 marks `moneta-kernel fold_recall` as "(no_std, conditional)", with a speed gate (>1 s for a 100k-record repoint) and a mile-4b build. But the referee row (556) declares that the referee's EvalBuf carries raw "per-record attention runs (t f64, w f64, gen u32)", and says its oracle "calls the fold oracle, because features carry raw attention, not anchors". The workspace (567) gives `moneta-referee` "deps: kernel", and puts `fold_recall` in that kernel (566). So whenever the referee ships, which the paper calls "always, at mile 4" (556; mile 4 builds `moneta-kernel` and `moneta-referee` unconditionally, 655), a Rust `fold_recall` is compiled and run inside WASM. That happens whether or not the fold's speed gate is ever missed. Counterexample: the Python fold oracle rebuilds a 100k repoint in 0.4 s, so the gate passes and mile 4b says no Rust fold. The referee still executes a Rust fold on every score. Its only cross-check is V-ORACLE-REF, a whole-referee f64 comparison at mile 4. V-ORACLE-FOLD, the per-event vs per-batch fixture with the "per-batch clamp" sabotage, is scheduled for 4b (523) and would never run. The β branch has the same contradiction: "If R2 flips to β, this seam is struck" (558, 633), yet the referee's EvalBuf still takes attention runs rather than U. Under β the referee would either still fold in Rust or need a different EvalBuf (the brief's β path is "score a flat pool of (cos, U, label)… the fold stays in Python", pass1_rulings_brief.md:172). Decision on attack 10: the fold crate cannot be struck. Only its conditional label can. What is actually conditional is the `moneta-py` native binding that exposes `fold_recall` to the Python read path for repoints.
all.evidence: BLUEPRINT_v7.md:556 (EvalBuf attention runs; 'calls the fold oracle'; 'always, at mile 4'); :558 ('conditional'; gate; 'struck' under β); :566 ('moneta-kernel/ … fold_recall'); :567 ('moneta-referee … deps: kernel'); :523 (V-ORACLE-FOLD at 4b); :655 (mile 4 builds kernel + referee); :656 (4b 'fold_recall if its gate was missed'); :633; pass1_rulings_brief.md:171-172
all.proposed_fix: Rewrite the kernel row so that `fold_recall` (no_std) ships with the referee at mile 4. Move V-ORACLE-FOLD, including its per-event vs per-batch fixture and sabotage, from 4b to mile 4. Restate the conditional seam as "`moneta-py` binding of `fold_recall` for read-path repoints: only if the Python oracle misses the gate". In the β branch, say what replaces the referee's input: either an EvalBuf variant carrying U, folded in Python, with the fold leaving the referee; or the referee keeps folding and only V-POW is added. Do not write "the seam is struck".

verdicts.reason: The cited text matches the finding, and the paper does not resolve it. In BLUEPRINT_v7.md §6, the referee row's EvalBuf carries raw per-record attention runs `(t f64, w f64, gen u32)`. Its oracle "calls the fold oracle, because features carry raw attention, not anchors". So scoring in WASM requires attention→U folding inside the referee. The workspace sketch puts that fold in `moneta-kernel` (decay, fold_recall, total_order, the exp port), and `moneta-referee` has "deps: kernel". Mile 4 builds moneta-kernel and moneta-referee without any condition on the fold gate. Yet the kernel row is labeled "no_std, conditional", gated on a 100k repoint taking more than 1 s, and mile 4b lists "fold_recall if its gate was missed". V-ORACLE-FOLD, the check that carries the per-event vs per-batch fixture and the per-batch-clamp sabotage, is scheduled at 4b. So when the fold gate passes, a Rust fold ships inside the referee and V-ORACLE-FOLD never runs. The only cross-check left is V-ORACLE-REF, a whole-score f64 comparison whose fixtures are not required to include the per-event/per-batch case. V-POOL runs at mile 3 against the read path and does not substitute. The β branch has the same gap. The pass-1 brief's β seam is "score a flat pool of (cos, U, label)… the fold stays in Python" (pass1_rulings_brief.md, Rust/D1 implication). But v7 says only "this seam is struck and a pow(U, β) path plus V-POW replaces it" (kernel row; Half-life call row). It never changes the referee's EvalBuf, which still takes attention runs. Two small inaccuracies in the finding do not change the result. First, the referee is not unconditionally "always": it is conditional on fuel, memory and cross-runtime bit-equality, and falls back to a pinned Python subprocess. That condition is independent of the fold gate, so the contradiction stands. Second, the referee could fold through the kernel's `decay` without a function named `fold_recall`. The per-event order (G3) would still be unverified at mile 4. Calling this critical is defensible, because an unchecked Rust fold would score every proposal.
verdicts.better_fix:
The proposed fix is correct. Three refinements:
(1) State that the Rust fold at mile 4 is conditional only on the referee's own fuel and bit-equality gate, not on the 1 s repoint gate. If the referee falls back to the pinned Python subprocess (J1 downgrade), the Rust fold also leaves mile 4, so V-ORACLE-FOLD should be tied to "whenever any Rust fold is built".
(2) Also require V-ORACLE-REF's fixture set to include the per-event vs per-batch case, so the whole-referee check cannot pass on fixtures that never exercise the clamp.
(3) In the β branch, prefer the brief's option: an EvalBuf variant carrying precomputed U (pool rows `(cos, U, label)`), folded in Python, with the attention-runs section dropped and V-POW added. Then mark V-ORACLE-FOLD and the kernel fold as removed only in that case. Update the mile-4b row and the Half-life-call row in the same edit so the three places agree.

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute this finding. The paper contradicts itself as the finding describes.

1. BLUEPRINT_v7.md:556 says the referee's EvalBuf carries per-record attention runs `(t f64, w f64, gen u32)`, and that its oracle "calls the fold oracle, because features carry raw attention, not anchors". The WASM referee therefore has to fold inside WASM.
2. :566 puts `fold_recall` in `moneta-kernel`, and :567 gives `moneta-referee` "deps: kernel". Mile 4 (:655) builds `moneta-kernel` and `moneta-referee` with no condition attached.
3. :558 still labels `fold_recall` "(no_std, conditional)". Its gate measures how long a 100k-record repoint takes in the Python read path, which has nothing to do with whether the referee needs a fold. Mile 4b (:656) builds `fold_recall` only "if its gate was missed".
4. V-ORACLE-FOLD, the only per-event vs per-batch bit-identity check with the per-batch-clamp sabotage, is scheduled at 4b (:523). When the gate passes, a Rust fold runs in every referee score, and nothing covers it except the whole-referee V-ORACLE-REF (:521). V-EXCL (:524, mile 4) checks fold semantics but not kernel-vs-oracle bit identity per event.
5. The β branch at :558 and :633 strikes the seam, but the referee row still takes attention runs. pass1_rulings_brief.md:172 says that under β the seam is a flat (cos, U, label) pool and "the fold stays in Python". That would need a different EvalBuf, and the paper never says so.

One overstatement: the referee is not unconditional. :556 makes it conditional on fuel and memory fitting under X1, and on cross-runtime bit equality. If it is downgraded to a pinned Python subprocess under J1, no Rust fold is needed. That narrows the finding without refuting it: in every world where the WASM referee ships, a Rust fold ships too.

Severity: critical is defensible, because a check it relies on would silently never run. High would also be reasonable, since this is a paper-level inconsistency and nothing is built yet.
verdicts.better_fix:
Apply the proposed fix with three refinements.

(a) Tie `fold_recall` to the WASM referee, not to "mile 4" unconditionally. Suggested wording: "`fold_recall` (no_std) ships in `moneta-kernel` whenever the WASM referee ships, at mile 4. If the referee is downgraded to a pinned Python subprocess (J1), the fold stays in Python and V-ORACLE-FOLD is not run."

(b) Move V-ORACLE-FOLD's milestone at :523 from 4b to 4, with the per-event vs per-batch fixture and sabotage unchanged. Add V-ORACLE-FOLD to the referee row's Checks at :556.
